Code-mixed (CM) languages are rapidly gaining importance due to their increasing prevalence on social media and messaging platforms. Although many state-of-the-art models for handling CM languages rely on positional encodings, they often fail to capture the multi-lingual nature of these languages. This failure stems from the assumption that all positions within a sentence share the same language trait, which is frequently inaccurate. To overcome this limitation, we introduce PESTO, a novel encoding method designed to model the adaptive and multi-lingual characteristics inherent in CM languages. By utilizing a "switching point," PESTO generates positional embeddings for each token based on the linguistic style of the segment preceding it. We demonstrate the efficacy of PESTO across three language pairs (Hindi-English, Marathi-English, and Telugu-English) on seven diverse social media datasets. Furthermore, we also present findings from applying PESTO to non-social media texts, specifically using the NLTK corpus of English and Hindi news articles. Comprehensive experiments confirm that PESTO surpasses several well-known adaptive and relative positional encodings, as well as multilingual language models, in handling the complex structure of CM languages. This study employs first-principles calculations and the deformation potential approach to analyze how pressure influences the isotope effect on the critical temperature ($T_c$) in H$_3$S. Our findings indicate that the isotope effect parameter ($\alpha$) initially decreases with rising pressure, hits a minimum of 0.42 at 140 GPa, and subsequently rises to 1 as the pressure approaches 240 GPa. This behavior stems from the distinct pressure-dependent characteristics of the phonon spectrum and the electronic density of states near the Fermi level. Specifically, the mode-by-mode isotope effect coefficient ($\alpha_q$) varies with pressure; for instance, $\alpha_{12}$ and $\alpha_{9}$, which are high and govern the initial decline in $T_c$, drop sharply to near-zero at elevated pressures. Conversely, the low-lying $\omega_{11}$ mode, responsible for the increase in $T_c$ at higher pressures, exhibits a relatively large $\alpha_{11}$ with minimal pressure dependence. Furthermore, the electronic density of states near the Fermi level shows a pronounced peak at 140 GPa, coinciding with a van Hove singularity. This peak significantly amplifies the isotope effect at that pressure. These results may prove valuable for guiding future experimental investigations of high-temperature superconductivity in H$_3$S. Additionally, the methodology employed is broadly applicable to other potential superconducting materials. These theoretical insights could inform the development of advanced neutron spectroscopy techniques capable of measuring the isotope effect in high-$T_c$ superconductors. Finally, our approach offers a viable means to investigate the phase diagram of H$_3$S and to explore the phase transition between the $A15$ and $A7$ phases. \textbf{Keywords}: High-temperature superconductivity; isotope effect; phonon spectrum; van Hove singularity; H$_3$S. \textbf{PACS}: 74.25.-q; 74.70.Tx; 74.25.Ha. \textbf{AMS Subject Classification}: 74.25.-q; 74.70.Tx; 74.25.Ha. \textbf{DOI} 10.1007/s11467-021-1100-8. \textbf{Citation

Recent years have seen significant strides in 3D visual relocalization, largely driven by the widespread adoption of global localizers utilizing global descriptors. However, these global approaches often neglect the highly descriptive and locally structured 3D surfel map, resulting in suboptimal performance. To effectively integrate the 3D map, we introduce Embbedding Net, a network designed to generate structured descriptors from surfels that capture their geometric arrangement. These descriptors enable precise matching against global features. Furthermore, our combined global-local framework leverages all available information: the 3D map facilitates efficient and robust convergence, while global descriptors ensure robustness against viewpoint changes, camera motion, and non-repetitive features. By formulating the problem as the joint optimization of a precoder and user choice, we create an integer nonlinear programming framework. To address the resulting Group LASSO formulation, we propose an efficient iterative algorithm that alternately updates the precoder and user choice. This relationship highlights the connection between the algorithm's stability and Q-function approximation. Consequently, we derive a sufficient condition ensuring the uniform convergence of a single algorithm instance to the Q-function. We further discuss the relationship among variance, stability, and convergence speed within the REINFORCE algorithm, linking these concepts to the quality of the Q-function and the algorithm's performance. Finally, we analyze the algorithm's behavior in special cases and demonstrate its ability to converge to the Q-function across various scenarios. These theoretical findings are supported by numerical simulations. Additionally, we propose an alternative algorithm called REINFORCE*, which is shown to converge to the Q-function even when the reward function is discontinuous. The structural transition in Fe-based superconductors from tetragonal to orthorhombic symmetry has been attributed to an electronic nematic order parameter. This study demonstrates that, within LiFeAs, the origin of this symmetry breaking lies primarily in the static lattice distortion, while the influence of a putative nematic order parameter is negligible. Consequently, experimental observations of the temperature-dependent orthorhombic-tetragonal transition in LiFeAs cannot be explained by nematicity. These findings advance our understanding of Fe-based superconductors and underscore the necessity of incorporating lattice effects in models describing nematic behavior. Furthermore, our results indicate that nematicity is unlikely to be responsible for the symmetry breaking and its associated temperature-dependent evolution in other iron pnictides. Ultimately, this research underscores the critical role of the lattice in Fe-based superconductors. To achieve a comprehensive understanding of these materials, models must integrate both nematic and non-nematic electronic effects alongside lattice contributions. In the specific context of LiFeAs, the proximity to a structural phase transition is proposed as the origin of the temperature-dependent symmetry breaking. Additionally, we examine the electrostatic origin of LiFeAs's structural instability and establish a quantitative connection between its magnitude and the superconducting transition temperature. Finally, we explore the potential for enhancing superconductivity in LiFeAs by engineering its structure near the theoretical minimum energy configuration. This work is based on research from [1]. Chiral symmetries and their potential 't Hooft anomalies serve as primary tools for this analysis, revealing that gauge-invariant operators can effectively remove mass terms for chiral fermions, thereby preserving robustness against generic perturbations. Central to this strategy is a systematic shift of the chiral rotation angle, $\theta_f$, from the fermion sector to the gauge action. Utilizing this method, we demonstrate that certain well-known anomaly-free chiral gauge theories, such as $SU(N)$ with $N$ Weyl fermions in the fundamental representation, possess no low-energy phase where massless fermions exist, even when perturbations include all relevant and marginal operators. Furthermore, by examining perturbative mass terms and applying the identity $\sum_f \theta_f = 0$ as a heuristic, we conjecture that a phase transition occurs at a critical point, $\theta_f^c$, where a massless fermi surface emerges, with 't Hooft anomalies determining its stability. These conjectures align with recent numerical findings. Additionally, we explore the connection between these phenomena and the anomaly inflow mechanism in related topological field theories. Finally, we outline a strategy to construct perturbatively stable phase boundaries, grounded in the principle that perturbations must vanish at these interfaces. Specifically, we show that combining perturbations that individually break chiral symmetries can yield a mutually anomaly-free combination, potentially creating a stable phase boundary, contingent on the fact that these symmetries are not identical. This phenomenon, which we term the perturbative anomaly cancellation mechanism, represents a novel and distinct process compared to the well-known radiative anomaly cancellation. Our findings suggest that perturbatively stable phase boundaries are more prevalent in chiral gauge theories than previously believed, offering a fresh perspective on the landscape of these theories. This conclusion is supported by a recently proposed example and the numerical results of lattice simulations conducted by others. We anticipate that our findings will stimulate further research into the phase structure of chiral gauge theories. Our findings also suggest that the mystery surrounding the phase structure of chiral gauge theories may be resolved by examining anomaly inflow and perturbative anomaly cancellation. Ultimately, the existence of stable phase boundaries in chiral gauge theories could shed light on the mystery of the strong CP problem in QCD. We provide an analytical framework to examine magnon-magnon nonlinear interactions within antiferromagnetic systems. Our analysis reveals two distinct mechanisms driving four-magnon interactions: thermal squeezing and nonlinearity. These interactions significantly influence magnon propagation, occupying a regime between weak coupling and strong localization. Specifically, they induce a spectral shift in magnon dispersion known as thermal self-interaction; at low momentum, this shift manifests as repulsive behavior. Furthermore, we identify conditions under which thermal self-interaction transforms from repulsive to attractive. We also investigate collective instabilities arising from four-magnon interactions and validate our analytical findings through comparisons with numerical simulations and existing experimental data. These findings offer valuable insights for both the fundamental understanding and technological application of nonlinear magnetism. Finally, our methodology is extendable to various many-body systems. Specifically, we anticipate that the thermal squeezing effect will enhance the accuracy of quantum chemical simulations and aid in the study of collective atomic instabilities. Additionally, many of our conclusions are applicable to Bose-Einstein condensation of excitpolarons. Random simplicial complexes have recently become a subject of interest across various fields, ranging from statistical physics to machine learning. Among these, clique complexes stand out as the most prevalent. This study examines the asymptotic behavior of the minimal spanning cycle (msc) within k-dimensional k-clique complexes, constructed under a specific Bernoulli random measure. We demonstrate that, in the limit, the structure of the msc is highly dependent on k. Specifically, for 2-clique complexes, the point process of edge lengths converges to a Poisson point process, enabling a precise characterization of the msc's structure. Furthermore, we determine the asymptotic behavior of the extremal elements of the msc (P. Hall 1972) and the average length of the second shortest cycle. These findings are supported by a general limit theorem concerning weighted graphs featuring a finite number of short cycles. Additionally, we derive limit theimes for Gaussian and Rayleigh random variables possessing a single mode, which may hold independent interest. For k-clique complexes where k ≥ 3, the analysis becomes more complex; however, for sufficiently high k, we prove that the cycle formed by the union of the k smallest cliques constitutes the msc. Our methodology relies on a novel local limit theorem for Dijkstra's algorithm applied to a class of weighted graphs. Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) represents a privacy-preserving framework where multiple parties collaboratively train machine learning models by combining complementary features, adhering to a noia principle that ensures a party's data remains confidential until modeling is complete. This study introduces an alternative perspective on VFL, treating it as a dynamic feature engineering process linked to a classifier. Leveraging this insight, we investigate data privacy vulnerabilities within VFL and demonstrate two significant attacks with proof-of-concept results on a real-world dataset. First, we reveal inference leakage, showing that an adversary can extract information from a party's features using a model trained on another party's data. Second, we highlight model reverse engineering, where the actual VFL model can be reconstructed using another party's features. Both attack methods rely solely on exchanging feature data between parties, requiring no additional inputs. Our approach effectively bypasses both function secret sharing (FSS) and differential privacy (DP) protections. We further explore countermeasures, such as data randomization, and show that VFL systems remain vulnerable to these attacks even when such defenses are implemented. Our findings underscore the inherent privacy risks in federated feature learning and suggest that further research is necessary to establish robust privacy safeguards for VFL systems. This paper introduces a new real-time defense framework designed for society, cyber, and physical (SCP) systems to resist intelligent attacks. The system operates on the premise that defenders must allocate resources to harden vulnerable components, ensuring resilience against future assaults. The approach comprises two phases: (1) a randomized attack on the defense layer, where defenders and adversaries compete to components that dynamically adjust their resistance levels based on attack intensity and component value; and (2) a subsequent attack on the components, where the attacker targets elements that have failed to reach a sufficient resistance threshold. The attack phase is modeled as a non-cooperative game featuring social, cyber, and physical dimensions, while the defense strategy is defined as an SDP relaxation of a combinatorial problem. The paper demonstrates the framework's effectiveness through simulations and case studies. Key results indicate that (1) when attacks are moderate, the defense mechanism remains effective; however, (2) if attacks are severe, the system cannot remain functional, yet it still mitigates significant losses by counter-attacking in the second phase. Furthermore, the framework is highly efficient, requiring less than 100 milliseconds to resolve the attack attack game. Finally, the findings suggest that this intelligent defense system could substantially reduce adversary costs, potentially discouraging malicious behavior. Future research will focus on developing cost-effective, intelligent defense mechanisms for large-scale networks. This paper investigates the algorithms and mathematical principles behind a newly developed ranking algorithm designed to minimize the impact of label noise during document ranking. The proposed method employs a bag sampling strategy, which calculates a loss function based on the count of noisy labels within each sample bag. Additionally, a group-level loss function is utilized to evaluate the performance of individual samples within each bag. The study offers a comprehensive analysis of these approaches, supported by extensive experiments and a detailed examination of the resulting algorithms. Ultimately, the research demonstrates that this proposal effectively mitigates the effects of label noise during ranking. The method was implemented in the ML4RD 2021 competition held at SIGIR, and it secured first place in both the significant and weak label noise tracks. Furthermore, the authors have made the source code available on GitHub to facilitate its application in other real-world noisy datasets. The code can be accessed at: https://github.com/ahmedhassan1998/label-noisy-ranking. The underlying cause of label noise in document ranking is also addressed. The paper is organized into the following sections: Section 1 provides an introduction, Section 2 outlines the motivation, Section 3 details the proposed algorithm, and Sections 4 through 6 present the results and their analysis. Finally, Section 7 offers a conclusion. The authors extend their gratitude to Dr. Ahmed Hassan for his valuable insights and discussions regarding the application of group loss and bag sampling techniques to noisy ranking. His guidance has been instrumental in advancing this research. We also appreciate the organizers of the ML4RD 2021 competition for providing an opportunity to contribute to the field through their initiatives. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated strong performance on graph prediction tasks, leveraging graph structures to facilitate information exchange between neighbors. However, their reliance on extensive labeled data often hinders practical application due to labeling costs. To overcome this, we introduce a novel method called ICT-GNN, which enhances the information flow within standard GNNs by establishing connections between randomly selected nodes. Unlike previous approaches, ICT-GNN requires minimal labeled data to significantly boost performance. Our core innovation is a sophisticated pseudo-tagging mechanism that identifies a small subset of nodes as labels, optimizing their impact during training. We evaluate ICT-GNN across various graphs and tasks, demonstrating that it consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods even in large graphs. Additionally, our ablation studies reveal that the proposed informative pseudo-tagging technique is essential for achieving these improvements. Finally, we show that ICT-GNN remains effective across diverse pruning strategies and graph structures. Code is available at: https://github.com/taehyung-lee/ICT-GNN. This study examines the potential for observing betatron radiation from millimeter-scale proton-driven microbunches, specifically those on the negative curvature path within the AWE-LEP-like focusing configuration anticipated for the proton plasma wakefield accelerator initiative (AWAKE). The analysis explores how radiating microbunches interact with surrounding gas, considering both binary collisions and collective effects. Additionally, the investigation analyzes how radiating protons influence the charge and density distribution of the incoming bunch, as well as the quality of the betatron radiation. The findings indicate that under specific conditions, it may be feasible to detect betatron radiation from these radiating microbunches. Furthermore, while radiative energy loss during the acceleration phase could pose challenges for achieving the target of 1 TeV electron energy in AWAKE Run 2, this issue could be mitigated by adjusting the electron plasma density. These conclusions regarding the detectability of betatron radiation from accelerating proton microbunches are based on a comprehensive analysis of the physical processes involved, utilizing a multi-physics simulation approach. Specifically, a hybrid simulation technique is employed, integrating the particle-in-cell (PIC) method with the hybrid Monte Carlo (HMC) method. This approach enables the investigation of betatron radiation emitted by millimeter-scale proton-driven microbunches, capturing both the statistical behavior of numerous particles and the individual interactions between specific particle pairs. The study also evaluates the impact of initial proton space charge forces on the final charge of the accelerated electron bunch and the overall beam quality. Furthermore, the analysis explores the feasibility of detecting betatron radiation from these microbunches by comparing the number of radiating and non-radiating photons against detector thresholds. The results also address the charge capacity of the electron beamline and its influence on achieving the target of 1 TeV electron energy. Finally, the study examines the effect of the drive electron density on the final energy of the accelerated electrons. Overall, the study demonstrates the feasibility of detecting betatron radiation from accelerating proton microbunches and provides a framework for analyzing such radiation, which could facilitate the study of betatron radiation from proton bunches in future linear colliders. This study addresses a critical challenge in distributed decision tree learning: how to train trees effectively across multiple servers while maintaining differential privacy. We introduce a privacy-preserving algorithm that is both scalable and provably accurate, designed to function without relying on any assumptions about input data distributions. Our approach offers two practical implementations for training large tree ensembles: one that is both scalable and accurate, and another that is accurate but not scalable. We validate the efficacy of these methods by applying them to distributed privacy-preserving image classification tasks. Additionally, our findings demonstrate that distributed private decision tree training can achieve performance comparable to centralized private training. As this is the first work to successfully apply differential privacy to distributed decision tree training, we believe our methodology will serve as a foundational framework for future research in this domain. This paper introduces a variant of Bregman proximal gradient algorithms designed to solve a regularized Jensen-R\'enyi divergence minimization problem. By leveraging the equivalence between Jensen-R\'enyi divergence and a regularized Kullback-Leibler divergence under the simplex constraint, we apply Bregman proximal gradient algorithms utilizing Kullback-Leibler as the reference function. For the $\beta=0.5$ case, we demonstrate the presence of a saddle-point structure within the algorithm and prove its convergence. Furthermore, we establish the convergence of the algorithm for arbitrary $\beta \in (0,1)$ under specific conditions. Finally, we apply this method to analyze the convergence dynamics of a game involving two players. Our results indicate that, consistent with standard proximal gradient theory, the algorithm converges linearly at the first order and superlinearly at the second order. These findings are supported by experiments conducted on both synthetic and real-world datasets, which illustrate the algorithm's convergence behavior and highlight the impact of the $\beta$ parameter. Additionally, our computational performance compares favorably against state-of-the-art methods. The source code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/ElafMohamed/BPG}. We introduce a new chain event graph model that encompasses both the structured chain event graph average differential equation and logistic chain event graph average differential equation models. Utilizing approximate Bayesian Markov sampling, we estimate the posterior distribution for the average differential equation parameters of this chain event graph model, with the graph structure itself serving as a hyperparameter. By applying Bayesian Markov sampling, we determine the model choice probability for each state within the graph. Consequently, we can visualize the resulting average differential equation system based on a selected model choice for the chain event graph. This method facilitates model choice across all states in the graph, extending beyond the limited two-way model choice currently available for linear and logistic chain event average differential equations. We demonstrate the application of this model choice procedure using a case study derived from data collected during the 2009/10 academic year at the University of Cambridge. The data, gathered via a weekly diary method, tracks student performance in a statistics and probability module, specifically focusing on attendance, exam results, and module withdrawal. Our results indicate that the logistic chain event graph model provides the superior fit for this specific university module. The proposed modeling approach offers greater flexibility than previous studies, which relied solely on chain event models. Furthermore, it surpasses models limited to logistic differential equations by accounting for the dynamic, time-dependent nature of transition rates between graph states. The methodology is implemented in the R package `chmcmc`, which is accessible at http://www.r-forge.r-project.org/projects/chmcmc. The package also includes a demonstration utilizing the Cambridge student data. The online version of this article, available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s11222-021-09997-8, is supplemented with additional material. Specifically, Figure 10 illustrates the logistic chain event graph model selected via Bayesian model choice, showing transition rates between states for every pair of connected state sets. This expanded figure is provided in the online publication. Additionally, the appendix demonstrates a model choice algorithm applied to a simple three-state chain event graph. The linear chain event graph model is also fitted to the Cambridge student data; however, it yields a poorer fit than the logistic alternative. We introduce and analyze a dynamic integration method that blends Hamiltonian dynamics with a Tikhonov regularization term to achieve at least local strong convergence toward the solution of an optimization problem featuring non-smooth regularizer and Tikhonov regularization at an accelerated rate. Specifically, we demonstrate that the direct and natural transition of this system at rate $\frac{1}{t}$ into one featuring solely a Tikhonov regularization term yields a trajectory with logarithmically local strong convergence to the least norm solution of the target problem, provided the Hamiltonian is coercive and its sublevel sets are bounded. Finally, numerical experiments utilizing both a quadratic objective function and one derived from compressed sensing data confirm the effectiveness of these findings. This approach extends the results of [20] and offers an alternative convergence rate to that established in [12]. Furthermore, our results align with those in [11] and [15], which address convergence to the least norm solution of Tikhonov problems featuring non-smooth regularizers, though our direct methods and proofs differ from those papers. Our approach also draws inspiration from [16], where a dynamical system incorporating friction, inertia, and Tikhonov regularization with a non-smooth potential function exhibits local strong convergence to the least norm solution. However, the primary distinction lies in our demonstration of the direct and natural convergence of the damped inertial system—transitioned directly into one with only a Tikhonov regularization term—toward the least norm solution, rather than the pointwise limit of the damped inertial system with vanishing Tikhonov regularization. Additionally, the direct transition method employed here offers a straightforward proof of convergence to the least norm solution. Our primary objective is to provide a new approach for achieving local strong convergence to the least norm solution of Tikhonov problems involving TMC functions, with a focus on the direct transition strategy. Our results also offer a positive answer to an open question posed in [11]. Finally, the direct transition method utilized in this paper represents a distinct approach from the one used in [15]. Overall, this paper demonstrates that the direct transition of a damped inertial system with vanishing Tikhonov regularization to a system retaining only the Tikhonov regularization term—achieved by selecting the switching time as $T^* = \frac{1}{t}$—yields local strong convergence to the least norm solution of the target problem, assuming Hamiltonian potential coercivity and bounded sublevel sets. Robots typically navigate walls by maintaining a constant distance, but they frequently exhibit disorderly transition dynamics when shifting between them. This study demonstrates that such transitions inherently generate disorder, characterized by diverse temporal patterns arising from spatial heterogeneities in robustness. Specifically, disordered onsets and quenchings emerge when a robot enters from free space to a wall, while quench disorder is observed when moving from a wall to free space. Furthermore, transitions involving two different walls are invariably disordered on the quenching side, though free-space onsets can be either ordered or disordered. Finally, we establish that this disordered behavior cannot be explained by simple mean-field approximations and must instead result from the activation of many free modes. Overall, our findings indicate that achieving orderly transitions requires the explicit suppression of these free modes. These results provide a foundational framework for guiding future wall-following robots toward more efficient transitions and free-space navigation. Additionally, this problem represents a novel instance of disordered onsets and quenchings, where order-to-disorder transitions occur when crossing critical points in one direction, while disorder-to-order transitions are observed in the opposite direction. To our knowledge, this specific duality has not been previously documented. Furthermore, this work underscores the necessity of developing new navigation algorithms that explicitly account for spatial heterogeneities in robustness. Consequently, this research underscores the vital role of complexity theory in advancing robotics. Finally, this work is based on the first author's PhD thesis. Plants are vital for human survival, yet understanding their growth remains a significant challenge. Although image data is abundant, growth dynamics are hard to capture; existing methods that estimate growth rates from images are often inaccurate and fail to generalize well. This paper introduces GrowSpace, a novel method that learns a space of growth patterns and maps plant images to this space. Specifically, we design a space that encodes one-dimensional growth over time and utilize a convolutional autoencoder to embed images into it. Our experiments demonstrate that GrowSpace achieves significantly more accurate growth estimation than prior approaches and exhibits superior generalization to unseen domains. Additionally, we show that the model can be used for data augmentation, enhancing the performance of other techniques. We further investigate its utility in non-intuitive applications, such as identifying plants that appear healthy but are actually suffering from diseases or nutrient deficiencies. Finally, we apply the method to an interactive mobile application for gardening, enabling users to simulate how their plants will grow in the future based on current images. The code and application are accessible at https://growspace.gmu.edu. Furthermore, we have made our dataset available at https://github.com/GrowSpace/GrowSpaceDataset. Please see our paper for a step-by-step tutorial on using the GrowSpace application. In summary, GrowSpace is designed to (1) accurately estimate plant growth, (2) enhance other deep learning techniques, and (3) facilitate interactive mobile gardening. We provide details on the method's capabilities and applications, including interactive mobile gardening. GrowSpace is expected to benefit both the computer vision and mobile gardening communities. The normalization of spectral biomarkers is essential for ensuring both technical and biological reproducibility in imaging studies. However, the current landscape lacks universally agreed-upon normalization procedures, and existing ex vivo methods are not directly applicable to in vivo imaging due to significant differences in spectral profiles. This discrepancy often leads to reduced reliability in clinical implementations. To address this, we propose a unified framework designed to enable reliable longitudinal follow-up and multi-center comparisons in clinical imaging. This study evaluates various imaging and chemical parameters to identify robust and transferable biological markers suitable for normalization across diverse platforms. We demonstrate that certain markers remain unaffected by technical variations in excitation energy, instrument response, and system geometry. Although the research focuses on fluorescence spectroscopy, the proposed framework is equally applicable to Raman, RIRS, and other vibrational spectroscopy modalities. These findings offer a pathway to normalize spectral data, facilitating multi-center studies and establishing a foundation for future clinical translation. Consequently, we introduce the Image Biomarker Normalization Initiative (IBNI), which provides an open-access repository of reference samples and standardized normalization protocols. This resource serves as a starting point for the broader effort to normalize imaging biomarkers and supports clinical decision-making through reproducible and reliable methods. By enhancing the reproducibility of spectral imaging biomarkers, we aim to improve the diagnosis and monitoring of diseases. The IBNI is freely accessible at https://ibni.org. We invite researchers from both academic and industrial sectors to collaborate with us in further developing these normalization procedures. Please contact info@ibni.org for more information. This paper outlines the methodology for pre-processing 2,000 publicly accessible color portraits from the non-institutional MORPH-II database, which depicts individuals from diverse racial backgrounds. Our approach, built upon the pytorch-image-preprocessing (TIP) framework within the opencv-python package, involves five primary procedures: colorization, face detection, face alignment, luminance conversion, and pixel normalization. The outcomes of these procedures are evaluated using the Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) metric, which quantifies the discrepancy between real images and those generated by the pre-processing pipeline. Using a validation subset of 200 images, we achieved a highly realistic synthetic portrait generated by the pre-processing pipeline with an FID score of 20.85. Furthermore, we conducted an ablation study to assess the individual impact of each pre-processing step on image realism. This study utilized mean squared error (MSE) calculated across channel-wise mean and standard deviation values to quantify the difference between pre- and post-processed images, thereby supporting the selection of hyper-parameters. Ultimately, the ablation study demonstrated that the specific hyper-parameters chosen for this pipeline effectively enhanced the realism of the portrait synthesis. We investigate the production of primordial black holes (PBHs) within a curvaton model featuring a step-function potential. In this framework, the curvaton field remains frozen until it reaches a specific threshold, where it begins to roll down the potential; subsequently, it is eventually dominated by and decays into the radiation energy density. The primary objective is to generate ultra-heavy PBHs with a mass of approximately $10^{16}$ g, which would remain stable against evaporation for the entire history of the universe. We demonstrate that the operating curvaton model can successfully produce such massive PBHs in this mass range. Furthermore, we establish a correspondence between the curvaton parameters and the resulting PBH mass and abundance. We also analyze the constraints imposed by PBH evaporation and dark matter density on the model's parameter space. Additionally, we assess the compatibility of this scenario with Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) data. Our findings indicate that while the model can produce PBHs in mass ranges up to $\sim 10^{14}$ g, the resulting dark matter density is insufficient to account for the total dark matter density of the universe. Consequently, an operating curvaton model alone cannot resolve the $s_8$ tension. Finally, we explore how this scenario can be tested by future CMB experiments, such as the Cosmic Microwave Background Stage-4 (CMB-S4). High school students often face challenges in grasping the necessary academic requirements for college success. To tackle this issue, we introduce a novel "high school to college" mapping that employs a specific latent variable model capable of handling data sparsity. The latent variable, termed the high school diploma value (HDV), encapsulates a student's grade 12 standing. Our findings indicate that the proposed model surpasses existing alternatives, including school profiles based on standardized test scores and GPAs, as well as the number of Advanced Placement (AP) courses taken. Furthermore, we demonstrate how these models can be utilized to highlight academic pathways for a sample of high school seniors from Washington state. Notably, students from certain high schools have already discovered these pathways and are enrolling in institutions where their HDVs are highest. Additionally, we provide a user-friendly web application for accessing the proposed model's results, which includes a feature allowing students to input their own high school information to generate a customized pathway map. This study introduces a novel vehicle platoon formation control framework that integrates differential games with analytical methods. While traditional formation control relies on fixed station positions, this approach dynamically generates target positions for formation controllers. Specifically, differential game solutions serve as these position references. For linear platoons, differential games provide efficient and robust solutions; however, analyzing non-linear differential games is challenging due to the difficulty of obtaining closed-form solutions. Consequently, we utilize numerical solvers to obtain these solutions and employ formation controllers to ensure platoon stability. Simulation results validate the proposed methodology and underscore the necessity and efficacy of employing dynamic vehicle position data rather than static geographic locations. The primary advantages of this method include its robustness, scalability, and the ability to manage nonlinear dynamics. Furthermore, this technique is applicable to various vehicle configurations, such as triangular and diamond formations, by simply providing the appropriate formation matrix. Additionally, the method supports cooperative maneuvers within the platoon. Ultimately, this proposed approach holds significant promise for future autonomous driving applications. **Keywords:** Formation Control, Vehicle Platoons, Differential Games, Autonomous Driving.

This study addresses the issue of interacting features in logistic regression, where interactions between variables cause significant changes in predicted outcomes. We introduce a method utilizing constrained logistic regression, featuring convex objective functions with lightweight constraints, to identify a subset of interactions necessary for achieving target objectives. Specifically, for a prescribed budget of interaction terms, the model selects the minimum number required to maintain a desired level of accuracy. We provide convergence guarantees for this approach within a distributed environment using bregza divergence-based objective functions and demonstrate its effectiveness across six real-world datasets. Furthermore, we propose two novel models employing sparsity constraints on interactions to maximize interpretability. For both relation and image classification tasks, we evaluate the trade-off between interaction count and interpretability, showing that the proposed models generate sparser interaction sets compared to existing methods. Additionally, we extend both formulations to support online learning, which is particularly beneficial for time-sensitive applications. Online experiments conducted on two image classification datasets confirm that our online formulations learn a sparser selection of interactions than offline approaches. To enhance scalability, we develop two online algorithms based on these formulations and validate their performance on two web applications. Finally, we demonstrate superior results on both synthetic and real-world datasets by learning interaction structures that align with human preferences. Detecting misinformation is crucial for safeguarding public discourse, and such information often disseminates rapidly through news headlines. While various studies have characterized the linguistic traits of headlines promoting fake news, these characteristics vary significantly depending on the specific outlet. To bridge this gap, we introduce a dataset of headlines sourced from 250 news websites. We demonstrate that Transformer-based models can effectively identify headlines using this diverse dataset. Our analysis reveals that Transformers achieve state-of-the-art performance, surpassing BERT by an substantial 11.23% and traditional text-based models by a considerable 20.29%. Furthermore, we examine the types of headlines the model successfully identifies to gain deeper insights into the mechanisms of news headlines. Finally, we explore the potential applications of our model within the news industry. The dataset and associated code can be accessed at https://github.com/ahmedmohd123/nh-detectors. All experiments were conducted on the Amazon EC2 cloud platform. Mohamed Ahmed, Mohamed Elsayed, and Mohamed Afify.

We establish the phase diagram for a frustrated Heisenberg antiferromagnet on a chiral honeycomb lattice within an applied field aligned with the pseudo-triangular axis. Utilizing series expansions and quantum Monte Carlo simulations, we identify multiple distinct phases: a unique chiral spin liquid (CSL) state, several conventional spin liquid phases characterized by gapless spinon excitations, and various magnetically ordered phases. Notably, our simulations of both amorphous and polycrystalline samples indicate that thermal fluctuations enable the system to reach the gapless CSL phase at low temperatures without becoming trapped in a magnetically ordered state. These findings suggest that CSL states in geometrically frustrated Heisenberg models can be reached equilibrium states in real materials even when minor disorder causes some spins to form short-range ordered clusters. Finally, we discuss a potential candidate material for this previously unexplored phase: the chiral honeycomb lattice found in $\kappa$-(ET)$_2$Cu$_2$(CN)$_3$. This is supported by recent neutron scattering data showing excitations consistent with the gapless CSL phase. Furthermore, we predict that applying a magnetic field along the pseudo-triangular axis will induce a field-induced CSL state in this material. Consequently, we propose that experiments on this compound, under both zero field and finite field conditions, can help clarify the phase diagram and the nature of spin correlations in this system. These insights could advance the broader understanding and investigation of CSL phases in other materials. Finally, we note that while our study focuses on the Heisenberg model, the identified CSL phase is particularly promising for materials exhibiting Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions, as it represents a CSL with a finite chirality. This contrasts with CSL phases in isotropic Heisenberg models, where chirality vanishes due to chiral symmetry. Thus, we anticipate that the phase diagram of Heisenberg models in chiral lattices, whether amorphous or polycrystalline, will serve as a valuable theoretical framework for analyzing CSL phases in various materials. Our comprehensive numerical and analytical framework is well-suited for this purpose. In conclusion, this study significantly expands the theoretical understanding of CSL phases, even in the absence of dipolar interactions. We believe these findings will inspire further research into the rich and previously unexplored phase diagrams of Heisenberg models on chiral lattices. Finally, we hope these theoretical results will encourage the experimental community to investigate the possibility of the CSL phase in this phase diagram

These approaches rely on fast algorithms to compute convolution and cross-correlation operators between visibilities and calibration models, leveraging the fact that regular-grid interferometers produce visibilities on uniformly spaced frequency channels that satisfy the convolution theorem. We introduce a novel autoencoding conditional Generative Adversarial Network designed to diversify portfolio distributions. This approach leverages historical returns to synthesize optimized future returns. Our empirical findings indicate that diversifying portfolios by fitting generative adversarial networks yields superior risk-adjusted returns compared to diversifying the underlying underlying conditional GAN. Furthermore, the model successfully eliminates exposure to specific factors, demonstrating robustness in the empirical process. The methodology is fully automated, requiring no manual intervention from users. Additionally, we highlight that utilizing disintegration in the generative process allows for the creation of tailored portfolios based on arbitrary factors. Finally, we emphasize the model's flexibility and ease of adaptation to various contexts. In summary, our results suggest that the proposed method is both effective and practical for portfolio diversification.

This study presents the application of a Bayesian neural network to classify blazar light curves from 2008 to 2019, utilizing Fermi-LAT data. The dataset was compiled by selecting sources across all blazar classes, characterized by their long-term, medium-term, and short-term variability patterns. This paper introduces a tensor-level merge operation for hypergraphs, defined via their adjacency hypermatrices, and investigates properties of this operation along with the spectral behavior under such merges. The operation encompasses both hypergraph disjoint and disjoint-like tensor direct sums as specific instances. When applied to hypergraphs without self-loops, the adjacency matrices of the resulting merged hypergraphs correspond to the sum (or convolution) of the original adjacency matrices plus a constant matrix, effectively extending the concept of hypergraph disjoint tensor direct convolution to include self-loops. Furthermore, the problem of determining the largest eigenvalue of the merged hypergraph is reduced to a tensor norm issue, which is subsequently addressed through an iterative algorithm. These findings provide foundational support for the development of various types of hypergraph tensor merges.

This work introduces a specific class of conditional measure flows, termed "regular" conditional measure flows. It is demonstrated that the Stratonovich integral with respect to such flows can be transformed into the Ito integral with respect to a corresponding "related" measure flow. This transformation relationship gives rise to a novel class of conditional measure flows, termed "special" conditional measure flows. A key characteristic of these special measure flows is that their conditional diffusion components satisfy a specific partial differential equation, which arises from the conversion between Stratonovich and Ito integrals via the specified Stratonovich measure flow. This PDE is expressed using the conditional measure flow's conditional density functions and their partial derivatives. The paper concludes with classical applications of these findings. In each case, the Stratonovich process is defined by a conditional measure flow, and its solution is derived using the Ito formulation of the equivalent measure flow. Furthermore, this resolution provides a solution to the original Stratonovich process. Finally, the authors propose a conjecture regarding the solvability of conditional measure flows based on this approach. Specifically, if a conditional measure flow is regular, its Stratonovich integral can be converted to a (special) related measure flow, thereby offering a solution to a class of equations involving functions of the Stratonovich integrand that were previously unrecognized. Additionally, the paper addresses a conjecture by B. Szabó concerning a class of equations featuring the measure flow on the right-hand side, for which regular Stratonovich processes have been identified. We introduce a concept of quasi-character analogous to that in Boolean algebras and investigate its fundamental properties. This concept gives rise to an upper spectral representation of a group, which shares several characteristics with the maximal torus representation of a real Lie group. Furthermore, we define manifold-like structures on two spaces: the collection of all finitary quasi-characters and the group itself. By leveraging the upper spectral representation, we construct a map that assigns to each group its standard structure space, thereby generalizing the concept of a locally compact Hausdorff topological group. In the context of permutation groups, we calculate the dimension of this standard structure space and compare it with the dimension of the space of all finitary permutations within the same group. These computations support the hypothesis that the standard structure space of a permutation group is homeomorphic to the set of all finitary quasi-characters of that group. The study of this hypothesis constitutes the content of our research. This paper focuses on developing the theory of standard structure spaces for groups and computing the standard structure space for permutation groups. Subsequent research will address the validity of this hypothesis.

This study investigates a novel semantic parsing framework designed for cross-domain text-to-SQL translation. Although previous efforts have concentrated on modeling parsing mechanisms, text encoding, and SQL decoding, they often overlook critical translation dimensions such as semantic preservation, schema adaptation, and database schema structures. To address this, we propose an auxiliary task that learns to predict relevant database schemas to enhance the parsing process. Furthermore, we incorporate a cross-domain feature engineered from this prediction to reinforce the translator. We assess our method's robustness across three diverse public SQL datasets, with results showing that our approach surpasses state-of-the-art models in accuracy. Additionally, we have open-sourced the related code and models, which can be accessed at https://github.com/brucewang99/Text2SQL-Cross-Domain-Parsing. Finally, we conclude by outlining four essential aspects that text-to-SQL semantic parsing systems must address to achieve effective generalization in cross-domain scenarios. Model predictive control (MPC) is widely adopted in multi-robot navigation due to its ability to handle complex constraints and optimize performance over time. The approach utilizes a novel Bayesian network to analyze multi-agent behaviors and generate future predictions alongside associated uncertainty metrics. Leveraging these predictions and their inherent uncertainties, we develop a robust likelihood function to create a non-linear MPC that prioritizes both collision avoidance and energy efficiency. Simulation results validate the proposed method's efficacy in navigating crowded spaces while remaining resilient to a variety of obstacles and interference patterns. Furthermore, experimental data from multi-robot system simulations successfully demonstrates the method's high reliability. This work holds significant promise for advancing safe navigation technologies in densely populated settings. We report the discovery of Andromeda XXV (And XXV), a previously unknown dwarf galaxy located in the halo of the Andromeda (M31) galaxy. Based on our analysis of deep imaging data, we determined a distance to And XXV of 780 ± 10 kpc, positioning it within the M31 halo. The galaxy exhibits a projected half-light radius of 1.4 ± 0.1 kpc and contains 1000 ± 200 red giant candidates. By integrating these findings with existing literature, we derived a systemic heliocentric radial velocity of -290 ± 10 km/s. Furthermore, we identified a 1.5 kpc-long tidal tail extending from the system. Our investigation into the kinematics of 100 red giant candidates revealed that their velocity dispersion is consistent with expectations for dwarf galaxies of this nature. We also examined And XXV's dynamical state by calculating the mass-to-light ratio within the half-light radius using the Cauchy estimator, yielding a value of 1.0 ± 0.2. This result suggests a low concentration of dark matter in the galaxy's center. Additionally, we found that And XXV is not on a stable orbit around M31 and is unlikely to be gravitationally bound to it. We propose that And XXV represents a member of the M31 group rather than a satellite of M31. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for theories regarding the formation and evolution of dwarf galaxies within the Andromeda halo. Finally, we show that combining WCN with confidence-based DST yields superior performance compared to DST alone, highlighting the potential of modeling ASR ambiguity for enhancing dialogue systems. A universal access structure encompasses the complete collection of committees derived from a universal partition of the participant set. We establish bounds for this minimum required subset size, demonstrating that for both large $n$ and large $s$, the necessary information amounts to approximately $\log_e(n/s)$. Continual learning (CL) involves training deep networks across a stream of tasks defined by independent input-output mappings, with the goal of retaining performance on previous tasks while learning new ones. Although numerous CL techniques exist, many simply adapt existing baseline methods rather than addressing the core challenge of catastrophic forgetting. This paper introduces two fundamental causes of forgetting in CL: (1) the continuous nature of training causes data from old tasks to become statistically irrelevant over time, leading to a drift in parameter updates away from their previous values; (2) performance on old tasks relies on the intersection of subspaces spanned by outputs for each class, which collapse as parameters shift to fit new tasks. We propose a straightforward baseline that combats forgetting by explicitly tracking and regularizing towards the model's historical average, alongside a dynamic regularization scheme that preserves subspaces for each old class. This approach surpasses all recent state-of-the-art CL methods using fewer parameters and minimal memory overhead, even on complex visual tasks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this technique effectively mitigates forgetting in non-CL scenarios, such as multi-domain image classification and multi-lingual machine translation. Finally, we conduct an empirical analysis of how training continuity and regularization influence CL performance. To our knowledge, this is the first work to identify the statistical drift in parameters as the root cause of forgetting in CL. The code is accessible at: https://github.com/DeepMind/mean-shape-replay.

We extend prior research [1] by analyzing infra-linear ($\gamma < 3$) and ultra-linear ($\gamma > 3$) degree distributions in addition to the previously studied normal case ($\gamma = 3$), where $\gamma$ denotes the exponent of a power-law degree distribution. Our prior work demonstrated that infra-linear networks are significantly harder to infer than ultra-linear or normally distributed networks, whereas ultra-linear networks are marginally more difficult than networks with normal degree distributions. Automatic Program Repair (APR) has garnered significant research interest in recent years. Traditional APR methods rely on heuristic rules to transform program code, yet they struggle to address complex bugs. Consequently, machine learning-based approaches have been widely explored to overcome these limitations. Nevertheless, such systems are susceptible to adversarial bugs—specifically, unit tests that act as "traps" to deceive repair algorithms. This paper introduces Adversarial Mask Generation (AMG), an adversarial training technique designed to identify these deceptive test cases. AMG utilizes a mask-based mask propagation strategy to detect adversarial bugs by generating adversarial programs and automatically extracting trap tests through program conformance analysis. Experimental evaluations across three distinct APR systems demonstrate that AMG successfully discovers 44 previously unknown adversarial bugs, outperforming existing methods. Furthermore, assessments on a large-scale dataset reveal that AMG effectively detects adversarial bugs in 60% of cases, with a detection rate exceeding 60% across all system types. Finally, testing confirms that AMG-identified adversarial bugs exhibit high effectiveness in preventing false repairs. The source code for AMG is publicly accessible at https://github.com/zhijun-liu/AMG. We hope this tool will assist APR researchers in avoiding adversarial bug "traps" and encourage further exploration of this domain. Additionally, we welcome contributions from the community to discover more such bugs. Our issue tracker is available at https://github.com/zhijun-liu/AMG/issues. Please submit any adversarial bugs you identify through this platform. We anticipate that AMG will serve as a valuable tool for enhancing the reliability of program repair efforts. This paper investigates the capacity region of a Generalized Feedback Interference Channel with Confusion (GIFC), a model featuring two encoders, one decoder, and one confusion decoder, all equipped with feedback links. Utilizing the information spectrum method, we determine the GIFC capacity region by defining a joint confusion entropy rate and establishing achievable rates based on cooperative joint decoding with confusion. Our analysis demonstrates that the confusion decoder's feedback expands this region, with the extended amount bounded by the conditional confusion rate mutual information. We arrive at the final result by applying time-reversal and convexification techniques. Notably, the derived bounds are achievable only by the confusion decoder; conventional feedback effects do not broaden the capacity region for standard users in GIFCs. Finally, we illustrate our findings through an example of a Binary GIFC with Confusion (BIFC) featuring an XOR gate, which serves as a practical benchmark for evaluating new GIFC designs. This specific BIFC model also functions as a representative example of a De Bruijn graph, a structure with applications in DNA storage and security. Furthermore, the study addresses a specific sub-case of the GIFC where the confusion decoder's output remains independent of the primary decoder's input, given the transmitted symbols and confusion; this scenario is particularly relevant to DNA storage systems where the confusion decoder represents a readout that may yield incorrect sequences. These findings offer a foundation for the analysis and design of GIFC architectures in DNA storage contexts. In ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions, the initial geometry is determined by the impact parameter and participant distributions, which vary with collision energy. This work introduces 3-dimensional flow as a novel metric for assessing collision geometry. Defined as the slope of the invariant yield versus transverse momentum ($p_T$), 3-dimensional flow exhibits a strong correlation with the initial spatial profile. Consequently, it serves as a valuable tool for investigating both the collision geometry and the equation-of-state (EoS). The study compares two distinct EoS scenarios to demonstrate how 3-dimensional flow reflects its underlying parameters. The findings indicate that 3-dimensional flow is highly sensitive to the speed of sound ($c_s$) within the EoS, thereby offering a novel approach to probe the chiral transition region. In summary, 3-dimensional flow represents a straightforward yet effective quantity for experimentally determining the EoS. These results were derived using TRENTo initial-state models. Additionally, the 3-dimensional elliptic and triangular flow coefficients ($v_2$ and $v_3$) are examined to assess their sensitivity to the EoS. Finally, to validate these theoretical findings, 3-dimensional flow is calculated for Au+Au collisions at various RHIC energies, with direct comparisons made against PHENIX data on inclusive $p_T$ spectra and $p_T$-integrated particle yields. All outcomes are compared against full hydrodynamic simulations utilizing TRENTo initial conditions and the same EoS as the input. Detecting COVID-19 in its early stages is crucial for mitigating its severe impact on human lives. While deep learning has proven highly effective in automated diagnosis, concerns persist regarding the potential privacy leakage associated with training these models on sensitive medical data. This paper introduces ADV-CE, a novel adversarial framework designed to enhance the privacy robustness of complex neural networks during the early diagnosis of COVID-19. Within this approach, an adversarial network generates synthetic data to train the primary model, ensuring it remains resilient against inference attacks even when public datasets are accessible. Extensive experiments using both synthetic and real-world data reveal that adversarial training substantially improves privacy robustness without compromising performance on clean data. Furthermore, ablation studies confirm that critical characteristics of the proposed method are indispensable to its overall efficacy. Consequently, ADV-CE offers a privacy-preserving solution that maintains high diagnostic accuracy, making it suitable for deployment in real-world clinical settings. Addressing the privacy challenges in initial COVID-19 detection represents a significant advancement that could transform the field of automated diagnosis. Future research will explore generalizing this research to enable the detection of other diseases while preserving patient privacy. Given the global scale of this challenge, such efforts hold the promise of significantly improving healthcare systems worldwide. Decentralized learning has recently gained significant attention, particularly in the context of wireless network planning. However, existing approaches typically require a central server to coordinate communication among workers engaged in training, such as neural networks. This study investigates wireless scenarios involving multiple workers participating in a common transmission system, where a central server is either unavailable or impractical to operate. We propose learning a graph neural network to handle inference tasks locally at each worker using only local data. These local predictions are then aggregated through a lightweight wireless communication protocol to generate a global prediction for the entire worker set. Our approach allows the model to leverage information from all workers while performing accurate inferences and maintaining low communication overhead. To our knowledge, this marks the first application of graph neural networks to decentralized learning. We validate our method experimentally by applying it to two real-world datasets: a synthetic synthetic network traffic graph and a real-world New York taxi network. Results demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance in both accuracy and communication efficiency. Furthermore, we explore various model designs and demonstrate that our method is particularly well-suited for graph-structured data. Researchers employed statistical methods, including Spatial-Temporal Scan Statistics, Global and Local Indicators of Spatial Association, and Principal Component Analysis. The results revealed a notable spatial-clustering pattern within homicide rates during the study period, alongside a gradual decline in overall rates. However, this reduction was not uniform across all municipalities, as specific areas maintained persistently high homicide rates throughout the years. These findings underscore the need for targeted public health interventions in these high-incidence regions. The research methodology and associated data could prove valuable for other locations facing similar challenges. We evaluate the impact of frequent and frequent accelerated SGD on minimizing objective functions characterized by benign nonconvexity. Robotics is increasingly leveraging robotic dexterous manipulation, particularly grip-based handling, to enhance its practical utility. However, current robotic grasping methods, whether derived from data or based on models, remain constrained by limited training data, resulting in poor generalization to objects not previously encountered. While robotic dexterous manipulation in data-driven contexts is a burgeoning field, the creation of large-scale, diverse grasp datasets remains a significant challenge. This paper introduces DexGraspNet, a novel dataset featuring a vast collection of synthetic grasps for everyday objects. The comprehensive data comprises 1.2 million diverse grasps across 10,000 distinct items. We demonstrate the efficacy of DexGraspNet both empirically and theoretically. First, we show that the extensive and varied grasp data enables a method to learn a universal gripper by training a single gripper controller to handle all objects using an efficient gradient descent algorithm. Second, a gripper trained on DexGraspNet achieves a successful grasp success rate of 81% on entirely unseen objects. Furthermore, by utilizing a single gripper trained on this large-scale dataset, we can manipulate all objects within the set using a straightforward and efficient closed-loop path planning algorithm. Finally, we provide theoretical insights into the relationship between dataset size and grasp performance. Our theoretical analysis indicates that grasp success rates improve as the number of examples grows, but they also plateau once a certain volume of examples is reached. To our knowledge, DexGraspNet is the largest robotic dexterous manipulation dataset available, offering valuable empirical insights for future research in robotic dexterous manipulation. The dataset and a suite of robotic manipulation tools are available at https://github.com/ChengyuanLi1999/DexGraspNet. **Methods:** The proposed sequence employs a non-cartesian radial sampling scheme for the 4D-3D-TSE module, utilizing a low in-plane resolution and a short readout window. The 3D-TFLA module is designed to be highly robust against free-breathing through-plane motion. A respiratory navigator is employed to retrospectively sort the acquired data into respiratory phases. The radial sampling strategy is optimized to ensure uniform angular coverage. The resulting data is reconstructed into a series of 3D volumes using compressed sensing. The study demonstrates the efficacy of this method in both phantom experiments and clinical applications.

**Results:** In free-breathing phantom studies, the average radial sampling points per slice were 11.7, 10.5, and 10.3 across three slices with simulated motion amplitudes of 10, 20, and 30 mm, respectively. Furthermore, the free-breathing approach reduced scan time from 14 minutes to 8 minutes.

Model compression aims to enhance inference speed and lower computational costs, making it vital for deploying models in edge environments. Prior approaches typically involve training a small backbone to distill knowledge from a large pretrained teacher, ensuring the backbone can cover the teacher's knowledge. However, these methods fail to account for information flow, leading to significant losses when knowledge is compressed. To address this, we introduce InDistill, a knowledge extraction framework that maintains information flow during compression. InDistill features a teacher with multiple decoding heads, where each head is responsible for distilling knowledge from a specific layer, preventing information loss. By controlling the layer-wise compression ratio, we maintain a compression granularity that aligns with information flow. We validate InDistill across various tasks, including image classification, semantic segmentation, and classification and detection tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that InDistill achieves state-oftheart results with substantially higher compression ratios compared to previous methods. Non-local grazing, where animals move between distinct vegetation patches, can trigger complex interactions between livestock and plant ecosystems. This phenomenon may initiate a feedback loop involving both vegetation and livestock, thereby altering the conditions under which stable coexistence is possible. We investigate this mechanism by integrating the concept of non-local grazing into a well-established dryland vegetation model. Our findings indicate that this factor can either enhance or diminish the stability of the system. Specifically, we determine a critical threshold for the length of the grazing cycle; when this cycle exceeds this threshold, the system enters a periodic state characterized by alternating high and low biomass levels. Furthermore, our results suggest that as the length of the grazing cycle increases, the stability of the coexistence system may fluctuate between different ranges. Finally, our analysis reveals that both the grain size and kernel type of the non-localization function significantly influence both the existence and stability of the system. These insights are corroborated through numerical simulations. Ultimately, our model and associated results provide valuable insights into the intricate dynamics of both non-local grazing and the ecosystem at large. Additionally, our findings may offer valuable perspectives for sustainable agricultural practices and the development of appropriate policies. Finally, our approach employs a non-local integral equation framework grounded in a well-established mathematical foundation. This methodology avoids the need for ad-hoc approximations of non-local grazing within traditional reaction-diffusion systems, a limitation that has previously hindered both theoretical and experimental investigations of non-local grazing effects. We anticipate that our findings will inspire further research into the effects of non-local grazing. Finally, our work may also contribute to advancing the mathematical foundations of non-local interactions. CountSketch is a widely used dimensionality reduction method that projects high-dimensional vectors into lower dimensions via randomized linear measurements, enabling the recovery of $\ell_1$-norm sparse vectors from compressed data. Although numerous theories and empirical results indicate that CountSketch remains robust against adaptive inputs, a complete theoretical proof has been absent until now. This paper fills that gap by establishing the resilience of CountSketch to adaptive $\ell_0$-norm vectors, demonstrating successful reconstruction even in the strongest adversarial setting where data is adaptively revealed based on prior reconstruction outcomes. Specifically, in instances where all previous predictions result in zero loss, the proposed CountSketch algorithm maintains constant relative loss for future predictions. Furthermore, this adversarial resilience extends to input sequences where total loss is non-zero, allowing the algorithm to achieve constant additive loss relative to the total loss of prior predictions. These findings represent the first theoretical results of their kind for CountSketch in adaptive scenarios. Additionally, the results generalize to count-based reconstruction methods applicable to count-data distributions, such as Poisson counts. Notably, the analysis does not rely on any statistical assumptions regarding the input sequence. The study begins by proving CountSketch resilience for adaptive inputs with known sub-Gaussian norms before extending the analysis to sparsity norms. Finally, the paper concludes by examining CountSketch's resilience to adaptive inputs within count-data distributions. The theoretical results are supported by empirical evidence. Finally, the count-based results are demonstrated to be tight. The code is available at: https://github.com/ashishgarg123/CountSketch. We introduce ipie, a Python-based auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (AFQMC) code designed to compute quantum expectation values for bosons and spin systems at finite temperatures. Specifically, it calculates unique ground and excited states, along with their associated quantum correlation functions and energy gaps, for extensive systems. The ipie framework supports a suite of advanced variational and projection techniques, including constrained auxiliary-field transformations, constrained imbedding, and the maximum entropy principle. Its auxiliary-field and Monte Carlo algorithms are highly parallelized across heterogeneous computing environments, including multi-core CPUs, multi-node clusters, and, since version 2.0, NVIDIA CUDA-enabled GPUs. We validate ipie's capabilities using representative models of bosonic and spin systems, specifically the Bose-Hubbard and $J_1$-$J_2$ Heisenberg models. We introduce a novel approach to the auxiliary-field Monte Carlo sign problem within bosonic systems that eliminates unnormalized configuration rejections, thereby boosting computational efficiency on both single and multi-core CPUs. Furthermore, we demonstrate the superiority of our maximum entropy algorithm over the constrained imbedding technique when determining excited states. The ipie code is freely accessible at https://github.com/iee-group/iee. This work serves as a tutorial for utilizing ipie to investigate bosonic and spin systems. A quantum network represents a future architecture that leverages quantum phenomena to deliver superior communication capabilities. In this study, we present a quantum version of the Prisoner's Dilemma applied to competitive HFT within such a network. The game features two players, Alice and Bob, who function as automated trading agents utilizing quantum strategies. We demonstrate that a quantum HFT network networked via the Internet enables the emergence of quantum dominant strategies that surpass the Nash Equilibrium found in both classical and other quantum implementations of the game. Specifically, at certain confidence levels, the expected payoff for the dominant strategy in our model is approximately 1.5 times higher than the classical scenario. Furthermore, we establish a link between the payoffs of the Prisoner's Dilemma and the profit functions used in our trading model. This connection reveals that the profitability of the dominant strategy is governed by the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index, which measures market concentration. Consequently, our findings indicate that quantum HFT networks can yield substantial profits for market participants, thereby driving the rapid advancement of quantum network technology. This research holds particular relevance for the current era of high market volatility. Additionally, our study highlights the economic advantages of quantum networks and suggests that quantum strategies could provide a substantial edge in highly competitive trading environments. This work serves as a proof of concept for future investigations into quantum HFT networks. To achieve this, we have developed a functional HFT network and an automated framework for running the Prisoner's Dilemma game, which are included as supplementary materials. These tools can be utilized to validate the economic benefits of quantum strategies in HFT networks. This document examines $n$-variable real-valued functions and their relation to partial derivatives, focusing on concepts such as continuity, (Schwarz) differentiability, and (Haar) almost differentiability. The primary objective is to establish sufficient conditions for the differentiability of an $n$-variable function based on the differentiability of all its partial derivatives, assuming $n \geq 2$. To achieve this, we substitute the classical mixed partial derivative theorem—which requires $\mathcal{C}^1$ differentiability of the original function—with a weaker variant that demands continuous values. This alternative version suffices to prove Baire category conditions for differentiability. We present four theorems addressing specific scenarios: first, if every partial derivative is Baire differentiable, then the original function is twice Baire differentiable; second, if all partial derivatives are $\mathcal{C}^1$ smooth, then Baire differentiation can be applied to the original function a second time; third and fourth, conditions are provided for determining higher-order Baire differentiability. These four theorems generalize established results from lower to higher dimensions. Additionally, we explore a "weak" version of the first theorem, which relaxes the requirement for continuous values and instead assumes that partial derivatives possess Baire pointwise derivatives. Finally, we present examples and counter-examples to demonstrate that, regarding higher-order differentiability, conditions based on continuity are strictly stronger than those based on Baire differentiability. In summary, this work presents novel findings and insights into how differentiability of an $n$-variable function relates to the differentiability of its partial derivatives. It is available as arXiv:2101.01012 [math.CA]. Keywords: Differentiability, Partial Derivative, Continuous Function, Baire Differentiability, Almost Differentiability.

This paper introduces a novel computational framework designed to measure vocal entrainment between conversation partners. Unlike prior approaches that focus solely on extracting features from individual signals, our method incorporates conversational context by utilizing the inter-speaker cross-correlogram of syllable timings. Furthermore, we provide an extensive statistical analysis of experimental data to validate the reliability and effectiveness of this novel entrainment metric. We also compare our findings against two existing entrainment measurement techniques and demonstrate the superior performance of the inter-speaker cross-correlogram. Finally, we illustrate the applicability of this method to conversation analysis by employing the measure to investigate turn-taking dynamics in simulated conversations generated by neural network-based virtual assistants. To facilitate future research, we publicly release the feature extraction code alongside the experimental dataset. The dataset includes acoustic recordings from simulated virtual assistant dialogues, as well as both scripted and real-world recordings of human-human conversations. Code and data can be accessed at: https://github.com/ahmedhassan1999/context-aware-computational-method-for-measuring-vocal-entrainmen.
