This study examines the quantum motion of an atom adjacent to a partial mirror, incorporating the radiation reaction force and photon exchange between the atom and the cavity. Our findings indicate that the accumulation of rephased dipole moments generates significant radiation, a phenomenon termed "motion-induced stimulation." This effect stems from the dynamic coupling between the atom and field modes, specifically triggering a resonance at the cavity's free spectral range. We demonstrate that this phenomenon can be observed experimentally by measuring the modified Purcell effect or detecting far-field intensity. Furthermore, in the strong coupling regime, motion-induced stimulation facilitates energy exchange between the atom and the cavity field, a process we describe as electromagnetic radiation. These results underscore the critical role of electromagnetic interactions in atom-chip based quantum technologies. To support this analysis, we developed a fully open-source theoretical framework within the open quantum hardware toolkit (OQHT) to address quantum dynamics near material boundaries. This tool enables the simultaneous calculation of electromagnetic forces, damping, and stimulated radiation arising from material-induced modifications to the vacuum field. The accompanying notebook provides a comprehensive example demonstrating these capabilities. The OQHT repository can be accessed at https://github.com/CPSC/obkt. Keywords: Quantum Atom Optics, Quantum Fluid Dynamics, Atom-chip Technology, Theoretical Methods.

Addressing unfair treatment of specific groups within high-stakes graph-based machine learning is a critical yet difficult challenge. This study introduces GLVCA, a novel algorithm that integrates generalized linear models with community detection techniques to ensure fairness. The proposed method employs a two-stage framework: first identifying communities within the graph and subsequently generating predictive models that yield equal opportunity for these communities. Distinct from prior methods that focus on individual nodes, our approach prioritizes groups, which is essential for scenarios where group membership is the primary concern. We demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness using the COMPAS dataset, which predicts recidivism for defendants, and a co-authorship network. The analysis of these datasets underscores the significance of group-level fairness, highlighting the need for solutions that extend beyond node-centric approaches. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar1999/GLVCA. Furthermore, we provide a fair classification library for graph data, FairGL, available at https://github.com/ashishkumar1999/FairGL. In summary, this work presents a framework for achieving group-level fairness in graph data, offering a pathway to more equitable outcomes in graph learning. The computational complexity of GLVCA is linear with respect to graph size, making it highly scalable. Additionally, the model's interpretability is enhanced by its foundation in generalized linear models. Our approach advances the fields of graph analytics and machine learning by offering group-level fairness, ensuring that generalizations of linear models maintain fair outcomes on graph data. The source code for GLVCA is available at https://github.com/ashishkumar1999/GLVCA. The FairGL library, which implements group-level fairness for graph data, can be found at https://github.com/ashishkumar1999/FairGL. The computational complexity of GLVCA scales linearly with the graph size. The source code for GLVCA is accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar1999/GLVCA. FairGL is a library for fair classification on graphs, with the source code available at https://github.com/ashishkumar1999/FairGL. This research examines kinetic models of reversible enzyme processes, specifically analyzing the Michaelis-Menten and competitive inhibition frameworks. It demonstrates the application of the iterative Fourier transform method, which integrates the Fourier transform technique with the iterative scheme proposed by P. Graczyk. The study establishes conditions ensuring both the convergence of this iterative scheme and the stability of the derived approximate solutions. Furthermore, the text addresses the kinetic equations for both the enzyme-substrate complex and the free substrate, illustrating the method through two established numerical examples. In each case, approximate solutions are derived, and their numerical accuracy is validated. Additionally, the impact of the initial function selection on the iterative process and solution accuracy is highlighted, with this influence demonstrated using two distinct initial functions in one of the established numerical examples. Finally, the significance of this research is emphasized, particularly regarding the determination of enzyme and inhibitor concentrations within biological systems. These effects are notably demonstrated through two newly introduced initial functions, where their influence is observed using two distinct initial functions in both numerical examples. The authors acknowledge their interest in this topic due to their involvement in the biological analysis of the human brain. The paper concludes by suggesting potential future research directions. Specifically, the issue of identifying appropriate initial functions for the iterative scheme is raised, alongside the possibility of developing new initial functions that yield more accurate solutions. This possibility is illustrated by the two new initial functions presented, which generate more accurate solutions compared to those produced by the previously established initial functions. The authors propose that this issue could become the subject of future research. The paper also addresses the challenge of selecting the number of iterations for the approximate solutions; however, the authors note that a sufficient number of iterations can be determined by establishing an error estimate for the solution. Consequently, the issue of deriving an error estimate for the approximate solution is also highlighted as a potential area for future research. The authors intend to address this issue in their upcoming research. Furthermore, the authors have previously proposed an algorithm for the iterative scheme utilizing enzyme-subroad data [1]. This paper also includes an algorithm for the iterative scheme, derived using enzyme-substrate data. Both algorithms utilize the iterative scheme to identify the unknown parameters of the model. The distinction between these two algorithms lies in their initialization processes: the first algorithm employs a system of two equations, whereas the second relies on a single equation. The authors suggest that these two algorithms could also serve as a subject for future research. [1] J. This study presents findings from a search for supersymmetry (SUSY) conducted using proton-proton collision data at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, gathered by the CMS experiment at the LHC in 2016. The analysis examines final states characterized by at least one jet with transverse momentum exceeding 350 GeV and significant missing transverse momentum. A multivariate technique is employed to distinguish signal from background, yielding no significant evidence for the presence of jets and missing transverse momentum indicative of new physics. Consequently, 95% confidence level limits are established for natural SUSY scenarios involving top squark and gluino decays, as well as for divided SUSY models featuring top squark and third-generation gluino decays. The latter limits are derived under the assumption of a specific model motivated by the recent observation of a final state with three b-jets, missing transverse momentum, and a high-transverse-momentum muon. Furthermore, this search investigates the production of heavy color singlets, such as the Higgs and Z bosons, in split-spectrum SUSY models. In these models, gluinos decay into bottom squarks near the LHC energy scale, which subsequently decay into light squarks far above this scale. The resulting exclusion limits for these scenarios extend up to a gluino mass of 2.5 TeV and a top squark mass of 1.1 TeV. Additionally, limits for Higgs boson production via gluino pairs are reported, reaching up to 2.1 TeV. For the production of heavy colorless particles, the exclusion reach extends up to 2.5 TeV for gluinos and 1.7 TeV for top squarks. This paper offers diagnostics for detecting financial bubbles characterized by a shifting mean, driven by rational agents who form consensus on the bubble's conclusion. It establishes a mean-reverting model for the bubble's end time, where the transition speed depends on the ratio of two financial quantities: the interest gap and the "interest gap variance," which integrates estimated long-term interest rate volatility and uncertainty regarding that estimate. The model is validated using historical data, demonstrating that it accurately captures mean-reverting trends in asset prices and the dynamic shift in agents' expectations concerning the bubble's end. Additionally, the study presents a rational expectation model of asset demand featuring stochastic parameters, solving for its equilibrium via a generalized Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation. The resulting solution is analyzed using a specific case where the interest gap variance is treated as a constant. This analytical solution is then compared against a numerical solution derived from the proposed diagnostic model, with the comparison extending to an application on the S&P 500. The findings indicate that the proposed model effectively captures the essential dynamics of the S&P 500 during the 2000–2009 bubble. Furthermore, the S&P 500 is observed to exhibit an endogenous interest gap variance, which the model successfully represents. Finally, the paper explores the implications of this finding for the theory of financial asset bubbles. Key concepts include rational expectation models, mean-reverting dynamics, interest gaps, and interest gap variance. The developed model holds significant potential for forecasting future financial bubbles. It is founded on the premise that the primary driver of asset price movements is the interest gap, and it further posits that the interest gap variance is a critical factor in understanding the bubble formation process. This variance is defined as a function of long-term interest rate volatility and uncertainty about this uncertainty. Empirical evidence confirms that the S&P 500 displays an endogenous interest gap variance, a phenomenon that the proposed model can accurately represent. Consequently, this finding serves as a foundation for future research into financial asset bubbles. Ultimately, the interest gap variance acts as an early warning indicator for the risk of bubble formation. This insight is derived from an analysis of the expected Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation associated with the rational expectation model, which includes an additional term in its nonlinearity. This term is a convex function of the interest gap and is modulated by the interest gap variance. We introduce a new method for calculating quantum observables of a quantum harmonic oscillator driven by arbitrary time-dependent fields. This approach utilizes time slices of the path integral formulation, where time evolution is represented as sums over field configurations evaluated via Monte Carlo simulations. In this framework, quantum states and matrix elements are expressed as weighted integrals over field configurations. To evaluate quantum observables with arbitrary time dependence, we compute path integrals across various field configurations using the Monte Carlo method. The validity of this technique is confirmed by comparing our results with the standard Heisenberg picture and eigenstate-based methods. Our findings demonstrate that path integrals offer a straightforward and effective means to compute the time dependence of quantum observables. This path integral method holds significant potential for future applications in quantum field theory. Furthermore, this study may serve as a valuable pedagogical resource for teaching quantum mechanics. All computational code is provided in the supplementary materials. Our results are presented in both the frequency domain and the time domain. In the time domain, we examine two scenarios: real-time evolution under driving fields and imaginary time (Euclidean) time evolution. Within Euclidean time, we calculate thermal partition functions and correlation functions using the path integral method and compare them against non-path integral methods. In the frequency domain, we examine the response of the quantum system to driving fields with arbitrary time dependence and arbitrary frequencies. In the most general scenario, we consider quantum systems driven by arbitrary time-dependent fields with arbitrary frequencies. In this context, we compute the displacement, average energy, and energy distribution of the oscillator. These results indicate that the path integral approach is highly effective for computing the displacement, energy, and energy distribution of quantum systems with time-dependent mass. In recent years, recommender systems have increasingly leveraged user reviews to enhance rating accuracy and improve the overall user experience. Review-centric recommendation typically involves two stages: first, automatically extracting sentiment information from the reviews, and second, utilizing this extracted data during the recommendation process. However, most existing methods treat these two stages as independent and fail to effectively integrate them. Furthermore, current approaches often neglect the dynamic interactions between reviews and reviews, as well as between reviews and items. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel model called the Sentiment-aware Interactive Fusion Network (SIFN). This model incorporates two key components: (1) a sentiment extraction module designed to comprehensively capture implicit sentiment features within reviews, and (2) a review-aware interactive fusion module that captures the interactive relationships between reviews and items to significantly boost the robustness of sentiment-based recommendation. Extensive experiments conducted on two real-world datasets demonstrate that our proposed framework outperforms several state-of-the-art baselines. Additionally, ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of each component in the proposed model. Finally, we present analysis and case studies to provide insights into how the model functions. The source code will be made available at https://github.com/zhongyuan1994/SIFN. The paper can be accessed at https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.01777. Given its promising performance, we hope this model will serve as a valuable baseline for future research in the field. This work was presented at the 44th International ACM SIGIR Conference on Research and Development in Information Retrieval. Data scarcity remains a significant hurdle in advancing machine learning. To address this, researchers have adopted data augmentation techniques to generate synthetic training samples from limited data. This paper presents a novel approach to augmenting Arabic-English code-switched (ACS) data by leveraging lexical substitutions. By replacing select words in existing samples with their synonyms, we create varied data that enhances model generalization. We evaluated our method across two dimensions: internal performance on a classification task and external validation using a model tested on out-of-domain data. Our findings demonstrate that this approach yields measurable improvements in both internal and external performance. Consequently, we propose effective substitutions for Arabic and English words within ACS text and suggest that lexical substitution-based data augmentation holds great promise for training data-driven models on this underexplored linguistic domain. We introduce a generalized $\lambda$-deformation characterized by a map $\lambda: \Sigma \to \Lambda S^1$. Applying this deformation to two prominent $T$-dual models—the $T$-dual of the $AdS_3 \times S^3 \times S^1/\mathbb{Z}_2$ WZW model and the $T$-dual of the WZW model defined on $SU(2) \times SU(2)/U(1)$—yields families of non-trivial integrable membranes. These families encompass various supersymmetric configurations, including straight lines, helices, and membranes that oscillate periodically within the deformation space $\Sigma \times \Lambda S^1$. A distinguishing characteristic of these oscillating periodic integrable membranes is the presence of singularities in their equations of motion; however, we demonstrate that these singularities are benign and do not disrupt the validity of the equations of motion. Furthermore, we establish that maps possessing vanishing deformation velocity—whether periodic or fixed—remain both stationary and periodic. All solutions identified here exhibit novel features and differ significantly from their two-dimensional counterparts. This discovery suggests that membrane physics within generalized $\lambda$-deformations is substantially richer and more diverse than that of its 2D variant. Additionally, we investigate membranes with constant deformation velocity and construct 3-dimensional maps that are not solutions to the equations of motion but facilitate the analysis of these constant-velocity deformations. Our methodology relies on establishing the existence of a local bi-Hermitian structure on $M$ derived from a bi-Hermitian structure on $\tilde{M}$ and a map $\tilde{\lambda}: \tilde{\Sigma} \to \Lambda S^1$ satisfying a specific differential equation involving $\lambda: \Sigma \to \Lambda S^1$. This finding is crucial for constructing integrable membranes in generalized $\lambda$-deformations. Our findings offer a new perspective on non-Abelian T-duality and may prove valuable in string theory research. These calculations provide a foundational framework for exploring quantum membranes in these backgrounds. We introduce a straightforward technique for validating and enhancing the quality of hex meshes. Our approach links and processes hexagons within a 3D coordinate system to construct and manipulate a tets forest, a technique we term "HexTo" (short for "Hexagons to Tets"). This method is simple, rapid, and offers a robust quality metric, enabling the development of an automatic optimizer, "TetsBackToHex," for counteracting the inherent anisotropy of hex meshes. The transformation process introduces tets with quality exceeding 0.58, which is sufficient for our anisotropic Laplacian smoothing algorithm to effectively remove mesh anisotropy. To our knowledge, the 0.58 quality threshold is the highest reported for spring-based smoothing. Furthermore, the resulting optimized meshes maintain perfect hexagons, avoiding the need for non-manifold meshing or tetrahedralization. Our findings are demonstrated on a variety of models, including the "bunny" and "sue" scans, as well as anisotropic meshes derived from finite element discretizations. The entire methodology is highly efficient, supporting real-time optimization on a GPU. Our code is released under the BSD 3-Clause License and is available on GitHub. Relation extraction (RE) focuses on identifying the relationship between a pair of entities within a specific sentence. While prior research demonstrates that pre-trained language models significantly enhance RE performance, optimizing these models remains an ongoing challenge. This study investigates the impact of knowledge graph link prediction tasks, utilizing the same base language models, on relation extraction. The research aims to determine if incorporating link prediction can boost RE performance and to understand how different tasks influence RE within pre-trained models. Experimental results indicate that simultaneously performing node classification and link prediction yields the most substantial improvements for RE, particularly when evaluated on the RE only metric. Furthermore, it has been observed that models fine-tuned to perform multiple tasks retain strong performance on single-task evaluations. These findings offer valuable insights for advancing relation extraction in the era of pre-trained language models. The code is accessible at https://github.

Subsequently, the parameters within this formula are extracted using Matlab's Curve Fitting Toolbox through minimization. The resulting model demonstrates high accuracy, with all coefficients determined fittingly across both multi-finger and single-finger inverter technologies. Furthermore, the model's validity across diverse technologies is confirmed, enabling its application in predicting inverter delay for unmeasured cases. This capability facilitates the use of the model in simulation tools to enhance technology scaling studies. Additionally, the model's sensitivity to coefficient variations is analyzed to predict delay trends across multiple technology nodes. Finally, the model is integrated into a sizing tool to determine optimal fan-in and fan-out values for minimizing delay. Incorporating this delay model into sizing tools yields superior results compared to simulations that exclude it. Ultimately, the findings indicate that modeling inverter delay via fan-in and fan-out is more effective than relying solely on current and power dissipation. Overall, the results presented in this work demonstrate significant improvements over traditional characterization methods. Specifically, the delay model developed in this study is more accurate than the one presented in [1]. Furthermore, predicting delay using fan-in and fan-out within the sizing tool produces better outcomes than predicting it using only current and power dissipation. Consequently, this research demonstrates notable advancements over traditional characterization approaches. The animacy category encompasses all objects visible in the natural world and includes specific subcategories such as faces, bodies, animals, and scenes. While prior research indicates that the ventral temporal cortex (VT) organizes these categories in a manner consistent with their prevalence in the natural world, the precise nature of this organization remains unclear. To address this gap, we examined fMRI data from 10 participants using a Bayesian hierarchical model to analyze how the VT encodes both distinct visual stimuli (e.g., faces, animals) and broader categories (e.g., animate, inanimate). Our findings demonstrate that the hierarchical framework, which integrates visual details with category knowledge, offers a more accurate description of neural representations than models relying solely on visual information. Furthermore, we identified a gradient in the correlation between the hierarchical model and neural activity across VT, suggesting a progression from visual processing to the animation hierarchy. Our results indicate that face-selective regions show the highest agreement with the hierarchical model, followed by animate and inanimate object-selective areas, with activity in scene-selective regions showing the lowest alignment. These insights deepen our understanding of VT functional architecture and underscore the essential role of Bayesian hierarchical models in advancing neural decoding techniques. Finally, we introduce a novel method for assessing the quality of neural representations for animate and inanimate categories, a technique that may prove valuable for future decoding applications. Overall, this study advances our comprehension of VT organization by revealing the existence and significance of the animation hierarchy. By applying Bayesian hierarchical models, we not only deepen our understanding of neural mechanisms but also enhance decoding accuracy. These advancements pave the way for decoding tasks involving inputs previously deemed impossible, such as novel scenes. Furthermore, our ability to accurately represent the animacy hierarchy enables the decoding of virtual reality experiences, including virtual faces, animals, landscapes, and indoor settings. These capabilities underscore the critical role of the animacy hierarchy in organizing neural representations of the visual world. By accurately decoding representations of the animacy hierarchy, we can investigate how the brain adapts to virtual reality and how animacy representations are utilized during this process. This paper introduces a novel numerical framework designed to automatically identify and eliminate numerical artifacts in simulation mesh deformation algorithms. The proposed approach, termed the "convex optimization-based structure-maintaining filter," is inherently structure-preserving and artifact-free. By framing mesh optimization as a convex problem, the method enhances the stability and reliability of simulations that rely on deforming meshes. Additionally, the filter is versatile, enabling the creation of a wide range of diverse and flexible structure-maintaining deformations. The section presenting experimental results offers substantial evidence of the filter's effectiveness and capability to maintain mesh structure. Finally, the broader implications and potential applications of this approach are explored. The computational methodology is fully automated, requiring no user intervention, and the results are reproducible. Furthermore, the paper provides a comprehensive summary of the formation and solution of the mesh optimization problem, detailing all necessary steps to enable readers to replicate the results and apply the filter to their own simulations. To facilitate this, an open-source library has been developed and made publicly available. Consequently, the framework is accessible and applicable to any simulation requiring deformable meshes, offering users a straightforward and user-friendly tool for enhancing their simulation stability and robustness. Users can easily adapt existing deformation algorithms by incorporating the structure-maintaining filter to achieve superior outcomes. The filter is compatible with any mesh deformation algorithm capable of creating a deforming mesh for the specific simulation problem. To demonstrate versatility, two distinct mesh deformation algorithms are employed in the presented results, and the application of the filter to both algorithms is illustrated. Users are encouraged to utilize either algorithm alongside the filter to achieve their own results. Ultimately, the structure-maintaining filter serves as a highly effective tool for users to enhance their own deformation algorithms, and its application has been widely explored to demonstrate its effectiveness.

Type-ax (Type-X) and Type-I X-ray bursts have been observed in MAXI J1535-571 by various X-ray observatories, though its nature as a black hole or neutron star remains uncertain. This study employs the Insight-HXMT to track the evolution of the corona within MAXI J1535-571 during the 2018 outburst, focusing on energy ranges from 10 to 80 keV. We identified low-frequency, quasi-periodic fluctuations (LFQPFs) classified as Type-C, which align with findings from other sources during outbursts. Our analysis reveals a decline in corona size as the source brightens, a trend consistent with prior research. Furthermore, we examined the correlations between soft and hard components and their joint evolution alongside LFQPFs, finding that the corona appears softer during outbursts. These results suggest that the corona in MAXI J1535-571 functions as a hot, optically thin region situated above the accretion disc. Finally, we explore the potential link between these observations and the observed evolution of spectral states. The source's mass is estimated at approximately 10.4 solar masses. This investigation is part of the Insight-HXMT Science Working Group 11 initiative. [abridged] Keywords: accretion, accretion discs, accretion, neutron stars, black hole candidates, X-rays: binaries. This study investigates cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning from scratch, specifically within scenarios of dynamic partner adaptation. In typical real-world teaming contexts, partners often exhibit dynamic adjustments to one another, necessitating reliable adaptation. To address this, the paper introduces a new social intrinsic incentive termed "transfer empowerment," which quantifies the impact of an agent's actions on its teammates' future rewards. The accompanying framework, iGET, is designed to efficiently learn a reliable re-acting policy that dynamically responds to a partner's adaptive behavior. Through extensive experiments on multi-agent grid games and a real-world mobile application, the results demonstrate that the proposed method effectively learns a robust policy capable of reliably responding to partners' dynamic adaptations. Identifying materials from images is crucial for remote sensing and planetary exploration. However, current deep learning methods struggle to identify materials with a high success rate without extensive training datasets. This paper introduces a data-efficient approach utilizing a state-of-the-art contrastive learning framework. To enable material identification through contrastive learning without the need for material labels, we employ physics-based rendering to generate synthetic data by simulating the optical properties of materials found in the training images. This synthetic data is then used to train a generative model, which helps minimize the distribution gap between the training and testing sets, thereby enabling one-shot identification of materials in unseen images. Experimental results demonstrate the method's effectiveness in identifying any material in images with only a single example, requiring no material-specific labels. Furthermore, the approach outperforms existing techniques in few-shot material identification scenarios. For instance, identifying all materials in the OpenEarth dataset using just one sample per material achieves an average accuracy of 86.2%, compared to 60.1% for the next best method. Additionally, identifying all materials in the M3DST dataset with a budget of 10 images per material yields an average accuracy of 92.0%, surpassing the best existing method by 14.4%. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/1000x1000/Contrastive-Material-Identification. Our findings highlight the promise of contrastive learning for achieving one-shot material identification and offer a promising path for future research in this field. The source code can be found at: https://github.com/1000x1000/Contrastive-Material-Identification. Our results demonstrate that contrastive learning is effective for identifying materials and paves a promising avenue for future research in this domain. Lie 2-algebras, also known as categorical Lie algebras, constitute an important instance of Lie n-algebras, which are the linear algebraic counterparts of Lie n-groups. Defined as strict Lie n-groups, they operate within the symmetric monoidal (cartesian) category of vector spaces. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of various characterizations and equivalent definitions of Lie 2-algebras. Furthermore, we demonstrate how to construct a Lie 2-algebra from a strict crossed module of Lie algebras and its dual construction, derived from a cohomological perspective. Our primary focus remains on translating concepts from the theory of Lie groups and crossed modules into the language of Lie 2-algebras. Ultimately, we present the cohomology theory for Lie 2-algebras, which classifies extensions of this type of algebra, analogous to the role of cohomology in classifying Lie n-group extensions. We introduce a new end-to-end model for keypoint-based image matching, characterized by a global descriptor focused on local image attributes. Unlike traditional methods, our approach relies solely on global descriptors to generate interest points, eliminating the need for separate detectors. This strategy significantly reduces the number of interest points, thereby lowering computational costs and improving performance. To achieve this, we employ a transformer-based descriptor matching module that establishes direct, coarse-to-fine correspondence between local attributes across two images, bypassing the reliance on keypoint localization. Additionally, a multi-scale feature extraction network generates robust interest points and descriptors from low-resolution inputs, resulting in a smaller set of high-quality keypoints. Extensive evaluations on public datasets demonstrate that LoFTR achieves state-of-the-art results in end-to-end image matching, speed, and memory efficiency. Algorithms used to derive vector magnetic field data from the images of the Interface Boundary Observatory's [I]maging Spectropolarimeter [I]V (BIS) consistently display bias in both the inclination angle and horizontal field magnitude. This bias stems from the physical interaction between the instrument's input optics and the Sun's diffuse background, which causes off-axis light to scatter into the focal plane. We demonstrate that the bias in inferred inclination is directly proportional to the magnitude of this scattered light. By examining the geometry of the scattered light's incidence on the solar disk, we identify a "scattered-light shadow" that moves across the both polar input lenses as the Sun traverses the sky. This shadow is most prominent near the meridian and casts the most significant shade on the southern hemisphere of the disk. Consequently, bias in inferred inclination is most severe on the southern hemisphere when the scattered-light shadow intersects the scattered-light path. This phenomenon is clearly evident in time-series data collected as the scattered-light shadow crosses the southern hemisphere. We also observe a corresponding bias in the inferred horizontal field magnitude, which is strongly correlated with that magnitude. Finally, we introduce a correction method that effectively mitigates this bias in both inferred quantities. This approach is straightforward to implement and can be easily integrated into existing inversion algorithms for future data collection. This is particularly relevant for the upcoming Solar [O]bservatory for Lunar and Solar [O]bservations (SOLIS) VI mission, which will employ BIS instruments to deliver high-quality vector magnetic field data for the interplanetary medium. This anticipated data is essential for solar physicists and solar dynamo theorists to refine their models of solar magnetic fields. We demonstrate the efficacy of this correction method on data collected during SOLIS' first year of operations. Our findings indicate a substantial reduction in bias, with mean errors in both inferred quantities dropping from 15° to 2°. Furthermore, we show that a previously reported correlation between inferred inclination and Sunspot Region Magnetic Flux Density is significantly diminished after applying this correction. This correlation was previously attributed to scattering effects, as the bias in inferred inclination is more pronounced when scattered light is present. Ultimately, we conclude that SOLIS' VI instruments will be able to provide high-quality vector magnetic field data for the interplanetary medium, provided that a correction for scattered light is applied. We also note that a similar correction is applicable to all current SOLIS instruments. We have developed a generic correction method that can be easily adapted for use with any SOLIS instrument. This study introduces a novel demand-side management framework where consumers determine both their energy consumption levels and pricing. To ensure privacy, consumers utilize an aggregative game to independently select a pricing strategy without disclosing consumption data to the provider. The service provider then uses this strategy to set rates for each time slot. Concurrently, consumers act as players maximizing their own utility by scheduling energy apportionment and billing prices, while also optimizing their individual costs by minimizing payment and maximizing the value of deferred energy use. To evaluate the proposed method, we developed an intelligent demand-side monitoring system equipped with advanced sensing capabilities. This system gathers consumption data to estimate aggregative strategies and reveals the sensing protocol. Finally, through extensive simulations involving both synthetic and real-world data, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach. Our results indicate that the framework successfully incentivizes consumers to adopt pricing strategies that mitigate peak demand, thereby enhancing overall system efficiency. Furthermore, the results confirm the framework's effectiveness even when aggregative estimates contain significant noise. The experiments also show that the sensing protocol achieves near-optimal performance with a minimal number of sensors. This study examines the impact of numerical errors on the weak and strong convergence rates within von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem. By substituting the exact spectral measure with an approximate one, the associated error in convergence rates can be quantified. Additionally, we introduce and analyze the lazy projection method, a variant of Yudin's Nesterov acceleration technique. This approach aims to enhance the weak convergence rate for von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem when applied to self-adjoint operators. In the context of quantum measurements, this theory offers a pathway to accelerate the convergence of state vectors toward their target subspaces. Notably, our analysis demonstrates that the lazy projection method requires no additional computation relative to the original von Neumann dynamics. Finally, we present specific applications of this theory for a quantum search algorithm. In this application, the lazy projection method functions as a modification to the Grover algorithm, effectively accelerating the strong convergence rate of the search vector toward the target state. We also evaluate the computational cost of these acceleration methods and conduct numerical simulations to validate the theoretical predictions. Furthermore, we address the impact of lazy projection on the search vector's overlap with other eigenstates and demonstrate that this overlap can be minimized by appropriately selecting the parameter for the lazy projection method. Finally, the computational cost analysis for lazy projection is also considered.

To effectively compare morphological complexity across languages, one must first understand the specific properties these complexity metrics aim to assess. However, validating the hypotheses underlying grammatical complexity theories remains a significant challenge. This study utilizes hidden Markov models to characterize complexity within an established typology and probabilistic grammars. By employing probabilistic grammars as proxies for specific languages, the research validates the foundational hypotheses of grammatical complexity and evaluates the accuracy of various complexity measures in identifying particular grammatical properties. The outcomes indicate that no single measure is entirely accurate; rather, a combination of different measures is required to adequately cover a language's entire grammatical property set. Furthermore, certain proposed hypotheses are contradicted by as few as 10 probabilistic grammars, underscoring a critical need for validation using larger typological datasets. Finally, the study demonstrates that grammatical complexity can be quantified through morphological inventories, aspectual systems, and agreement mechanisms. These inventories are linked to language family size and geographic distribution, suggesting that languages with greater complexity are more likely to belong to larger families and wider geographic groups. Consequently, languages have evolved toward greater complexity by acquiring additional morphological features rather than losing existing ones. These insights enhance our comprehension of language complexity and inform our analysis of how languages are grouped into families and are distributed across regions. We investigate the lensing effects of substructure in the dark matter halos of galaxy clusters, focusing on the impact of small-scale subhalos on weak lensing signals. Our analysis reveals that the abundance of subhalos can be constrained by measuring the weak lensing power spectrum across scales of $\sim 100-500 \, h^{-1}$ Mpc. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for both $\Lambda$CDM and self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) models, subhalo abundances align with cold dark matter (CDM) predictions up to an overdensity threshold of $\Delta \rho / \rho \lesssim 10^{-3}$. However, SIDM models predict a more pronounced suppression of subhalo density at higher overdensities compared to CDM. This occurs because subhalos in SIDM models tend to lose mass through scattering interactions with the smooth intracluster medium, whereas subhalos in CDM models remain isolated from the surrounding medium. Consequently, subhalos in SIDM models are less susceptible to stripping by tides or dynamical friction. Finally, our findings indicate that subhalo abundances in SIDM models can be well approximated by reinterpreting $\Lambda$CDM halo mass functions, provided the halo mass is substituted with the halo mass within an inner boundary that excludes the region affected by subhalo stripping. This approach effectively bypasses the distinct accretion histories of subhalos in CDM and SIDM scenarios. Overall, our results suggest that current and upcoming weak lensing surveys can significantly enhance constraints on SIDM models, thereby strengthening the case for self-interacting dark matter. Additionally, we find that subhalo abundances in SIDM models are consistent with observations of galaxy rotation curves and dwarf spheroidal galaxies. In contrast, stellar or dynamical lenses are unlikely to contribute substantially to the specific weak lensing scales examined in this study. Future weak lensing surveys will further refine constraints on subhalo properties in galaxy clusters, potentially advancing our understanding of dark matter. Our analysis also serves as a proof of concept for using weak lensing to study dark matter properties within intracluster gas. Finally, our findings are directly applicable to studying subhalo abundances in virialized dwarf and giant elliptical galaxies, as well as dwarf and galaxy clusters, given their similar dynamical histories. This is particularly relevant for SIDM models, where subhalo abundances are primarily determined by the density of the intracluster medium.

This paper establishes new findings for nonlinear elliptic equations defined on $C^2$ domains in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and utilizing measures as right-hand sides. Specifically, we demonstrate the existence of a unique weak solution that satisfies a H\"older continuity estimate. As a secondary application, we derive the existence and uniqueness of solutions for the polyharmonic operator, where the solution exhibits a logarithmic Hölder continuity condition. Additionally, we investigate the existence and uniqueness of weak solutions for an elliptic operator that includes the square root of the Laplacian, again employing surface measures on the boundary as source terms. Our approach relies fundamentally on establishing appropriate Hölder estimates for the fractional Laplacian within bounded domains, a result we prove in a separate publication. The proofs for our primary results are entirely self-contained. Our methodology integrates various techniques, including weighted Sobolev-Poincaré inequalities, potential theory, and estimates for the Laplacian with surface measures, all of which are utilized in their full capacity. We also provide several novel and potentially useful lemmas and theorems that may have broader applications. Notably, in the final section, we present a novel and significant result regarding the existence and uniqueness of weak solutions for elliptic operators involving $\sqrt{-\Delta}$. This represents a substantial advancement over prior work, as it extends these findings to cases where the right-hand side is a surface measure on the boundary. Furthermore, our methodology appears well-suited for addressing broader classes of nonlinear elliptic equations. Finally, we demonstrate the applicability of our results to nonlocal elliptic equations, thereby extending existing literature in this area. This work introduces a novel material model designed to identify cobalt-abundant compounds within the Y-Co-B system. By integrating an evolutionary search algorithm with an electrostatic material model, we successfully synthesized new materials featuring high Co concentrations. The minimum energy structures derived from this approach were subsequently analyzed using density functional theory. Among the resulting ground states, several are anticipated to exhibit superconductivity. Furthermore, we provide detailed characterizations of a number of these superconducting materials. Notably, YCo$_{2.5}$Fe$_{0.5}$-based compounds demonstrate exceptionally large Pauli susceptibility, indicating a significant influence from nonmagnetic impurities. Additionally, YCo$_{2}$-based materials are predicted to possess a substantial density of states at the Fermi level. These findings underscore the model's efficacy in discovering unconventional superconductors within this material family. Finally, our results align well with existing experimental data, and we have identified several promising candidates for future experimental investigation. Specifically, YCo$_{2}$-based materials are predicted to exhibit metallic behavior, while YCo$_{2.5}$Fe$_{0.5}$-based compounds are expected to display semiconducting properties. This represents a distinct example of the similarity principle applied to magnetic materials. Furthermore, YCo$_{2}$-based compounds are anticipated to be paramagnetic, whereas YCo$_{2.5}$Fe$_{0.5}$-based compounds are predicted to display itinerant ferromagnetism. These outcomes underscore the robustness of the proposed model. Ultimately, the study demonstrates the model's capability to identify a range of stable materials exhibiting diverse physical properties within the Y-Co-B-Fe system. The discovered materials are characterized by a combination of high T$_c$, semiconducting behavior, and a moderate density of states at the Fermi level. These attributes are highly desirable for Josephson junctions and thin-film devices. Consequently, this approach offers a promising avenue for developing new materials in this category. A comprehensive database of these materials is available at http://www.dam.bristol.ac.uk/DCM/Database/YCoBFe.html. Risk-aware bidding is essential for effective participation in competitive bidding auctions, yet its complexity, combined with the need for real-time decision-making, makes developing practical tools highly non-trivial. This study addresses these challenges by introducing an adaptive, risk-aware bidding framework tailored for display advertising auctions. Unlike existing approaches, our method explicitly accounts for budget constraints, aiming to maximize benefit while ensuring the total spend remains within the allocated budget. We evaluate bidding strategies based on risk aversion and introduce ARAR, an novel algorithm that utilizes ad impressions to dynamically adjust bid prices in real time. Through numerical simulations, we demonstrate that our approach surpasses current state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, adaptive risk-aware bidding not only boosts revenue but also enhances the quality of competitive bidding across all relevant sectors. Additionally, our tool is accessible as an open-source software package on GitHub. To our knowledge, this remains the first software implementation of adaptive risk-aware bidding for display advertising. Classical particles follow a single trajectory, whereas quantum particles are described by a wavefunction that can be expressed in different bases. A notable example is the quasi-probability distribution within phase space, which can display negative values. It has been established that if all possible trajectories are considered, every feature of a quantum system can be accounted for classically using these as the fundamental variables. This raises a compelling question: do specific subsets of wavefunction realizations, which exhibit fewer classical negatives in their wavefunction-based trajectories, offer a guidance-based trajectory description? In this work, we examine how Wigner negativity influences mixing and measurement within both open and closed quantum systems. We conclude by addressing the implications of these findings for the study of quantum guidance. arXiv:2101.03004v1 [quant-ph] 7 Jan 2021.

In the two-way limit analysis of quantum key distribution, a fundamental condition for condition-number limit analysis involves selecting a random seed for privacy amplification from a non-uniform marginal distribution derived from a source key, which is subsequently conditioned. This study establishes that the achievable secret key rate remains invariant whether this random seed is generated locally or externally. This insight resolves the previously open problem regarding the secure key rate attainability using an external random seed under this analysis method. Furthermore, the proposed analysis framework is applicable to the one-way limit analysis utilizing random degenerate LO operations. As a practical application, the achievable secret key rate for quantum key distribution over twisted-pair telecommunication lines is calculated for a concrete concrete example. The results indicate that the secret key rate using an externally generated random seed under the one-way limit analysis with random degenerate LO operations is equivalent to that achieved via the two-way limit analysis with source key post-processing. Additionally, it is demonstrated that the secret key rate under the one-way limit analysis with random degenerate LO operations can be significantly larger than when post-processing is applied after key generation. Consequently, this confirms the superior performance of employing externally generated random seeds for privacy amplification. To achieve high secret key rates, it is essential to utilize externally generated random seeds for privacy amplification, even in scenarios involving high-transmission-fidelity two-way communication. This conclusion is supported by the limit analysis method. Furthermore, the research suggests that new key generation methods should be explored to achieve high secret key rates. To achieve this, the limit analysis method serves as a valuable tool for evaluating the security of arbitrary key generation methods. The same conclusion holds true for the case of post-processing the output of quantum key distribution from a twisted pair. This paper introduces a generalized definition of Bertrand curves within the timelike domain and investigates the conditions under which a timelike curve and its corresponding Bertrand partner share a semi-metric distance. Finally, we examine the properties of both timelike Bertrand curves and non- Bertrand curves in this generalized sense. Although the study is conducted in a semi-metric framework, the proposed generalization remains applicable to Riemannian spaces. We anticipate that these results will be valuable for research into geometric properties and dynamics alongside physics and mathematics. We investigate the spin-dependent (SD) scattering of relativistic dark matter within the context of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) acoustic spectrum. Dark matter may possess a spin, enabling it to interact with thermal nucleons via SD forces. If the dark matter density is substantial and it possesses an anisotropic alignment with the baryon density, the SD scattering cross-section can significantly reduce the primordial free electron density. This reduction suppresses Thomson scattering, leading to increased CMB polarization and large-scale temperature anisotropies. Furthermore, we demonstrate that relativistic dark matter can transfer significant momentum to nucleons, causing a shift in the CMB temperature spectrum. Our analysis reveals that SD interactions with nucleons can generate a notable temperature dip at the first acoustic peak while simultaneously boosting polarization amplitudes. These effects could be observable in current or upcoming CMB datasets, offering a distinct signature for SD dark matter interactions. Additionally, we explore how these phenomena might be leveraged to constrain SD cross-sections using existing CMB measurements. Finally, we examine the potential of future experiments, such as the Simons Observatory and the Cosmic Stage 4 initiative, to further probe SD interactions with relativistic dark matter. This research offers a novel framework for investigating dark matter properties through precision cosmological observations. Our findings indicate that SD interactions with relativistic dark matter can substantially alter the thermal history of the universe, potentially explaining the unexpectedly low free electron density measured by cosmic microwave background observations. This could help resolve tensions between cosmological and laboratory determinations of interstellar electron density. We also highlight that SD interactions with dark matter could provide a new perspective on the electron reionization process. Our results suggest that relativistic dark matter is a viable candidate for generating additional ionization, thereby reducing the required degree of reionization to align with observational data. These findings underscore the critical role that relativistic dark matter could play in the ionization history of the universe. Our study highlights the necessity of incorporating relativistic dark matter into cosmological models, as it could significantly influence the thermal evolution of cosmic plasma. This note employs Faulhaber's Formula to demonstrate the rapid convergence of the alternating series defining the odd Bernoulli numbers at $n=1, 2, 3, 4$. It further utilizes Faulhaber's formula, alongside the Faulhaber-Faulhaber correspondence and the Prouhet-Tarry-Escott problem, to elucidate the structure of the non-alternating series for these same odd Bernoulli numbers. The approach is grounded in a direct proof of Faulhaber's formula that avoids the standard induction method. Additionally, the text briefly outlines an application of the Prouhet-Thompson sequence, which is linked to the Prouhet-Tarry-Escott problem, in deriving the structure of the odd Bernoulli numbers $B_{1}, B_{2}, B_{3}, B_{4}$. The note concludes with a discussion of an open conjecture concerning the relationship between Faulhaber's formula and the Prouhet-Thompson sequence. This formulation serves as an alternative to the conventional induction proof of Faulhaber's formula, potentially offering students a more intuitive and efficient means of grasping the structure of odd Bernoulli numbers. It is anticipated that this perspective will prove valuable to mathematicians and educators in mathematics education. Reward learning offers a promising approach for training reinforcement learning agents by utilizing human feedback. However, existing methods often require training on large datasets, resulting in significant training time expenditures. This paper addresses this issue through three key contributions. First, we demonstrate that data sorting can substantially reduce training time without compromising performance by ensuring that early samples are more informative than later ones. Second, we introduce a visual inspection method for human feedback, which enhances both the quality of the information and reduces the time needed to provide it. Third, we propose a novel reward learning framework called Cluster Reward Learning (CRL), which combines data sorting with visual inspection. We present an efficient algorithm for CRL based on visually aided cluster ranking and prove its convergence. Experiments across eight continuous control environments demonstrate that CRL achieves superior sample efficiency compared to state-of-the-art reward learning techniques. Furthermore, we validate that our method effectively reduces training time through both theoretical analysis and empirical evidence. Overall, we show that data sorting and visual inspection work synergistically to provide substantial sample savings and time efficiency. The source code and experimental results are available at https://github.com/ChengdaLi1996/CLF. Our implementation is also integrated into OpenAI Gym's new reward learning API, which supports popular data sorting techniques such as heuristic Bellman decomposition, maximum likelihood estimation, and preference learning. This API significantly lowers the barrier to entry for researchers interested in exploring reward learning. Within the framework of noncommutative space-time, we investigate nucleon structure characteristics, including Dirac and magnetic form factors, the axial vector form factor, and flavor-dependent nonlocal vector form factors. It is demonstrated that flavor-dependent form factors exhibit distinct characteristics even at low energies. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that flavor-dependent contributions can significantly influence flavor separation uncertainties regarding partial quark momentum fractions. Current global fits indicate a preference for the momentum distribution of anti-quarks within the nucleon to be heavily suppressed in noncommutative space-time. These findings suggest a need to re-examine the momentum distribution of anti-quarks in nucleons, particularly within the context of the anti-quark gluon condensate. Finally, our results establish a lower bound for the noncommutative parameter as $10^{-33}~\mathrm{GeV}^{-2}$. This bound is derived by utilizing the bound for the anti-quark gluon condensate established in arXiv:1903.07100 [hep-ph]. Additionally, we propose that the lower bound for the noncommutative parameter could be enhanced by incorporating data from the flavor-moment of the nucleon. Specifically, we utilize the flavor-moment dataset from the PACMAN collaboration [arXiv:1709.00004 [nucl-ex]] and the flavor-momentum data from the DIS collaboration [arXiv:1709.00002 [nucl-ex]]. The central value for the lower bound is determined to be $10^{-29}~\mathrm{GeV}^{-2}$, utilizing the flavor-momentum data from the DIS collaboration. We also calculate the flavor momentum fraction $\bar{x}_u(x)$ for the up anti-quark, which is found to be significantly smaller than the up quark momentum fraction $x_u(x)$. This calculation relies on the first moment of the flavor momentum distribution, $\Delta E_q$, derived from the flavor momentum data provided by the DIS collaboration. We also determine $\bar{x}_d(x)$ for the down anti-quark, noting that it is not significantly suppressed compared to the down quark momentum fraction $x_d(x)$. The down quark momentum fraction $x_d(x)$ is derived using the down quark momentum distribution $d(x_d)$ from the DIS collaboration, which is based on their flavor-momentum data. We recommend that future research utilize the flavor-momentum data from the DIS collaboration

This study examines the Toric code on a triangular lattice within the regge limit, demonstrating that the star operators simplify to the form $ZZZZ\ldots Z$. The resulting Hamiltonian is highly frustrated, yet its ground state remains degenerate with degree four, characteristic of a topologically ordered phase. Furthermore, we offer a graphical depiction of the star operator utilizing the zigzag graph, which is the regge limit of the Potts graph. Within this framework, the star operator is represented by the collection of $ZZZ\ldots Z$ operators situated on a graph featuring the greatest diameter among all graphs sharing the same boundary. This finding suggests an extension of the Nussinov theorem to the regge limit, positing that a "geometric line" emerges in this limit. We also propose a method for embedding the regge-limit star operator into a hierarchy of quantum states, thereby generating a family of gapped Hamiltonians capable of describing ground states in the topologically ordered phase. Additionally, we investigate the properties of the topologically degenerate states in this system, revealing that they differ in their linking numbers, which vary both classically and within the regge limit. Finally, we outline a pathway to generalize these findings beyond the regge limit. These results are derived through a classical analysis of the Potts model, a quantum operator algebraic approach, and a direct verification of the star operator on the smallest system. Surprisingly, all derived conclusions remain valid in the limit of zero Potts weight, even though the star operator fails to maintain the $ZZZ\ldots Z$ form in this specific limit. To address this discrepancy, we introduce the concept of "quasi-geometric lines," which are more prevalent than their quantum counterparts. The paper concludes with a discussion of these findings and their broader implications. This work was conducted in collaboration with J. Sun, Y. Zhang, and Z. We investigate the $\sigma$-model approximation for a class of "interlaced" or "complex interlaced" random band matrices, extending findings previously established for real interlaced random band matrices. These interlaced matrices consist of free random band matrices perturbed at specific sites by a finite-rank complex matrix possessing zero mean. We demonstrate that this specific class of perturbation suffices to characterize the universal properties of arbitrary finite-rank interlaced random band matrices. The sigma-model action is derived from a self-consistent equation involving an auxiliary matrix that serves as the coupling constant. The universal large-$N$ behavior of interlaced random band matrices is subsequently obtained via the saddle-point method. Finally, we confirm that the universal properties of weakly interlaced random band matrices align with the saddle-point approximation of the sigma-model action. Additionally, the weak interlacing scenario is examined within the sigma-model framework. In the limit of large interaction $D$, we demonstrate the localizability of the system. However, for arbitrary interaction $D$, we show that the large-$N$ behavior corresponds to a deformed Wigner semi-circle law, consistent with the saddle-point approximation. This study extends the methodology developed in arXiv:1905.07704 to the case of complex interlaced random band matrices. While the large-$N$ behavior remains identical in both cases, the definition of the interlaced matrices differs: in the real case, perturbations are real symmetric matrices, whereas in the complex case, they are general finite-rank complex matrices. This distinction leads to a significant difference in the sigma-model approximation. In the real case, the coupling constant is a single real number; conversely, in the complex case, it is a matrix with $2+2D$ elements. Consequently, in the complex case, we can derive a more general large-$N$ behavior for arbitrary $D$ by solving a more general self-consistent equation. We explicitly solve this equation for $D=0$ and $D=-1$. Furthermore, we establish that the sigma-model approximation yields a deformed Wigner semi-circle law for the large-$N$ behavior of complex interlaced random band matrices, thereby confirming a conjecture regarding real interlaced random band matrices. Finally, we show that the large-$N$ behavior of complex interlaced random band matrices is universal and independent of the specific nature of the perturbation matrices. We investigate a novel, meaning-permutation-invariant objective for pre-training on dialogue utterances, which links surface forms to semantic representations without relying on noisy annotations. This approach models the dialogue pre-training task as a game involving two players: a speaker who perceives words as a permutation of meanings, and a listener who must infer these meanings from the observed vocabulary. Consequently, the model is trained to identify utterance permutations that align with the listener's internal meaning space. Experiments on the CoSIE and SimpleDialog datasets demonstrate that our method generates stronger semantic representations for dialogue understanding, outperforming baseline objectives that connect utterances to either out-of-domain or in-domain semantic representations. Additionally, we find that our objective effectively links surface forms to both dialogue and general domain semantics in a shared representation space. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/taehyunglee/MDL.

Algorithmic interpretability is essential for establishing trust and confidence in machine learning (ML) systems. However, the current landscape of definitions and metrics for algorithmic interpretability is fragmented and lacks a unified framework. This paper proposes a research agenda for creating a comprehensive, unified model of algorithmic interpretability, grounded in human learning theories and supported by a literature review. We present a model where algorithmic interpretability is quantified by the cognitive complexity required to learn the input-output behavior of ML algorithms. This approach is demonstrated using childhood education materials, such as the Cognitive Assessment Test (CAT) and Stanford-Binet tests, which have been widely employed to assess human cognitive development. The proposed model and metrics offer a robust foundation for future research into algorithmic interpretability. Specifically, we introduce the Cognitive Assessment Test (CAT) score as a metric for algorithmic interpretability and illustrate its application through a case study involving ML-based medical diagnosis systems. Additionally, we demonstrate that algorithmic interpretability metrics can be derived from general human learning models. Finally, we show that algorithmic fairness metrics can also be formulated based on these proposed metrics for ML interpretability. This research aims to foster a holistic and unified research direction for algorithmic interpretability. The code and codebooks for the case study are available at: https://github.com/ChinmayKale/ML-CAT. Our findings indicate that the cognitive complexity of ML algorithms can be effectively measured using educational tests originally designed for children. This demonstrates the viability of our approach and provides a practical example of how to evaluate the cognitive complexity of ML algorithms. The proposed research framework establishes a unified and holistic foundation for algorithmic interpretability, aligning with educational theories and cognitive development models. By providing a clear and comprehensive understanding of algorithmic interpretability, we offer a solid basis for advancing research in this critical domain. Our work demonstrates that a model of algorithmic interpretability, derived from human learning theories, can serve as a viable and effective foundation for further investigation. Anomaly detection remains a critical challenge in numerous real-world applications, particularly when anomalies are rare and data is unbalanced. Isolation Forest (iF) is a popular anomaly detection method that excels in unsupervised and semi-supervised settings by isolating data points to cluster them effectively. However, the inherent tree structure of iF presents significant computational hurdles, including high memory usage and slow training times, which limit its applicability in resource-constrained environments. This paper introduces TiWS-iForest, a novel approach designed to overcome these limitations. By integrating the principles of the Wolf Shear (TiWS) algorithm into iF, we enhance its computational efficiency regarding execution time, memory consumption, and scalability. TiWS-iForest operates by sampling small, localized patches of the original dataset to train tree sub-samples, thereby reducing computational costs. We evaluated this method across various anomaly detection benchmarks, comparing its performance against state-of-the-art iF variants. Our results demonstrate that TiWS-iForest delivers competitive accuracy while significantly improving computational performance, making it ideal for demanding applications such as TinyML and FPGAs. Furthermore, we illustrate its effectiveness in unusual TiWS-iForest scenarios, including large-scale anomaly detection and anomaly detection within small, localized datasets. This paper introduces a novel statistical framework for analyzing extreme values that aligns with the point pattern component of a Poisson process. By reparameterizing the intensity function through extreme value theory constraints, the model gains the flexibility to incorporate covariates at both block and within-block levels. This approach unifies the methodologies of peak-over-threshold and block maxima analysis. A Bayesian perspective enables the simultaneous estimation of the shape and scale functions while inferring jump points to capture the underlying intensity. These results are applied to determine optimal thresholds for peak-over-threshold analysis and to classify weather systems responsible for extreme precipitation. Furthermore, a specific model implementation is utilized to assess the consistency of jump point estimates derived from bootstrapped posterior samples. This analysis is performed on two datasets: simulated data from a known Poisson process and the High Resolution Environment and Climate Data (HR-ESD) from the European Climate Data and Research Centre (CDR). The findings of the HR-ESD analysis are compared against traditional peak-over-threshold and block maxima methodologies. Additionally, a Shiny application is made available to facilitate the use of the Poisson process reparameterization. Finally, a discussion addresses potential extensions of this work. Recent advancements in Natural Language Processing (NLP) have significantly boosted the role of knowledge graphs, which offer structured context for enhancing model performance. While recent years have seen growing interest in learning representations from vast statistical data, there remains significant potential for leveraging curated common-sense knowledge graphs like AtOMIC (Alice in Wonderland Temporal Movie Instance Annotation) and MaRIa (MIT Movie Relational Annotation) to aid model design. These resources capture multimodal knowledge regarding events, actions, and their relationships. This paper presents the COMET-ATOMIC 2020 shared task, organized under ACL 2020, aimed at advancing two critical research directions: representing common-sense knowledge graphs using symbolic methods and integrating them with deep neural networks. Both directions focus on video question answering. Participants were tasked with inferring action classes from video clips by utilizing the structural knowledge encoded in these graphs. The competition featured two tracks: Symbolic and Hybrid, with 30 teams registered. This shared task highlights ongoing efforts to harmonize symbolic and sub-symbolic approaches within knowledge graphs and NLP. The paper details the datasets, evaluation metrics, and baseline methods, while also summarizing the performance of participating teams. Finally, it offers a comprehensive analysis of the results, particularly for the Hybrid track, and outlines key lessons for future work. A repository of code and data is available at: https://github.com/comet-kb/comet-atomictask2020. The findings are expected to guide ongoing and future research into applying common-sense knowledge graphs to NLP. Website: https://comet-kb.github.io/comet-atomictask2020. This article outlines the pipeline developed to manage data reduction and compression for the Hi-GAL survey, a comprehensive survey of star-forming regions conducted with the HIFI instrument on the Herschel Space Observatory. Designed to facilitate both online reduction and interactive data access, the pipeline produces compressed, calibration-reduced data in FITS format. The initial release of this pipeline was published in *Herschel Science Operations Status Report*, and it has since undergone further development and refinement. This paper describes those updates and demonstrates the pipeline's functionality through a series of examples. Additionally, we illustrate how users can access and analyze the resulting data via the Hi-GAL Data Archive. We argue that the approach presented here offers a flexible framework suitable for similar data pipelines, and we conclude by highlighting potential future enhancements. The source code is available at https://github.com/Hi-GAL/HiGAL_Pipeline. The repository also includes a collection of demonstration data files. Specifically, a FITS file containing calibration-reduced, compressed Hi-GAL data is available for download from the Hi-GAL Data Archive at https://archive.higal-survey.org/index.php?d=20120612T111111&i=HISS_20120612T111111_001. This file covers the HISS observation of the NGC1333-IR21 source at 160.0 GHz (400.0 um) within the HI-GAL survey. Accessing this file triggers the online data reduction pipeline, resulting in a new HI-GAL data release. To showcase this reduced data, users can visit https://archive.higal-survey.org/plotter/, which displays the data in FITS, SPY, and JPEG formats and provides plotting tools for 1D and 2D data. This platform also supports the creation of Hi-GAL survey plots for publication. Furthermore, users can access and plot HI-GAL data in SPY and JPEG formats via the Hi-GAL Survey Web Portal at https://www.higal-survey.org/. This service integrates with the Hi-GAL Data Archive and offers plotting capabilities for 1D and 2D data, including a plotting tool for HI-GAL survey data in FITS format.
