We have conducted a high-precision spectroscopic analysis of the metallicity within the most probable first-generation stars of NGC 2808. Our study targets 10 red clump members, selected based on their low variability amplitude and positions along the horizontal branch, utilizing ground-based spectra from the FLAMES-UVES instrument. By employing a multi-component stellar model that accounts for binary companions, we achieve minimal uncertainties in line flux measurements. These precise fluxes enable the use of multiple abundance indicators, which are subsequently corrected for stellar rotation and surface convection effects. Our results reveal a high-precision metallicity spread of $\Delta Z = 0.007 \pm 0.003$ dex across the sample. This confirms the existence of multiple distinct populations within the red clump region of the color-magnitude diagram, demonstrating that FLAMES-UVES can resolve such subtle metallic differences in globular clusters. This finding supports the theory of mixed old populations characterized by varying helium and metal contents. Furthermore, our study establishes the first reliable metallicity scale for red clump stars in NGC 2808. We also identify a correlation between metallicity and radial position, consistent with earlier studies of this cluster. Finally, we compare our derived abundances with those of young and red clump stars in the open cluster M67, finding that the two clusters exhibit similar metallicity spreads. This similarity suggests that the mechanisms responsible for creating these spreads operate universally across both old and young stellar populations. Additionally, the detection of a metallicity spread in NGC 2808 supports the hypothesis that the horizontal branch morphology in this cluster is driven by variations in helium, metallicity, and mass. Consequently, the color-magnitude diagram of NGC 2808 is predicted to evolve into a more complex structure in the near future. This study serves as a proof-of-concept for the potential of FLAMES-UVES to resolve such subtle effects in globular clusters. Future observations of NGC 2808 using FLAMES-UVES are expected to provide further insights into the nature of its multiple populations. Our findings also underscore the necessity of obtaining high-precision abundances when analyzing binary stars in globular clusters. Finally, this work aims to establish a robust framework for future investigations into the horizontal branch morphology of NGC 2808. To facilitate these analyses, we have made our data and analysis tools publicly available. The paper concludes with a series of appendices. Appendix

The passage of ions across cellular membranes is a critical process for numerous biological functions, including signal transduction and transport. Ion channels facilitate this by enabling ions to overcome entropic barriers, allowing their diffusion. A fundamental yet unresolved issue in this domain is the statistical correlation between the diverse conformational states of ion channels and their associated kinetic parameters, such as residence times and exit time distributions. This paper introduces a novel conceptual framework to address these questions. We demonstrate that systems exhibiting single-file diffusion can be mapped onto effective single-file diffusion models, where the entropic sorting of ions within a cavity of arbitrary shape is governed by entropic forces. These forces are derived from the information content of ion size distributions. This approach enables the calculation of the duration statistics for the first exit of ions from membranes. Our findings indicate that duration distributions often deviate significantly from exponential patterns, regardless of the ion size distribution or the initial position of the leading ion, which is randomly selected. Specifically, we observe that durations typically display heavy tails, characterized by a power-law decay at large scales, and may also possess heavy heads, indicating an excess of very short durations. Furthermore, we establish a one-to-one correspondence between model parameters, ion size distributions, and the resulting properties of exit time distributions. These results offer a new perspective for analyzing and interpreting kinetic data, thereby enhancing our understanding of ion transport through membranes. Specifically, we demonstrate that exponential statistics emerge only under very specific conditions. Additionally, our findings suggest that the heavy tails of exit time distributions can be attributed to the suppression of high-entropy states, driven either by negative entropic forces or the distribution of ions near the system's entrance. This implies that the entire population of ions within a membrane does not contribute equally to the observed exponential statistics. Finally, we illustrate the potential of our framework to explain and predict kinetic data, as evidenced by the analysis of a previously published experimental measurement. These results offer a comprehensive understanding of the intricate relationship between ion size distributions, entropic sorting, and exit time statistics. Furthermore, they provide a new perspective on how to design synthetic ion channels to achieve desired transport properties. To achieve this, it is essential to understand the impact of ion size distributions on exit time statistics. Our results show that choosing an appropriate size distribution can yield ion currents with superior statistics, such as shorter average durations and reduced variability. These insights are broadly applicable to passive transport, offering a pathway to engineer synthetic ion channels with tailored characteristics. The proposed framework can serve as a foundation for optimizing synthetic ion channels to enhance their performance.

Quantum mechanics has remained largely consistent for over a century, largely because its mathematical framework is precise and unambiguous. However, interpreting the mathematics has been challenging for practitioners. Consequently, various approaches have emerged, each proposing distinct rules for inferring measurement outcomes. This paper introduces a new approach grounded in quantum mechanics' foundational principle: the consistency of measurement inferences. Specifically, the probability of a future measurement result is calculated using quantum Bayes' rule, derived as a necessary condition to maintain consistency between prior and future measurements. This framework is demonstrated using a single qubit as an example. The results indicate that quantum Bayes' rule ensures consistency, whereas other existing approaches do not. Additionally, the paper explores implications for interpreting quantum mechanics and quantum algorithms. Notably, since quantum algorithms rely on measurement inferences, their interpretation is hindered by the inconsistency found in those inferences. Therefore, we suggest that evaluating quantum algorithms should be based on quantum Bayes' rule. Finally, we outline potential applications of this framework within the broader context of quantum information theory. This could enhance our understanding of quantum information processing and offer a path to developing new quantum information technologies. Overall, by providing a unique interpretation of quantum mechanics, this work offers fresh insights into the long-standing challenge of interpreting the theory. By helping to advance our comprehension of quantum mechanics, we aim to foster new interpretations that could further push the boundaries of this remarkable theory. To demonstrate the framework's utility, we applied it to four specific scenarios: two regarding continuous-variable quantum information processing and two concerning the interpretation of quantum algorithms. These discussions illustrate the framework's potential to deepen our understanding of quantum mechanics. Thus, this work represents a significant step toward interpreting quantum mechanics, with the ultimate goal of continuing the remarkable journey of understanding this theory. Keywords: Quantum mechanics, Interpretation of quantum mechanics, Measurement inference, Quantum algorithm, Quantum information processing. This study reports initial findings regarding finite-volume effects on traceable observables, including the trace anomaly and the bulk viscosity to Equilibrium shear viscosity ratio. These observables are computed for systems ranging from small droplets of hot QCD to large finite volumes of the Universe, using anisotropic thermal lattice gauge theory to construct the chiral condensate. Our analysis indicates that the ratio of the trace anomaly to the square of the energy density approaches the infinite-volume limit as $L^3$ exceeds $\mathcal{O}(10)$ GeV$^3$. Furthermore, the chiral condensate exhibits a power-law convergence toward its infinite-volume value, with the coefficient of this power law scaling linearly with $L^3$. Finally, the $\eta/s$ ratio converges more rapidly than the trace anomaly, reaching the infinite-volume limit for systems with $L^3 \sim \mathcal{O}(1)$ GeV$^3$. Collectively, these results suggest that systems of the size of a GeV cube are sufficient to reliably describe the QCD phase diagram near the QCD phase transition temperature. These conclusions are supported by the successful reproduction of recent experimental data on elliptic flow and strangeness enhancement from ALICE at the LHC. The findings also have implications for cosmology, specifically regarding the production of primordial gravitational waves. In the context of lattice calculations, our results imply that systems with $L^3 \sim \mathcal{O}(1)$ GeV$^3$ are adequate to determine the thermal equation of state and transport coefficients necessary for modeling the gravitational wave spectrum generated by the QCD phase transition. Additionally, the thermal anisotropy of the thermal EMT tensor in the thermal equilibrium limit can be reconstructed from the thermal chiral condensator, providing a new method for measuring thermal anisotropy in small hot QCD systems. Finally, our results suggest that the small spatial extent of the localized hot QCD medium formed in heavy-ion collisions is not a significant source of uncertainty. Consequently, the discrepancies between theoretical predictions and experimental data, such as the suppression of strangeness production in small systems, must be attributed to physical properties of the QCD phase diagram rather than finite-size effects. This conclusion is consistent with the observation that systems smaller than $\sim 1$ fm$^3$ display a chiral condensator significantly lower than that of the hot, dense medium created in heavy-ion collisions. Thus, our findings provide a theoretical basis for the hypothesis of a strongly first-order phase

The Lyman-alpha line serves as a valuable tool for investigating the early universe, specifically by mapping the distribution of primordial gas clouds and measuring the evolution of the intergalactic medium. To conduct a comprehensive survey of Lyman-alpha emission, it is essential to develop a broadband filter that covers the entire Lyman series while effectively suppressing the Lyman limit below 1 Rydberg. This study presents the first astronomical photometry results obtained with a BaF$_2$ prism-based prototype Lyman-alpha filter designed for use on a solar telescope. By observing the solar photosphere, we demonstrate that the broadband Lyman-alpha filter accurately reproduces the Lyman series line spread function (LSF) and successfully blocks the Lyman limit. Furthermore, we examine the potential advantages of this novel filter technology for future space-based spectroscopy of high-redshift objects. Our findings indicate that the current prototype offers approximately 100 times more spectral resolution than broadband Hubble Space Telescope spectra of the high-redshift universe, with transmission rates of 80% across the 6–90 $\mathring{A}$ bandpass. Additionally, the Lyman series accounts for roughly 50% of the total energy output, while the continuum contributes approximately 50%, and the filter effectively suppresses the continuum outside the Lyman series. Future enhancements to this technology could include optimizing the filter's transmission profile, further reducing the series-to-Lyman-limit energy ratio, and implementing tunability across the entire Lyman series bandpass. These advancements would significantly enhance the capabilities of future space-based spectroscopy. Ultimately, the tunable BaF$_2$ prism-based Lyman-alpha filter holds the potential to uncover new scientific discoveries in the Lyman ultraviolet range. This paper introduces a new image indexing approach designed to dynamically update an index as new images are added and existing ones are removed. Specifically, the system employs a search structure where each node represents an index term, containing a single image at its leaves. Compared to current methods that index each individual image, our proposed dynamic indexing method reduces both time and space complexity. The study includes the formulation of this new indexing technique, its implementation, and empirical evaluation through benchmarking against an existing state-of-the-art indexing solution. Results indicate that our method is 1.5 to 2 times faster than the existing approach. The benchmarking utilized a dataset of 10,000 natural images, for which we provide a summary of key image-retrieval statistics. Furthermore, we address a specific retrieval scenario to demonstrate the efficiency of our indexing method. The accompanying source code is available at https://github.com/ahmedhaleem/DynamicImageIndexing. Our method is particularly efficient for large image retrieval applications where images are continuously added and deleted. The paper includes detailed formulations of our approach, including theoretical complexity analysis, alongside a comparison of retrieval performance against the existing state-of-the-art indexing method. Finally, we provide recommendations for selecting image retrieval applications that would benefit most from our proposed dynamic indexing solution. Our approach is applicable to any image retrieval system that relies on a similarity metric. We have applied this method to two types of similarity measures: a low-dimensional one derived from color histograms and a high-dimensional measure based on deep convolutional neural network features. We conclude that our dynamic indexing method is 1.5 to 2 times faster than the existing state-of-the-art indexing method while maintaining the same retrieval performance. Our implementation is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ahmedhaleem/DynamicImageIndexing. The paper also provides sample images from our dataset to illustrate the retrieval performance of the proposed method. Additionally, we detail the steps taken to develop a deep convolutional neural network feature extractor for image retrieval and present a comparison of our results with those of an existing state-of-the-art indexing method. The search complexity is $O(N/K)$, where $N$ is the total number of images and $K$ is the rank of the term matrix. The update complexity is $O(K)$, representing the complexity per insertion or deletion. The space complexity is $O(N/K)$, reflecting the complexity per insertion. These results are supported by complexity analysis, retrieval performance comparisons, and comparisons with other state-of-the-art solutions.

The keyless communication framework eliminates the need for a secret key by utilizing publicly accessible channel information as a keyless security source. This process begins with channel inputs generating correlated outputs at the transmitter and receiver, which are then processed to extract a common random randomizer. Subsequently, this randomizer is utilized to generate a shared secret key derived from the mutual randomness inherent in the channel. While existing keyless frameworks typically assess security solely during key generation, this paper investigates security across the entire protocol, paying particular attention to the initial randomizer generation phase, which has been previously overlooked. To address this, we propose a generic analysis method for AWGN channel outputs that quantifies the uncertainty of a randomizer relative to channel inputs and random Gaussian noise. Our security analysis demonstrates that amorphous noise is essential for unconditionally secure communication in AWGN channels. Furthermore, we evaluate security performance under different amorphous noise models and confirm that keyless communication with amorphous noise achieves superior security compared to traditional error-correcting code-based methods. Finally, we extend our security analysis from deterministic channel inputs to random ones and demonstrate that our analysis remains valid for finite-alphabet channels. To our knowledge, this represents the most general and complete security analysis ever conducted for keyless communication. Additionally, we introduce a novel security metric for keyless communication that quantifies the uncertainty of a random randomizer given channel outputs. Our analysis of this metric is the first of its kind for keyless communication and is expected to be the only such analysis achievable. We also discuss practical security applications, including secure channel estimation and channel tracking. In these applications, we analyze secure channel estimation in a MIMO system and propose a new approach for secure channel tracking. To our knowledge, this marks the first security analysis of keyless communication applications. We have made our code available on GitHub. Our findings regarding secure channel estimation and tracking are also the only available security analyses for these specific keyless communication applications. Consequently, this work provides the most general and complete security analysis ever performed for keyless communication, covering the full protocol, finite-alphabet channels, channel estimation, and channel tracking. Additionally, we have made our codes available on GitHub. This paper offers the only security analysis for keyless channel tracking. Furthermore, this research provides the most general and comprehensive security analysis for keyless communication, addressing the complete protocol, finite-alphabet channels, channel estimation, and channel tracking. This study re-examines the motion of a dispersionless (point) particle within a washboard potential, which is essential for direct tunneling diodes, semiconductor lasers, and Josephson junctions. While analytical solutions exist for the equation of motion, they have been neglected because the dominant approximation yields a well-known linear equation. In contrast, the full equation yields a solution expressible as an elliptic integral, enabling a new perspective on the dynamics. We derive an expansion formula using Bessel functions to calculate the period as a series, even for high velocities, and use it to identify a "resonant" regime at low speeds where the expansion fails. This resonant state represents a novel phenomenon involving a combination of standard coherent tunneling and delocalization across the entire potential landscape. Within the tunneling region, we demonstrate that the apparent linear equation actually describes coherent tunneling with an exponentially small anharmonicity. Finally, we explore the physical implications of these findings for the devices mentioned above. Notably, in the context of a shunted Josephson junction, we show that this resonant phenomenon corresponds to phase slips, a concept previously understood through numerical or experimental data but now clarified by our approach. These insights could be valuable for analyzing recent experiments on quantum phase slips. Furthermore, the proposed method for analyzing current-phase relations offers a fresh approach for designing and interpreting Josephson devices intended for quantum computing. A key finding is the existence of resonances in both experimental current-phase relations and those generated by quantum simulator devices. These findings underscore the critical need for precise control over environmental conditions when utilizing Josephson junctions in quantum computing applications. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 derives the solution; Section 3 examines low-velocity motion, including the tunneling regime; Section 4 addresses high-velocity motion; Section 5 discusses applications to Josephson junctions and quantum computing; and Section 6 offers concluding remarks. This study presents flexible local projections as a method for analyzing impulse responses. We evaluate the impulse effects of oil price shocks on the US economy using both OPEC and BP crude oil price indices. Our findings indicate that these Local Projection (LP) results align with previous economic literature. Specifically, we observe significant OPEC LP impulse effects: a prolonged but mild contraction in real GDP peaking at approximately 0.15 standard deviations after two years; a sharp, one-year decline in industrial production reaching about 0.3 standard deviations; and a sustained but moderate reduction in real consumption, falling roughly 0.25 standard deviations after three years. Conversely, the impulse effects on real investment, real net exports, and inflation prove to be OPEC-specific and remain economically negligible. Furthermore, we introduce an impulse response diagram that visualizes uncertainty bands alongside a median estimate, offering a more intuitive approach for communicating and interpreting LP results. Finally, we demonstrate that LP results are robust to variations in sample size and model specification. Overall, this paper advances both methodology and application by enhancing the flexibility and interpretability of local projections. Additionally, our impulse effects of OPEC provide fresh insights that complement existing economic research. Finally, the OPEC results fail to replicate for BP, underscoring the critical need to distinguish between the two sources. Specifically, the OPEC results suggest that oil price shocks exert a more substantial impact on the real economy than on the financial sector. This aligns with the OPEC definition of supply disruption, whereas BP results reflect price increases driven by market demand. These distinctions highlight the value of the OPEC price index for economic analysis. Overall, this study advances the methodology and applications of local projections. First, it offers a new approach for estimating impulse responses. Second, it provides a novel application by quantifying the impulse effects of OPEC oil price shocks. Finally, it demonstrates that the OPEC price index is particularly valuable for this analysis, as it effectively captures supply-side disruptions. These findings significantly enhance our understanding of the relationship between oil prices and the economy. Finally, this research exemplifies how local projections can significantly advance both methodology and application. First, it introduces a new approach for estimating impulse responses. Second, it quantifies the impulse effects of oil price shocks. Third, it distinguishes between OPEC and BP, demonstrating the value of OPEC for this analysis. These findings significantly enhance our understanding of the relationship between oil prices and the economy. Overall, this paper advances both the methodology and application of local projections. We investigate the angular Casimir effect by introducing a point charge within the bounded nontrivial quantum vacuum of "unbounded" Landau levels in a uniform magnetic field. The resulting torque confirms a Newton's 3rd law pair, where one component interacts with boundary dipoles, and the other pairs with the unbounded vacuum, effectively demonstrating the Casimir torque in Landau charge-occupied vacua. Furthermore, we identify a significant radiation reaction force component acting on a moving point charge in this Landau charge-occupied vacuum, alongside a novel, previously unreported radiative force component for a stationary charge, both of which possess real physical significance. These findings are supported by numerical calculations. Our research also suggests that radiation reaction components may exist for neutral particles in this unbounded Landau-occupied vacuum, though further investigation is required. The model system employed here, "unbounded" Landau levels filled with Landau charges, serves as a promising framework for future quantum simulations of quantum electrodynamics. Specifically, it offers a potential pathway to simulate the radiation reaction force of electrons in curved spacetime, as well as the equations governing motion under strong gravity, electromagnetism, and geodesic deviation. The latter could provide a quantum framework to test the strong equivalence principle, which is currently inaccessible to experimental verification. Additionally, our framework could facilitate new laboratory tests of quantum noninertial phenomena, such as the angular Casimir effect, which have hitherto been beyond reach. These and related proposals are also applicable to other unbounded charge-invariant vacua, including those of neutral particles and photons. Finally, our approach may advance the development of quantum test theories for quantum motion involving gravitational and electromagnetic fields, thereby supporting efforts to explore quantum aspects of gravity. The computational framework utilized in this study is also available for these and other purposes. The code was developed to examine quantum noninertial phenomena in "unbounded" Landau levels and to investigate the quantum motion of point charges in curved spacetime, specifically under strong gravity, electromagnetism, and geodesic deviation. The numerical code is also applicable to other quantum phenomena involving "unbounded" Landau levels, such as the angular Casimir effect, quantum noninertial phenomena, and the quantum motion of point charges in curved spacetime. Fine-grained named entity types present a significant challenge in Natural Language Processing due to their vast diversity and heterogeneous characteristics. In certain scenarios, types within the same class exhibit distinct attributes, such as celebrity subtypes being defined by roles like "singer," "actor," or "director." Consequently, modeling the relationships between a entity and its type becomes crucial for enhancing performance in various NLP tasks. Current approaches typically rely on transformer-based language models or vector representations, which fail to adequately capture the hierarchical and compositional structures inherent in these entities and types. To address this, we introduce the Refinement Entity Graph (RH), which employs a hierarchical structure to more effectively represent the relationships between entities and types. By integrating an attention mechanism, RH dynamically adjusts the importance of first-order neighbors, thereby refining the connections between entities and types. Furthermore, we adaptively weight the significance of specific neighbors for different types to further refine entity representations. We assessed RH's efficacy across two extensive datasets: NER-FG and WebTables. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms various baseline approaches. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/1234567890zhang/FGNET-RH. Finally, we release the NER-FG and WebTables datasets to the public to facilitate future research. The NER-FG dataset can be accessed at https://github.com/1234567890zhang/NER-FG, and both datasets are also available at https://github.com/1234567890zhang/WebTables. Additionally, access to the WebTables dataset can be found at https://github.com/1234567890zhang/data_preprocessing. Our results for the general class provide the sharp upper bound for this determinant. Dynamic models are essential for forecasting future system states, yet identifying their equilibrium or fixed-point configurations is notoriously difficult. Although existing approaches utilize optimization or root-finding techniques, they often suffer from high computational costs and sensitivity to hyperparameters. We introduce DynNet, a framework that adapts neural networks to predict an equilibrium's immediate vicinity based on the current state. This method is built upon fixed-point networks and employs a novel loss function grounded in continuous time-dynamics to ensure the preservation of important model dynamics. We demonstrate the method's effectiveness on both synthetic and real-world datasets. Furthermore, we apply it to forecast the dynamic outcomes of games involving various market and evolutionary scenarios. These cases illustrate how DynNet can achieve superior predictions of a game's future state compared to adaptations of other network architectures. This study introduces novel bounds for causal influence measures, including total influence, the causal influence score proposed by Shalhi et al. (2019), and the post-intervention causal influence developed by Nishiyama and Shimokawa (2021). The proposed bounds are expressed through the sums of absolute edge weights within a directed acyclic graph (DAG) that represents the causal structure of a specific post-intervention scenario. Notably, these bounds do not depend on specific functional forms or data distributions, and the same bound applies regardless of the target variable. We demonstrate that these findings yield highly accurate estimates of causal influence even with limited sample sizes and a small number of observed variables. Furthermore, we present an efficient algorithm for calculating these bounds in arbitrary high-dimensional settings and explore their application as regularizers for causal inference using linear structural equation models. Empirical results indicate the integration of this bounding approach into regularized estimation procedures leads to substantial performance gains compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, we establish connections to classical influence measures, such as centrality metrics in network analysis. Our extensive simulations and analysis of a real-world dataset reveal that a model incorporating these bounds achieves superior performance across multiple criteria when evaluated against top-performing alternatives. Finally, we provide Python code for the linear case and a command-line interface for practical implementation. This work establishes a new framework for quantifying how an intervention at one node propagates through a network of other nodes. We demonstrate that these bounds are effective for estimating causal influence, particularly in high-dimensional settings, and can serve as useful tools for regularization and scoring in causal inference tasks. This approach is highly scalable, supports parallel computation, and avoids the need to specify data distributions or causal targets. Empirical evidence shows these bounds can significantly enhance performance in causal inference using high-dimensional linear models, with this method now available as an option in the `pcalg` R package. We also illustrate how these results relate to various related concepts. The associated code implements these bounds for probabilistic DAGs, high-dimensional linear models, and Gaussian data, providing a practical starting point for researchers. We hope this contribution aids in quantifying node influence within causal networks. The code is accessible at: https://github.com/chenyuan1992/cibound. This paper focuses on the classification of stealthy attacks within linear time-invariant systems. Specifically, we examine linear dynamic systems with unknown parameters, where the goal of predictive monitoring is to identify attacks without compromising the system or triggering existing detection mechanisms. We introduce a general parameter expansion framework designed to maintain predictability, utilizing predictive classification to identify the presence of such attacks. The study derives the finite-sample error bounds for this approach and proves its asymptotic consistency. Additionally, we demonstrate the application of our predictive classification methodology through a real-world case study involving a water treatment plant. Finally, we provide an MATLAB repository link for accessing the implementation code. Keywords: Steady Attacks, Stealthy Attacks, Predictive Classification, Parameter Expansion.

Autoregressive models are currently leading state-of-the-art document summarization, yet they depend on extensive labeled data and often fail to generalize to new datasets. This limitation is particularly pronounced for low-resource Indian languages, where the scarcity of summarization labels further constrains model performance. To address this, we introduce GAE-ISumm, an unsupervised framework that utilizes a Graph-Based Encoder for Indian Summary Extraction. This approach first establishes a semantic graph from the input text and subsequently identifies summary sentences through the graph. Experiments across multiple Indian languages demonstrate that GAE-ISumm matches or exceeds human-generated summaries in quality. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/aryanbansal19/GAE-ISumm. Additionally, the paper includes a detailed analysis of the Indian language landscape to provide context for this work. The accompanying repository also features a comprehensive library of multilingual corpora and semantic graphs derived from various Indian languages. The framework's success in delivering high-quality unsupervised summarization is expected to serve as a robust foundation for future research initiatives. The paper is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.10555. Furthermore, our work has been accepted into the 2022 Computational Linguistics and Technology Challenges (CLT2022). This paper introduces S-rings of Cohen type, which are constructed as sub-S-rings within the specific S-rings of group type associated with regular nilpotent groups. We classify these S-rings of Cohen type alongside the sub-S-rings of group type in regular nilpotent 2-groups that are normal within the corresponding maximal S-ring. Additionally, the study examines the group of type automorphisms and morphic type elements for an S-ring of Cohen type. Finally, the paper presents a specific example of an S-ring of Cohen type that cannot be represented as a sub-S-ring of a group of type 1.

The autoencoder serves as a fundamental element in various machine learning tasks, functioning as an unsupervised model that learns data representations by mapping inputs to latent variables and subsequently reconstructing the original inputs from these latents. In supervised scenarios, it is frequently employed to create features or augment existing features. This paper introduces the Least Squares Variational Autoencoder, an unsupervised technique designed to mitigate over-regularization issues found in other autoencoder approaches. Experimental results demonstrate that the method successfully recovers complex latent variables and outperforms competing methods in both feature selection and classification applications. Additionally, empirical evidence indicates that this approach selects more discriminative features than alternative methods. Furthermore, the autoencoder exhibits robustness against noise, a trait not observed in other autoencoder models. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ahmedgaber/lsvae. The widespread adoption of the Internet of Things (IoT) has driven significant interest in developing smart applications, prompting researchers to explore secure architectures that minimize risks associated with unsecured devices. This paper introduces a low-cost, secure system for monitoring smart home appliances by leveraging private blockchain technology combined with RSSI-based signal strength measurement and trilateration for appliance localization. Within this framework, every smart device is treated as an IoT node; its transmitted signals are captured by an array of sensors, which then store a subset of this data on the private blockchain to ensure integrity and availability. Furthermore, the system utilizes these received signals to identify active nodes and compute the distances between appliances and corners using block data. Experimental results from a simulated environment demonstrate that this proposed method effectively localizes smart home appliances. The paper concludes by outlining potential future enhancements, such as integrating machine learning for localization and improving the system's scalability. Finally, the authors suggest adopting a hybrid approach that combines both private blockchain and public ledger technologies to achieve an optimal balance among security, scalability, and decentralization. This proposed system offers an affordable solution for secure localization within smart homes. Additionally, the authors intend to explore advanced signal processing techniques, such as time reversal and MUSIC algorithms, in future research to further enhance localization accuracy. Finally, the study examines the dual application of blockchain in this context: first, as a localization mechanism, and second, to mitigate the inherent security vulnerabilities of IoT devices. Regarding the latter, the authors propose employing a consortium blockchain model, where multiple entities jointly manage the network; this approach is considered superior to public or purely private blockchain configurations for smart home environments. The paper subsequently analyzes the advantages and disadvantages of such a consortium model and concludes by evaluating the potential for implementing this blockchain-based localization scheme in real-world settings. Finally, the authors address the challenge of ensuring system scalability when handling the data volumes generated by numerous appliances. To overcome the limitations of private blockchain, the authors propose a distributed cloud architecture that combines blockchain with cloud computing. The paper subsequently discusses the benefits and drawbacks of this proposed solution. Ultimately, the work envisions a distributed cloud framework built upon a hybrid blockchain structure comprising both public and private networks. The paper concludes by analyzing the security implications of such a distributed cloud architecture. This study introduces an adaptive deep learning-based method designed to enhance the spectral efficiency of Gray-coded modulation. Leveraging the flexibility of deep neural networks, the approach learns to assign bits to signal power magnitudes, thereby optimizing the energy distribution across analog-inherent channel effects. By employing a differentiable encoder paired with a maximization decoder, we demonstrate that this proposed scheme surpasses both established and recently introduced alternatives. Furthermore, our analysis of the deep learning framework reveals its intrinsic multi-scale and self-organizing characteristics. Specifically, these properties of the trained neural network bear a strong resemblance to the fundamental principles of the quantization-chain framework, a concept historically significant in quantization theory. Consequently, we illustrate that our solution achieves superior spectral efficiency compared to existing methods, such as probabilistic shaping combined with uniform or non-uniform constellation mapping. Additionally, simulations indicate that our scheme maintains robustness against imperfect channel state information regarding large-scale fading coefficients and demonstrates resilience to non-linear amplifier distortions. Finally, we successfully apply this proposed approach to massive MIMO systems equipped with non-ideal hardware components. In this context, our deep learning-based quantization chain outperforms traditional constellations and shaping techniques using L-shaping with either uniform or non-uniform power allocation. Notably, when implementing our method with a 16-L-shaping constellation featuring 4-level level-spacing quantization and 16-QAM, spectral efficiency gains reach up to 1.56 b/s/Hz. The results for the mass MIMO system are as follows: 1.52 b/s/Hz with LDPC decoding, 1.56 b/s/Hz with MMSE decoding, 1.49 b/s/Hz with LDPC decoding under non-ideal hardware, and 1.52 b/s/Hz with MMSE decoding under non-ideal hardware. Furthermore, by integrating this mass MIMO system with LDPC decoding and MMSE decoding, we observe an additional spectral efficiency gain of up to 0.04 b/s/Hz compared to our proposed proposal. This survey examines the current state of research in parameterized algorithmics and complexity regarding the upward planarity testing problem. Upward planarity involves determining whether the vertices and directed edges of a DAG can be positioned in 2D space such that every edge flows from bottom to top. This is a fundamental problem in algorithmic graph drawing, a key area of discrete algorithmic geometry. We focus on top-down drawings, where higher $y$-coordinates represent greater height. We analyze parameters derived from specific vertex subsets, such as sources, sinks, or cut-vertices, which are often available in domain-relevant applications. We discuss upward planarity testing, drawing, and saturation within the context of subset-based parameters, covering both complexity and the application domain of series-parallel digraphs. This class of digraphs is significant because its members admit linear-time upward planar embeddings, a property that does not hold for general series-parallel graphs. Finally, we outline several promising open problems and areas for future research. We aim to provide a comprehensive overview of existing results and potential directions, highlighting complex issues and open questions to inspire further investigation into upward planarity. Specifically, we address the complexity of upward planarity testing and drawing for vertex subsets, as well as the saturation level of series-parallel digraphs and other digraph classes regarding this parameter. Our review of parameterized complexity and applications is intended to inspire future research on upward planarity. We conclude with open problems and potential avenues for study, demonstrating that the field remains vibrant and full of exciting possibilities. Datasets generated through crowdsourcing are prone to noise, necessitating specialized techniques to ensure accurate classification of categorical outcomes. This study introduces a framework that combines ensemble modeling, an approximation of the "Human Softmax" distribution, and a suite of uncertainty metrics designed to evaluate human confidence in categorical predictions. The approach is first applied to a well-known benchmark task: classifying 20 US Senate elections into two categories, "Republican Majority" and "Democratic Majority," based on Senate composition. By integrating ensembles with entropy-based confidence measurement, the method surpasses the performance of any single model. Furthermore, it is extended to a more complex, noisy task involving the classification of 1,000 US states across eight categories—ranging from "Very Low" to "Very High"—for their propensity to experience heat waves. This generalization accounts for within- and between-category variability in human responses and handles errors in crowd-reported data. Results indicate that while ensemble modeling enhances classification accuracy, it does not fully resolve disparities in human agreement across different confidence levels or answer categories. These findings offer a robust strategy for analyzing categorical predictions, particularly in the presence of noisy crowdsourced inputs. The methodology is fully open and reproducible, with all necessary code and data available at: https://github.com/JamesJLambert/StateHeatWaveClassification. This study introduces a novel semiflow constructed from fractional linear operators acting on $C^1$ functions, demonstrating that its transfer operator on $C^0$ functions exhibits asymptotically exponential stability. The flow generated by this operator is analytic, and the transfer operator's transfer function belongs to the Wiener algebra of functions with absolutely convergent Fourier series. We derive explicit formulas for the leading eigenvalue and eigenfunction, providing upper bounds for the transfer function and eigenfunctions associated with the $n$th iterate. These estimates confirm the asymptotic exponential stability of the transfer operator. Furthermore, we establish the existence of a stable manifold for the transfer operator within a Banach space of functions with absolutely convergent Fourier series whose $C^k$ norms remain bounded. The WPDE governing the semiflow is formulated as a generalized Burgers equation. This equation features a nonlinearity that is locally Lipschitz in a Banach space of analytic functions and globally Lipschitz in a space of $C^k$ functions with $k$ sufficiently large. The WPDE is well-posed within a ball of small radius in a ball of $C^k$ functions. Additionally, the WPDE's transfer function is analytic, and its Fourier coefficients decay exponentially. Constructing covering arrays with strength $2$ and low size is essential for applications like high-speed software testing. This paper introduces a novel technique for deriving covering arrays from covering designs. Utilizing this approach, the authors have developed 44 new covering arrays, enhancing 20 existing lower bounds for strength $2$ covering arrays. Notably, this method enables the direct resolution of an open problem posed by Brouwer and Schrijver in 1978 regarding the minimum size of a strength $2$ covering array with 5 rows and 7 columns. Additionally, the method is applicable to covering arrays with a fixed number of levels, making it useful for designing software test suites. An online repository containing these covering arrays, along with the corresponding covering designs and additional methods for generating new arrays, is provided at the end of the paper. The arrays can be accessed here: http://www.cs.ubc.ca/~miller/smallcoverarraysV2.tar.gz. This approach is also a valuable tool for CS researchers engaged in software testing. We demonstrate that for any integer $k \geq 1$, the complexity class $\mathsf{NXP}_{d,k,2}(q)$—comprising the local correlations arising from nonlocal games played by $N$ players using $k$ copies of the $d$-dimensional maximally correlated state via noisy questions from an alphabet of size $q$—remains within $\mathsf{NP}$ whenever $N < q$. This finding contrasts sharply with a known hardness result for a slightly broader scenario and places most questions regarding the complexity of local correlations in these games within $\mathsf{NP}$. Additionally, we prove that determining the local correlations feasible for a network utilizing classical communication is complete for $\mathsf{coNP}$. Finally, as an application of our decidability proof, we establish a bound on the number of constraints necessary to approximate the local correlations of these networks. Specifically, the count of necessary inequalities grows exponentially with respect to $N$, $k$, and $\log d$, while remaining independent of $q$. Furthermore, we illustrate the utility of this approximation approach by deriving an upper bound for the local correlations of a notable non-local game involving multiple players. This problem has been conjectured to characterize the capacity of a network with quantum assistance, a setting conjectured to be undecidable. Consequently, our findings suggest the possibility of an upper bound applicable to the local correlations of this specific network. **Keywords:** nonlocal games, Bell inequalities, quantum networks, quantum communication complexity. **Acknowledgments:** We acknowledge financial support from the Spanish Ministry of Science and Innovation (grant FIS2017-84045-P), the Spanish Ministry of Universities (grant FPU15/03007), the Generalitat Valenciana (grant PROMETEOII/2017/030), and the European Research Council under the European Union's Horizon 2020 research and innovation program (grant agreement no. 724467). Automated crash replication and testing have garnered significant interest within the software engineering community. This paper presents a brief overview of the guided genetic algorithm (GA) proposed by Li et al., which is built upon the original genetic debugging algorithm by Wen et al. and the random crash reproduction guided by application traces method by Zhang et al. Li et al. suggest enhancing the state graph traversal guided by the trace by incorporating the concept of cut-edges, enhancing the mutation operator with random execution, and adding the recovery operator. Our objective is to assess the efficiency of this proposed approach, providing a limited empirical study of the guided GA method. The results of this partial replication are presented. This study is part of a broader effort to evaluate the algorithm using the JUnit testing framework for bug #32 in Mozilla's Firefox browser. The vortex lattice represents the dominant zero-field state of a superconductor in its charged environment. In spin-polarized doped quantum Hall superconductors, vortices form a distinct square-triangle lattice. We present experimental findings from underdoped YBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_{6+x}$ indicating a novel vortex lattice structure that merges characteristics of both square and triangle lattices. This study provides the first direct evidence of this hybrid grid in a cuprate superconductor. Furthermore, we outline the development of a vortex underdoping phase diagram, which identifies a critical underdoping level marking the shift from a square to a square-triangle vortex grid. This transition aligns with a previously noted change in pseudogap symmetry. Finally, we discuss the relationship between vortex lattice behavior and pseudogap symmetry. These insights are anticipated to enhance our understanding of high-$T_\textrm{c}$ cuprate superconductors. Additionally, the observed transition may elucidate the relationship between quantum Hall Landau levels and quantum spin dimerization. These high-field superconducting findings offer a framework for investigating various quantum phases in diverse quantum many-body systems. *This work was supported by the National Science Foundation (DMR-1805170), the Department of Energy (DEFG02-94ER45576), and the Simons Foundation (435962).* **Note:** This manuscript was submitted prior to the discovery of time-reversal symmetry breaking in YBCO [1]. Photons emitted from the QGP during its early evolution are highly sensitive to the plasma's viscosity; however, because the emission is distributed over a prolonged duration and a large volume, the observable photon spectra are dominated by the isothermal stage, rendering measurements of flow harmonics and their ratios ($v_n/s v_1/s$) largely insensitive to viscosity. In contrast, thermal photons, which can be detected experimentally, originate from the QGP formed after approximately $1\,\mu$s. Consequently, we demonstrate that while the yield of thermal photons is primarily governed by viscosity, the flow harmonics and their ratios are largely determined by anisotropic flow. This phenomenon arises because thermal photons effectively sample the anisotropic shape of the late-stage QGP. Furthermore, we establish that the photon $v_2/s v_3/s$ ratio exhibits a significantly more pronounced maximum at low viscosities compared to hadron $v_2/s v_3/s$ and dilepton $j_2/j_3/j_3$ ratios. This makes the measurement of the thermal photon $v_2/s v_3/s$ ratio a highly promising method for future flow measurements, offering a robust tool for investigating the viscosity of the QGP medium. Our study also examines various scenarios for implementing this measurement. Finally, we explore potential applications of thermal photon $v_2/s v_3/s$ in both current PHENIX data and upcoming PHENIX Run-3 and RHIC Beam Energy Scan experiments. Additionally, we suggest that ALICE, PHENIX, PHOBOS, STAR, and CMS at the LHC could measure this observable using existing datasets, as well as in the future with PHENIX, RHIC BES, PHOBOS, STAR, and ALICE. We conclude that thermal photon $v_2/s v_3/s$ serves as a valuable tool for constraining the viscosity of the QGP medium. Furthermore, we emphasize that future analyses should focus on extracting viscosity using flow harmonics that peak in the low-viscosity region, rather than relying solely on anisotropic flow. This approach is essential for achieving a more precise constraint on the specific viscosity $\eta/s$ of the QGP. We present a systematic investigation of finite-temperature magnetic ordering in two-dimensional (2D) triangular and kagome lattices using the stochastic quantum Ising approach. Our results demonstrate that this method is both accurate and effective for these systems. We identify a novel, robust, and fully ordered magnetic state on the kagome lattice that persists in the thermodynamic limit at zero temperature. This state exhibits in-plane propagation and belongs to the sixfold degenerate class of possible orderings. Additionally, we detect a competing state with fourfold degeneration, characterized by out-of-plane propagation. By examining the phase diagram of the 2D triangular lattice, we find that the stochastic quantum Ising method successfully predicts the sequence of magnetic phase transitions. Specifically, at zero external field, the system evolves from a paramagnetic phase to a magnetic phase with in-plane propagation (twofold degenerate), followed by the emergence of a stripe phase (sixfold degenerate) as the external field increases further. These phases are also observed in the 3D cubic lattice. Finally, we establish that the stochastic quantum Ising method yields accurate and reliable finite-temperature magnetic ordering in both the triangular and kagome lattices. This confirms that the approach can reliably identify the onset of long-range order in complex lattices, a finding that could have significant implications for high-temperature superconductivity research. Furthermore, our work suggests that lattice types with higher symmetry, such as hexagonal, can be investigated with comparable accuracy. Overall, the stochastic quantum Ising method proves to be a valuable tool for exploring finite-temperature magnetic ordering in both 2D and 3D lattices. These findings are derived from extensive numerical simulations of the quantum Ising model with single-site anisotropy. We also establish a correspondence with the classical Heisenberg model featuring single-ion anisotropy. Finally, our study predicts a unique phase diagram for the quantum Heisenberg model on a simple cubic lattice. To our knowledge, this marks the first comprehensive exploration of finite-temperature magnetic ordering in these specific lattices. Our findings may prove significant for high-temperature superconductivity studies. Furthermore, the stochastic quantum Ising method is applicable to studying magnetic ordering in lattices with multiple inequivalent sublattices. This study addresses the identification of treatment effects within large-scale multi-treatment experiments while managing the false discovery rate under dependence. To achieve this, we introduce a unified framework that encompasses previous solutions such as the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure and the large-scale effect identification (LSEI) method. By employing the dependence graph of an underlying latent factor model, we categorize identification problems into two categories: weakly dependent and strongly dependent. Our primary contribution lies in establishing the exact null distribution for a data-driven statistic under both dependency conditions and deriving the corresponding type-I error probability for the identification threshold. These theoretical findings enable the proposal of a generic factor-based procedure for identifying treatment effects under weak and strong dependence, with substantial gains achievable by utilizing the structure of the latent factor model. We validate the practical utility of our method through two real-world datasets: a large-scale agricultural experiment involving 1,010 treatment effects and a large-scale clinical trial involving 16,500 treatment effects. Furthermore, we extend the identification framework to scenarios where the number of treatments exceeds the sample size. Simulation studies indicate that our approach maintains strong type-I error control and achieves significantly higher power compared to existing methods across both dependent cases. The principle of cosmic expansion is fundamental to contemporary cosmology. Although this concept initially seemed counterintuitive, it is now universally accepted as the most logical explanation for observational data. Furthermore, it serves as a cornerstone of the Big Bang theory, which posits that the universe originated from an extremely hot, dense state and has been growing ever since.

Observations by Hubble in the 1920s revealed that distant galaxies are receding from Earth, a phenomenon that can be attributed to the expansion of space itself. Consequently, the logical approach to understanding cosmic expansion begins with a review of Hubble's key findings. The subsequent section provides mathematical derivations of Hubble's law, which demonstrates that the distance between any two points in the universe increases at a rate proportional to their separation. The final section compares the cosmic expansion model with the alternative scenario of an static universe. We will demonstrate that the static model fails to account for Hubble's observations and introduce the concept of Hubble volume, which suggests that the visible universe may not represent the total extent of the cosmos. Finally, we will illustrate how Hubble's observations are naturally explained by the Big Bang model.

Although numerous automatic inquiry reformulation methods exist, they rely on specific criteria to transform user questions and subsequently analyze Web documents to support location tasks. However, these criteria are often restrictive, limiting the approach's applicability. This paper addresses this issue by presenting QUICKAR, a technique that leverages crowdsourced knowledge to automatically reformulate inquiry questions for concept location. The QUICKAR framework encompasses three core components: (i) a rule generation engine that creates reformulation rules by mining inquiry reformulation knowledge from crowdsourced platforms, (ii) a rule refinement engine that enhances these rules using both automated and manual processes, and (iii) a rule ranking engine that prioritizes the refined rules to select the most effective reformulation. Experimental results demonstrate that QUICKAR successfully and effectively reformers inquiry questions to minimize search effort during concept location. Entrainment represents a fundamental trait of human interaction, yet quantifying this mechanism remains an open challenge. We introduce an unsupervised deep neural network model that characterizes entrainment by analyzing the acoustic similarity of speech samples exchanged between interactors. This approach enables the detection of entrainment events within both spoken and written exchanges. Furthermore, the model is robust enough to predict the magnitude of conversational entrainment even when the behavior is manipulated. Our results indicate that entrainment is more prevalent in human-human conversations than in human-AI interactions, and it demonstrates a strong correlation with subjective assessments of conversational naturalness. Additionally, during behavior transfer tasks, the model identifies that naturalness is maximized when human behavior is imprinted on a neural network trained to interact with another human. These findings collectively suggest the potential for enhancing naturalness in human-machine partnerships. To our knowledge, this marks the first effort toward developing a metric capable of measuring entrainment. Self-supervised learning (SSL) has emerged as a significant strategy for temporal action segmentation, offering an advantage over supervised methods by eliminating the need for extensive annotation. However, SSL approaches often depend on specific data distributions, rendering them unsuitable for generalization to unseen domains. To address this limitation, we introduce an SSL framework for temporal action segmentation that relies solely on the co-occurrence of actions within video segments. We developed a comprehensive protocol called Self-supervised Co-occurrence Action Analysis (SSCAP) to fully leverage this prior. In our approach, temporal segmentation labels are utilized to train a video classification model through a self-supervised objective focused on segment-level feature learning. Subsequently, we employ action-class-specific filters to identify and segment actions based on their co-occurrence patterns. Experimental results indicate that our method achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art supervised techniques while requiring significantly fewer annotations. Domain adaptation is essential for ensuring robustness in unsupervised scenarios and remains a rapidly evolving field. In contemporary research, the most prevalent setting involves domain adaptation without an independent source domain, which has led to the development of various methods. However, this paradigm is highly susceptible to performance degradation when the source domain shifts during the adaptation process. To address this issue, we introduce a novel Source-Free Domain Adaptation (SFDA) approach that remains effective even when source data is unavailable. Our method employs a hypothesis shift strategy, where hypotheses are generated from a domain-agnostic model trained on multiple domains. This design eliminates the need for source data and mitigates SFDA challenges. Additionally, we incorporate a self-training mechanism to enhance SFDA performance further. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that our proposed SFDA technique outperforms previous methods in terms of robustness and generalization. The code is accessible at https://github.com/Chenchen-Zhang/Semi-Supervised-Hypothesis-Shift.

Atmospheric retrievals serve as a critical instrument for both characterizing exoplanet and brown dwarf atmospheres and understanding their evolution. This work investigates the principles of grounding, a critical computational stage of ASP solvers. We introduce a formal model of grounding that encompasses both modern efficient approaches, such as those used in CLNFOIL and CNF2ASP, as well as older methods, including the principles underlying abctool and cnf2asp. Our model distinguishes between constructive and non-constructive ground instances, asserting that the former are essential for SAT encoding. Based on this model, we demonstrate the necessity of specific correctness principles for efficient grounding, illustrating how violations of these principles result in incomplete or inefficient grounding. We empirically evaluate the consequences of these violations across various ASP programs. Furthermore, we establish a sufficient condition grounded in the syntax of ASP programs to guarantee that all non-constructive ground instances are discarded. The paper concludes with a summary and an outline of future research directions. This model and our condition are available as open-source software. Additionally, we illustrate how automated static analysis can facilitate user guidance in effective grounding. All experiments were conducted using the solver aspic. This paper establishes the initial law for general quantum resource theories (QRTs), which are mathematical frameworks used to quantify non-resourceful resources within quantum systems. We demonstrate that under noiseless, resource-preserving transformations, the physically meaningful axioms of a resource monotone—functions that do not increase under these operations—are precisely those representable as convex roofs of strictly monotones. This formulation resolves an open question regarding the initial laws of quantum coherence. Additionally, we prove that while cardinality is the sole additive monotone for set-theoretic classical resources, nearly every quantum resource possesses at least one strictly monotone. These findings offer a comprehensive and nearly complete framework for resource representation in both classical and quantum domains. Furthermore, we investigate resource theories for non-coherence and non-stabilizer quantum resources at low resolution, revealing distinct behaviors in strictly monotone functions as noiseless transformations are generalized to include selective resource-independent operations. We conclude by proposing a potential generalization of the initial law to scenarios involving resource-consuming operations, such as measurements. Specifically, we conjecture that the axioms of monotones under such operations correspond to functions that are convex roof extensions of $f$-concave functions. Although this conjecture remains unproven, we validate it for two cases: non-coherence under decohering channels and non-stabilizer states under stabilizer states under Clifford unitaries. Consequently, our proposed resource representation may facilitate new resource theories or more efficient resource theories derived from states lacking significant structural similarity to stabilizer states. Overall, this work provides a robust foundation for formulating initial laws in quantum resource theories. Additionally, it may inspire the development of physical principles in physics through the analysis of the physical content of these laws. To achieve this, it is essential to investigate the historical development of the initial law and explore its relationship with physical principles. This paper addresses both objectives. Specifically, Section 2 examines the historical evolution of the initial law and its connections to physical principles, with a particular focus on coherence and non-stabilizer states. Section 3 then outlines several open problems and potential future research directions. Finally, Section 4 offers a comprehensive summary of the paper's contents. Finally, Section 5 provides an overview of the content. In this study, we prove a generalization of the initial law for quantum resources. This paper introduces a class of functions designed to estimate complex functions of probability distributions using simple, consistent, and asymptotically normal estimators. Data on the complex distributions is indirectly accessed through a sufficient statistic estimated via an estimator that converges at a rate $\sqrt{n}$. The study presents a general framework for developing these functions, which are demonstrated on a broad category of statistical models. The paper develops these methods within the context of dynamic programming. Specifically, it applies them to quantile estimation in DSGE models where sufficient statistics include estimated transition operators, including cases with noise in these operators. Additionally, the application extends to estimating general functions of distributionals derived from iterated application of transfer operators. Quantitative illustration involves estimating the value function in a simple linear model featuring transition operator noise. Furthermore, the approach is demonstrated by approximating the distribution of sample paths in a one-dimensional model with nonlinear transition operators. The methodology is also highlighted in the context of estimating the value function and policy function in a one-dimensional model characterized by a non-convex value function. Finally, the paper explores extensions to higher-dimensional models. Estimating the value function remains straightforward when the transition operator is linear, even if convexity fails. When transition operators are nonlinear, distributionals at any finite time $t$ can be estimated, though distributionals over the entire sample path cannot. This limitation is addressed in an appendix where estimation is performed using posterior distributions derived from a prior that favors model classes with a reduced number of parameters. This paper addresses inference for multivariate time series with infinite variance that are both non-linear and non-stationary, ignoring temporal dependence for now, with the goal of predicting future observations based on current data. We evaluate four distinct inference approaches, three of which are non-parametric, designed to improve prediction accuracy. Additionally, we conduct a simulation study to assess performance, and we apply each method to two datasets of economic interest, analyzing how different sample sizes influence prediction accuracy. Finally, we summarize the strengths and limitations of these methods to assist readers in selecting the most appropriate approach for their specific needs. Our focus remains on direct inference for predicting time series observations, rather than inferring underlying data generating processes. We present several contributions, including new estimation techniques, reviews of existing methods, and a systematic comparison aimed at guiding readers toward the most suitable method for predicting multivariate time series observations. These codes feature a code distance of $\Omega(n^{1/2 - \epsilon})$ and can be decoded in time $O(n^{1 + \epsilon})$ using a constant-size alphabet, where $n$ represents the number of physical qubits. Our approach extends the classical speed code construction by Kudekar, Savitzki, and Vardy (IEEE Trans. Info. Theory, 2019) to the quantum domain and employs the minimum-distance decoder under the assumption of a low error rate. We further demonstrate the existence of a family of quantum speed codes capable of decoding via a constant-size alphabet with a linear runtime bound. Additionally, we establish a general theorem that enables the adaptation of any family of classical binary linear codes, equipped with an $O(n^a)$ time minimum-distance decoder, to the quantum domain to achieve the same property. This finding enhances the recently developed general code construction method by Freedman and Haah (Proc. R. Soc. A, 2016). Finally, we provide a comprehensive discussion on the trade-offs among code distance, minimum distance, and decoder complexity for this proposed class of quantum codes. The group decision problem is defined as finding a group that dominates the graph. We establish that, assuming $NP\not\subseteq$ BSS, no distributed decision algorithm exists for distance-$r$ distance-$r$ dominating set (where $r\geq 2$) on sparse high-girth graphs in the BSS model when the group size is a non-constant polynomial of the input size. This result implies that no distributed decision algorithm can identify the group size as a function of the group size for any instance of a distance-$r$ distance-$r$ dominating set problem, thereby resolving a question posed by Peleg. Furthermore, for a distance-$r$ distance-$r$ dominating set problem on sparse high-girth graphs with a group size of $O(1)$, the problem is undecidable in the Turing model and difficult in the BSS model (specifically, it lacks a decision algorithm running in non-constant polynomial time). Consequently, no decision algorithm can detect whether a vertex subset serves as a distance-$r$ dominating set for this problem, meaning we cannot ascertain if a monochromatic distance-$r$ neighborhood exists for every vertex. This contrasts with the scenario where the group size is non-constant and grows with the input size, in which case decision algorithms exist to check if a group dominates the graph or if a group of a specific size dominates the graph. Additionally, we demonstrate that for any pair of vertices, a group dominating both can be identified in non-constant polynomial time, with the group size bounded by $O(r)$. Finally, we note that our results extend to distance-$r$ dominating set problems in general graphs, including those with short girth. Specifically, we show that no decision algorithm exists to find a group that dominates the graph in the BSS model when the group size is the square of the input size. This establishes a hierarchy among decision problems for distance-$r$ dominating set problems based on group size, revealing a trade-off between group size and decision algorithm efficiency. We investigate disordered higher-order topological insulators (HOTTIs) featuring point-like zero-energy corner states within two-dimensional (2D) square lattices. Unlike their extended surface or edge counterparts, these corner states exhibit finite size and are highly susceptible to localization by potential fluctuations, even when the disorder strength is extremely weak. Consequently, the system undergoes a bulk-surface transition, where the delocalized nature of the corner states changes from extended to localized. Utilizing numerical simulations, we analyze the evolution of corner-state properties throughout this transition. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the corner states possess a fractal dimension that diminishes from 0 to 0 as the corner-surface transition is passed. This behavior aligns with the multifractality spectrum of the bulk surface states at the mobility edge. Additionally, the fractal dimension at the mobility edge matches the multifractality spectrum at the corresponding scale, a phenomenon previously observed in the delocalized-localized transition of 1D lattice states at the Anderson mobility edge. This study provides new insights into the unique physical properties of disordered HOTTIs. Our findings may also hold implications for other systems hosting finite-size topological states. Finally, we suggest potential extensions of our work to higher-order topological states with line-like and plane-like configurations in lower and higher dimensions, respectively. This article presents a selection of recent searches for supersymmetry performed at the CMS experiment, which are reviewed within the context of the experiment's broader physics program and existing theoretical predictions. While the program extends beyond supersymmetry, this focus is adopted here due to the inherent theoretical synergy between the two fields. Supersymmetric particles, if they exist, would serve as components of physics extending the Standard Model and could offer viable candidates for dark matter. Furthermore, supersymmetry offers the potential to resolve the hierarchy problem and may provide the framework for Grand Unified Theories. Although no supersymmetric particles have been detected to date, the CMS experiment continues an aggressive and systematic effort to investigate the phenomenon both independently and in collaboration with other experiments. These efforts rely on sophisticated theoretical simulations that drive the selection of particles to search for and facilitate comparisons with other experimental efforts. This paper offers an overview of supersymmetric searches at CMS and their status. It is important to note that the absence of observed supersymmetric particles thus far does not disprove the concept; rather, it constrains the parameter space, prompting further refinement in searches for both observed and unobserved phenomena. Ultimately, supersymmetry remains a viable possibility. A successful experimental confirmation of supersymmetry would be transformative for particle physics. Conversely, if current searches continue to yield no significant findings, further refinement of supersymmetric models will be necessary. In either scenario, further upgrades to the CMS detector will be essential. With an anticipated luminosity of 300 fb$^{-1}$, the experiment will have the capacity to investigate numerous unexplored regions of the supersymmetric parameter space. Additionally, upgrades to the CMS detector will enable investigations into Higgs physics and dark matter, both of which are intrinsically linked to supersymmetry. These discussions will provide a current snapshot of the search for supersymmetry at the CMS experiment. For a more comprehensive overview, readers are directed to the comprehensive review by T. Plehn. Finally, given the space constraints, many specific searches are not discussed in detail; readers are encouraged to consult the original publications for those details. We introduce a neural radiance field technique designed to synthesize new views of scenes captured via CG-bright-field microscopy. In this microscopy approach, out-of-focus light is intentionally removed to render out-of-plane structures invisible, thereby providing depth cues for estimating scene depth from single images. Our method utilizes a neural network to estimate per-pixel scene depth and integrates this depth data with a neural radiance field to estimate scene radiance for novel view synthesis. The network learns a depth prior that varies based on the specific scene and is parameterized through a per-pixel latent code. The radiance field is represented by a three-layer fully connected network conditioned on the depth field and camera intrinsics. We demonstrate that our technique achieves state-of-the-art results in both depth recovery and view synthesis on two benchmark datasets: in-vivo retinal imaging and ex-vivo fixed tissue imaging. In contrast to previous methods, our approach offers a more efficient solution for view synthesis, achieving results comparable to Gaussian splatting. Furthermore, we show that our method can generate novel views from single images, whereas prior techniques are limited to generating at most two views from a sequence. Finally, we highlight the potential of our method for real-time applications by leveraging implicit neural representations and efficient rendering techniques. Specifically, we demonstrate real-time rendering on a single A100 GPU at 1280x720 resolution. Additionally, we show that a smaller, faster network trained on a reduced dataset can achieve high-quality rendering at 1280x720 resolution on a single RTX3090 GPU, meeting the requirements for interactive real-time rendering. To our knowledge, this represents the first fully differentiable and real-time solution for bright field neural rendering.
