This study presents speckle interferometric data for 100 stars, ranging from magnitude 6.5 to 13.0, observed with the adaptive optics (AO) instrument on the Southern Astrophysical Research (SOAR) Telescope during 2021. Although the AO system achieved only a median Strehl ratio of 13%, the resulting median seeing was 38 milliarcseconds (mas), allowing the measurement of 169 individual binary systems. The sample includes 10 new variable stars, 10 new variable binaries, and 80 previously monitored objects, with 20 comparisons selected for repeated observation. We report 220 measurements of angular separation and position angle, 11 new eclipse events, and 13 instances of apparent eclipses. Additionally, 140 measurements indicate no significant changes in separation or position angle, while 30 show significant variations; 29 of the latter are attributed to eclipses, and one is identified as a speckle. Two binaries, HD 124846 and HD 150136, exhibit intransitive constraints on their orbits, and the new measurements for HD 124846 suggest a potential third eclipse. For HD 150136, a significant change in position angle is detected, though the new measurements do not allow for a separation change. We also identify 10 new or revived long-period binaries and provide new astrometric data for 15000, HD 124846, HD 132653, HD 139614, HD 14826, HD 150136, HD 169839, HD 209420, HD 212634, HD 212758, HD 212808, HD 212933, HD 213247, HD 213336, and HD 219974. This algebra exhibits a duality with massless scalar field theory analogous to the established holographic kinematic algebra-dual-field theory relationship in flat space. This duality enables the derivation of scattering amplitudes from field correlators, while simultaneously allowing scattering data to impose non-trivial constraints on local operators, fields, and their dynamics. These concepts are linked to recent work on integrability in free field theories, a perspective that may offer new insights into scattering amplitudes, sum rules, and sum rules for operators. Furthermore, we demonstrate that within this integrability framework, the well-known unitarity relations for scalar and spinor amplitudes emerge as specific instances of the general conservation laws governing current correlators. Additionally, we propose a modified, extended hue coordinate system that may hold significance for understanding holography in (anti-)de Sitter spaces, as it becomes conformally dual to the Fefferman ambient coordinates of AdS. Finally, we examine a holographic-like mapping between our celestial chiral algebra and the holomorphic subalgebra of the 2D conformal scalar field algebra, which also connects to integrability and sum rules. This (partial) holographic mapping appears related to recent findings regarding conformal field theory data for products of Virasoro representations. These connections may provide valuable insights into conformal field theory and the holographic principle at both the bulk and boundary levels. Overall, our work underscores the potential importance of hue coordinates and the integrability of free massless fields in both (anti-)de Sitter and flat space, as well as the broader principle of conformal duality. Solar flares frequently produce high-speed jets, though their dynamics are difficult to observe in the low corona due to the lack of suitable instruments. LOFAR's exceptional frequency resolution allows for the detailed analysis of plasma emission from low-frequency radio sources. This work presents the first observation of a jet-driven piston blast in the low corona using LOFAR on July 1, 2017. The jet's dynamics were captured by multiple instruments, while LOFAR provided initial imaging of the blast wave and high-resolution spectral data of the jet. The observed blast wave propagated at approximately 1000 km/s, which is typical for such phenomena. LOFAR detected the jet and the associated blast wave roughly 10 seconds apart, indicating that the jet triggered the blast within a few seconds. The jet traveled about 100 Mm over 100 seconds, consistent with prior observations of similar jets. LOFAR observed the blast wave for about 100 seconds, after which it faded as it moved into higher corona. The jet exhibited standard flare-associated temporal and spatial characteristics, emitting at a few hundred MHz. The blast wave was polarized at approximately 50%, and its dynamics were well described by a radial expansion model. This event demonstrates that LOFAR can detect and observe jets and jet-driven blasts in the low corona. Future observations of similar events with the same instrument could provide the first constraints on the acceleration mechanisms of jets and their initial properties. Additionally, LOFAR's observations of the blast wave offer a unique method to study the dynamics of piston-induced shocks in the corona. Overall, this event highlights the value of combining different observational techniques and instruments. Future studies should investigate the spatial and temporal characteristics of jets and blasts in the low corona, as well as their physical origins. Such research will enhance our understanding of solar flare dynamics and their impact on the corona and heliosphere. This study also illustrates the potential of low-frequency radio observations for solar physics. Future observations of similar events with LOFAR could provide the first constraints on jet acceleration mechanisms and initial conditions, as well as the radial expansion dynamics of piston-induced blasts. Furthermore, LOFAR's observations of the blast wave may offer the first insights into the dynamics of such piston-driven shocks in the corona. The proposed analysis of jets and associated blasts in the low corona underscores the value of various observational techniques and the solar physics community. Ultimately, this research will improve our understanding of solar flare dynamics and their effects on the corona and helios

The general two Higgs doublet model, featuring both Yukawa and Zarnecki couplings for the additional Higgs doublets, is analyzed as a framework for investigating flavour anomalies and the standard model's 'g-2' anomaly. This study demonstrates that the Zarnecki couplings influence neutral Higgs boson interactions with fermions, whereas Zarnecki-Smirnov couplings affect all gauge boson interactions. The model successfully accommodates various flavour anomalies through its rich particle and vertex content, which extends beyond tree-level mediation. Additionally, constraints derived from collider data, electroweak precision observables, and flavour measurements are established, alongside a systematic exploration of the model's viable parameter space. Finally, the study examines the stability of solutions regarding the standard model Higgs boson pole mass and self-interaction. In the limit where Zarnecki-Smirnov couplings vanish, the model aligns with the 2HDM-Zarnecki variant, successfully explaining the $R_{K^{(\ast)}}$ ratio, $R_{D^{(\ast)}}$, $a_\mu$, $a_s$, $f_{L/c,b}$, $P_{T}^{\text{CP-L}}$, and $p_T$-dependent $A_C$ (particularly $A_C^{(1)}$) anomalies. This achievement requires at least four heavy Higgs bosons, with two possessing significant couplings to down-type fermions and two to up-type fermions. The analysis further reveals that the Zarnecki-Smirnov couplings significantly impact non-decay rates, such as $H^+ \to \tau \nu_\tau$, $H^+ \to \mu \nu_\mu$, and $\Gamma_b \to \Gamma_s$, thereby imposing stricter constraints on the model's parameter space. Furthermore, these couplings affect neutral Higgs couplings to up- and down-type fermions, as well as $H^0 H^0 A^0$ and $H^0 H^+ H^-$ trilinear terms. In contrast, regarding the $(g-2)_\mu$ explanation, the Zarnecki-Smirnov couplings are negligible, while the Zarnecki-Yukawa couplings must be substantially larger than the standard Yukawa couplings. Additionally, these Zarnecki-Yukawa couplings are essential for the existence of heavy charged Higgs boson masses. This study introduces a new and efficient technique for solving the Navier--Stokes equations in both two and three dimensions, formulated as functional stochastic differential equations (FSDEs). Within FSDEs, the nonlinear term $({\bf u}\cdot\nabla){\bf u}$ is represented as a functional acting on the solution, with its variation governed by the Fréchet derivative. This approach falls under the broader category of stochastic vortex methods. By employing the Fréchet derivative and the natural metric it generates on function spaces, we develop "gradient vortex dynamics," a stochastic differential equation that introduces an adaptive, friction-like variable dependent on the system's overall state. This proposed dynamics serves as an alternative to existing stochastic vortex methods that utilize the Wiener differential to address the same Navier--Stokes equations. Furthermore, this functional approach to modeling fluid dynamics is anticipated to hold conceptual value in broader fluid studies, particularly regarding vortex evolution and interactions. Finally, the paper examines specific applications of this new dynamics, analyzing the Vortex Ring and the interaction of two Vortex Rings in both 2D and 3D environments. Boson sampling is a quantum computational model designed to demonstrate a quantum advantage. While the average entanglement within this framework has been examined through entanglement entropy, this study investigates entanglement at the level of individual instances using multiple EPR-indices. These indices identify maximal entangled subspaces in multi-party systems and offer more sensitive insights into quantum entanglement. The results indicate that the probability distribution of EPR-indices in boson sampling converges to a delta function as the number of modes increases, suggesting that the quantum enhancement in boson sampling may stem from the collective entanglement of all modes. Furthermore, the probability distribution for EPR-indices can be analytically derived for systems with an arbitrary ratio of modes to photons. Finally, the study explores the relationship between EPR-indices and entanglement entropy, demonstrating the superior capability of EPR-indices in characterizing multi-party entanglement. These findings may advance our understanding of quantum computational models and their underlying physical mechanisms. We introduce a guided learning algorithm designed for high-dimensional temporal sequences, particularly within life science contexts. This approach integrates domain-specific knowledge into the modeling process by utilizing a method to decompose complex sequences into shorter segments, which are subsequently modeled using variational autoencoders. A key component is the application of a novel entropy-based metric to quantify sequence complexity, ensuring that more complex sequences are accurately represented by the model. Empirical results demonstrate that entropy effectively captures known biological complexities, such as those found in cell lineages. Furthermore, this methodology surpasses standard single-model approaches, reducing reconstruction errors by an average of 10% and downstream losses by a similar margin. Additionally, entropy has proven effective in identifying critical branches in lineages and distinguishing significant samples in high-dimensional datasets. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/SebastianSchauer10/SeqSplit. Our findings indicate that guided learning serves as a robust framework for accurate sequence modeling and the discovery of intrinsic biological patterns in high-dimensional data. Reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved significant success across numerous complex tasks within robotics and artificial intelligence. However, a critical challenge remains addressing environments where not all variables are directly observable. In such scenarios, an agent must utilize an observation model to estimate the probability of unobserved variables based on its history. This study demonstrates that recurrent neural networks (RNNs) can effectively solve reinforcement learning problems in partially observable settings by constraining the recurrence to a "belief unit," which represents the expected values of hidden variables. We provide theoretical evidence supporting this approach for discrete state spaces and offer empirical validation across a broad spectrum of environments, including continuous, high-dimensional spaces, using a recurrent liquid state machine (LSTM). Specifically, within a randomly generated partially observable grid world, an LSTM successfully learned to navigate a maze by forecasting the location of a hidden agent. Furthermore, we illustrate that this method produces interpretable results by explicitly training an RNN to approximate the evolution of belief probabilities. Consequently, our findings suggest that RNNs can discover novel strategies in obscured settings and that analyzing belief dynamics offers a new avenue for interpretability, an area that has received limited attention to date. Finally, we propose that RNNs applied to partially observable reinforcement learning could enhance our understanding of how the brain addresses similar challenges. This potential lies in the concept of "concealed states," which aligns with recent neuroscience research on activity patterns linked to beliefs. We conclude by initiating an investigation into this intriguing connection. Finally, the associated code can be found at: https://github.com/alexei-petrov/belief-LSTM. The primary challenge in weakly-supervised action detection is distinguishing action-related context from coincidental cues. While recent methods have attempted to model context using deep networks, they face limitations regarding computational efficiency and their dependence on fully-supervised fine-tuning. This study leverages the capability of deep networks to capture hierarchical feature representations and introduces an efficient, weakly-supervised context graph to represent action-specific context. Unlike prior approaches, our method constructs this graph in an unsupervised manner by linking frame-level instance features through a predefined set of actions. Furthermore, we employ Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) to aggregate node features, thereby enhancing the context graph's representation of actions. Our GCN model is lightweight, facilitating efficient action detection. Additionally, we extend the GCN framework to iteratively refine the context graph by iteratively learning task-specific edge supervision, thereby improving contextual representation. Experiments on standard datasets (UCF-101 and UCF-101-ext) demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods. The 2021 Image Similarity Challenge (ISC2021) aimed to identify matching images within a collection of 1,024 randomly gathered web images. Organized under the vision that large-scale image retrieval will become a fundamental tool for future image analysis and digital forensics, the competition evaluated various image similarity methods through detailed result analysis and ranking. This report details the challenge's organization and provides an in-depth examination of the top-ranked models—Clour, DFTNet, and ViT-SIM—along with a synthesis of key outcomes and breakthrough findings. Additionally, we outline promising future directions for large-scale image search, including the adoption of deep neural networks, self-supervised learning, and contrastive loss functions. We further emphasize the critical role of deep learning in robust image search, address common pitfalls in evaluation metrics, and propose avenues for enhancing both the quality and robustness of these models. Finally, we conclude by suggesting that multi-granularity image similarity research will be essential for future image search applications. Overall, we believe this challenge will significantly advance the field of image similarity. The source code and pre-trained models are accessible at https://github.com/Clour-Project/ISC2021. This study investigates nuclear matter properties at zero temperature under strong magnetic fields using the lowest-order current-vortex lock (LOCV) technique within a magnetic Walecka model. A key observation is that the magnetic field induces anisotropy in energy, momentum, and velocity due to quantized quark transverse motion into Landau levels. Specifically, transverse velocity and pressure (defined as $B\cdot P$) are anisotropic, whereas longitudinal velocity and momentum remain isotropic. Notably, for energies, the isotropic component exceeds the sum of the transverse and longitudinal contributions. In the strong-field regime, the velocity components align closely with those of cold nuclear matter, while the pressure components diverge significantly. At high densities, the isotropic pressure component surpasses the isotropic energy, whereas the sum of transverse and longitudinal pressure components remains below the energy. Furthermore, the LOCV method yields a softer equation of state compared to the static LOCV approach. These variations in nuclear matter properties relative to the magnetic field and chirality can influence the equation of state, which is crucial for understanding neutron star phenomena. Consequently, these findings may help interpret observational data regarding magnetars, pulsars, and binary neutron star mergers. Additionally, the LOCV framework can be extended to analyze quark matter, offering insights into magnetic field effects on the quark-gluon plasma. Privacy and security have become critical concerns in machine learning, particularly in scenarios where data remains distributed across multiple entities. Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as a promising solution to address these challenges while maintaining communication efficiency. This paper presents a comprehensive survey of state-of-the-art FL techniques, offering an in-depth analysis of various methods categorized into three types: aggregation-based, differential, and differential aggregation-based FL. We examine the principles, advantages, and limitations of each approach to guide future research and provide practitioners with the necessary guidance to select appropriate strategies for specific scenarios. Additionally, we evaluate the performance of federated models against centralised counterparts in terms of accuracy, efficiency, and security. Finally, we identify open challenges in the field and offer insights to direct the community's future efforts. Overall, this study provides readers with a systematic and holistic understanding of privacy-preserving FL, facilitating more informed decisions for both academic research and industrial applications. We conducted far-ultraviolet (FUV) observations of the Taurus, Perseus, Aquila, and A21 cloud complex using the FUV-M instrument aboard the Korean Faint Object Telescope and Satellite (KFTS). These observations targeted 15 molecular clouds to analyze their cloud structures and elemental abundances. The resulting FUV-M images reveal the cloud complex as a continuous structure featuring several bright regions, which are attributed to FUV emission originating from the cloud edges. By analyzing the FUV spectra of these edges, we determined the electron temperature and hydrogen abundance. Our results indicate that the FUV emission is primarily caused by the photoionization of interstellar hydrogen by ambient ultraviolet photons. Furthermore, the derived hydrogen abundances align well with values reported in previous studies. Finally, we provide a detailed analysis of the cloud complex's structure and physical conditions based on our observations. Specifically, the FUV emission from the cloud edges suggests that the clouds are not in pressure equilibrium. Additionally, the cloud edges appear to be expanding, driven by pressure gradients resulting from the ionization of interstellar hydrogen. These observations offer valuable insights for future studies of the cloud complex's structure and physical conditions. Overall, this study represents a significant advancement in FUV observations of the Taurus-Perseus-Aquila complex. Similar observations of other molecular clouds are expected to yield valuable results. This work is anticipated to significantly contribute to our understanding of the cloud complex's formation and evolution. Tables constitute a significant portion of scientific literature and are crucial for analyzing research findings. However, retrieving them from documents remains an under-researched area, primarily due to the non-standardized format of tables in PDFs. Existing solutions often rely on XML tags or utilize document structure in a limited capacity. This paper introduces the use of representation embedding for table retrieval in PDFs, leveraging a Graph Neural Network (GNN) to table representations. We also conduct experiments on retrieval tasks, comparing our GNN approach against a baseline that uses the PDF's document structure to achieve similar results. Finally, we perform an ablation study to evaluate the impact of various document structure features on global and local retrieval performance. Finally, our PDF-based representation models demonstrate competitive performance against state-of-the-art solutions on the PubTabNet dataset, which is the most widely used benchmark in the field. Furthermore, we introduce a new dataset, PDFTableRetrieval, specifically for table retrieval tasks, and provide open-source code for our document structure representation models at https://github.com/ahmedmohamed1999/Graph-Neural-Networks-and-Representation-Embedding-for-Table-Retrieval-in-PDF-Document. We introduce a two-stage hierarchy of cognitive hierarchies designed for multi-stage games under information insufficiency. Our cognitive hierarchy model incorporates the extensive form game structure, handling the possibility that players may lack knowledge about others' payoffs or strategies. We demonstrate that a fixed-point concept, where no player has an incentive to lower their level of thinking, serves as a prediction for such games. Furthermore, we establish an existence theorem for this equilibrium and provide an approximation method, similar to the continuous rationality approach used in single-stage extensive form games. We also analyze a series of examples, proving that our proposed solution concept can effectively guide player behavior in these scenarios. Additionally, we extend this framework to include the probability structure, thereby generating a series of first-order, second-order, and Nash equilibria. We demonstrate the utility of these concepts by applying them to a new class of multi-stage games with information insufficiency, a setting that extends beyond the scope of Selten's (1965) bank game. Our findings indicate that these solution concepts can successfully predict behavior in both the bank game and this broader class of games. Finally, we illustrate how these frameworks can be applied to environmental economics, where agents interact within a dynamic setting of insufficient information regarding others' cost functions. We show that our proposed solution concepts can predict the equilibrium outcomes of a two-stage technology adoption game. Finally, we present preliminary empirical evidence supporting the predictions of these frameworks. Specifically, we examine a two-stage experiment involving a technology adoption game and a public goods game. In both cases, we observe strong support for our proposed solution, with no significant evidence of higher-order beliefs. In the technology adoption game, we also find strong support for our framework utilizing first-order, second-order, and Nash equilibria. These results suggest that our proposed solution can serve as a robust prediction for behavior in this class of games. Approximate membership tests utilize a probabilistic data structure (PDS) to quickly verify if an item exists, allowing a controlled false negative where a member item might be reported as non-existent. This feature enables the detection of non-member items, as any item deemed non-existent is definitively not a member. However, identifying items that are actually members requires positive confirmation; without it, the focus remains solely on optimizing performance for non-members. We introduce a novel approach to reduce false positives by introducing a rare event flag on buckets, ensuring that every member item is eventually detected and flagged. This method results in a structure where the entire collection serves as a false-positive-free filter for all stored items. Experimental findings indicate that this optimization can significantly enhance the efficiency of the PDS. Specifically, for a PDS managing a dataset of 100,000 items within 1,000 buckets, performance improved by 40% to 60%. For datasets exceeding one million items with 1,000 buckets, the speedup reaches 60% to 80%. The implementation code and results are publicly accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar2000/amqf. Additionally, this paper presents a new PDS, the Universal Filter (UF), which is highly tunable and can be configured to function as a standard or advanced approximate membership test. The UF's design is straightforward, relying on a single bucket per item, a single hash function, and a single array. The technique for achieving false-positive-free filtering is also applicable to other PDS structures, such as Bloom filters. The paper provides a detailed analysis of the optimization's performance, including cost-benefit evaluations. Furthermore, the study examines the UF's suitability for various application scenarios. This study theoretically examines three-body recombination involving two polar spinor atoms in the presence of a third body, employing a density matrix formalism. The analysis identifies two distinct regimes: a weak-field regime where only one hyperfine state is populated and a strong-field regime where two hyperfine states are populated. The interaction between atoms is modeled via mean-field theory, while laser coupling between these hyperfine states is represented within the three-body framework. Numerical simulations of three-body recombination across different laser intensities reveal that in the strong-field regime, laser coupling between two atoms of opposite spins results in an effective spinor atom-molecule transformation. This phenomenon is characterized by the disintegration of molecules and the excitation of atoms to higher laser-coupled levels. These findings suggest the potential for developing spinor atom-molecule devices and spinor three-body engines. Furthermore, the study predicts a three-body induced atom-molecule dissociation at high laser intensities and outlines the specific regimes for complete atom-molecule conversion and equal population of laser-coupled levels. These outcomes are derived from solving the time-dependent three-body system equations and have distinct implications for recombination rate coefficients. Finally, the proposed model and predictions can be experimentally validated using existing cold-atom systems. Specifically, the predicted atom-molecule dissociation can be tested with ultracold KRb molecules, and the complete atom-molecule conversion can be verified using ultracold $^{87}$Rb atoms. To achieve these validations, laser coupling between atoms must be established through three-body radiative association. The proposed theoretical model and experimental procedures are expected to reveal novel phenomena and enable the investigation of various novel effects. Theoretically, the study elucidates the intricate dynamics of three-body recombination in spinor systems, while experimentally, it demonstrates the utilization of three-body radiative association. These contributions establish a foundation for advancing theoretical and experimental research into spinor three-body recombination. Additionally, the work addresses a significant gap in current three-body recombination theory by accurately describing the effects of laser coupling between atomic spin states. Ultimately, this research offers valuable insights for future advancements in quantum chemistry and atomic physics. Specifically, the study investigates the influence of laser coupling on three-body recombination, a factor previously overlooked in existing theories. The proposed theoretical framework and suggested experimental validations are anticipated to significantly contribute to the ongoing and future study of three-body recombination in spinor systems. This study introduces a novel Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) framework designed for incompressible multi-component fluid-structure interaction (FSI) simulations. The approach integrates a height function method to calculate the surface normal vector (NV) within a mesh-free environment, isothermal Navier-Stokes solvers based on the projection method for multi-component incompressible incompressible Navier-Stokes equations utilizing the viscous force model and the artificial thickness (AT) scheme. To enhance numerical stability and precision, a new, more stable and accurate calculation of the pressure Laplacian (PL) function is developed. Additionally, a new parallelized algorithm is presented to minimize the impact of kernel errors at fluid-structure interfaces, thereby significantly improving simulation accuracy. The framework is validated against a circular cylinder subjected to a uniform flow with a Reynolds number of 100, a square plate oscillating vertically within a binary fluid mixture, and a square plate undergoing pitching motion in a ternary fluid mixture. The results demonstrate the high precision and stability of the proposed framework. Finally, the AT scheme is applied to investigate the dynamics of a square plate oscillating in a binary fluid mixture, yielding a comprehensive understanding of the complex multi-component FSI behavior. The study examines the influence of various parameters, including the amplitude, frequency, fluid-structure Reynolds number, and the volume fraction of each component in the binary fluid mixture, on the dynamics of the oscillating square plate. Key findings include the identification of a symmetric mode at low Reynolds numbers and an asymmetric mode at high Reynolds numbers, where the latter exhibits a higher drag coefficient. Furthermore, it is observed that the amplitude of the plate's motion diminishes as the volume fraction of the heavier component within the binary fluid mixture increases. Finally, it is noted that the drag coefficient of the plate rises with the fluid-structure Reynolds number. These results provide valuable insights into the dynamics of square plates oscillating in multi-component fluid mixtures, a phenomenon that has not been previously explored. Machine learning is rapidly becoming one of the most critical areas in contemporary science and engineering, with quantum machine learning emerging as a promising new discipline that leverages the unique properties of quantum mechanics. While the theoretical foundations for classical and quantum algorithms addressing supervised learning are well-established, unsupervised learning remains a less explored domain. This study presents the first all-encompassing unsupervised learning framework designed for noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) systems. Utilizing the programmable superconducting quantum computer comprising 64 qubits developed by the University of Science and Technology of China, we experimentally demonstrated the implementation of various clustering algorithms within this system. These processes were optimized by exploiting the entropy of the quantum state, and the outcomes were evaluated using mutual information. By accessing the complete landscape of the quantum objective function, our approach demonstrates superior performance compared to the Hessian-based method proposed by Cerebras. Furthermore, the findings from this experiment validate the feasibility of quantum unsupervised learning on existing superconducting processors. Additionally, this research marks the inaugural publication to demonstrate quantum learning on such a machine, indicating that quantum technologies could soon become integral to data analysis systems. The source code for this study is available at: https://github.com/USTCSQ/QML4ICIP2021.

This study introduces Hopper, a multi-hop transformer designed for the spatiotemporal inductive bias inherent in video and visual forecasting. To address the temporal dimension, the model establishes a latent state updated via multi-hop attention, which generates an observation for the transformer transformer and manages uncertainty through a Gaussian distribution. For spatial inductive bias, Hopper decomposes the problem into two components: a shared spatial prior shared across all time steps, which is a temporal prior applicable to every spatial location. The spatial prior is parameterized using a global filter and a per-pixel local filter, while the temporal prior is defined by a shared mean and variance parameterized by a filter. We demonstrate that Hopper, an end-to-end trainable framework, can be inextricably linked to a statistical forecaster, yielding significant performance gains over other transformer-based baselines. Furthermore, our ablation studies indicate that Hopper outperforms other approaches on CUB-200, UCIC-PBZ, and GSS datasets. Additionally, the efficacy of the spatiotemporal inductive bias is validated through qualitative and quantitative analyses. Finally, we highlight Hopper's success across various video and forecast prediction tasks. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ashishgarg/Hopper. This work introduces a model-independent framework for determining the $W$ boson mass, utilizing top quark decay data from experiments. As a proof of concept, we examine the lepton-pair and $b$-jet yield relationship across various $W$ decay masses, based on Monte Carlo simulations. In a real experimental setting, this method would eliminate the systematic uncertainty of 30 MeV (at 1$\sigma$) associated with top quark decay modeling, which currently limits precision mass measurements. Furthermore, the approach is entirely independent of jet energy calibration. We demonstrate that this technique can be validated with existing data and that current measurements of the lepton-pair and $b$-jet yield correlation are already precise enough to significantly enhance the accuracy of the $W$ mass determination. Additionally, we show that the observed uncertainty in these measurements is primarily statistical, indicating that the method will substantially improve the precision of the $W$ mass measurement. This represents a crucial step toward a future $W$ mass determination that is independent of jet energy scale uncertainties. Our findings suggest that an analysis of the lepton-pair and $b$-jet yield correlation could be performed on the current CMS and ATLAS datasets, which have already achieved a precision of 10 MeV (1$\sigma$). This level of precision is sufficient to achieve a relative uncertainty on the $W$ mass of approximately 10$^{-4}$. Such accuracy is essential for the upcoming Standard Model test at the future circular collider. We also explore how to maximize the information extracted from top decay data in a future scenario involving an integrated luminosity of 300 fb$^{-1}$. This would enable a study of the $W$ mass using the lepton-pair and $b$-jet yield correlation with a precision of 5 MeV (1$\sigma$). This level of precision is three times better than what is expected from an analysis of top quark mass distributions and ten times better than the precision achievable from an analysis of jet energy and kinematic variables. Furthermore, the $W$ mass determination derived from the lepton-pair and $b$-jet yield correlation is independent of jet energy scale uncertainties. Consequently, the total uncertainty on the $W$ mass determination is reduced to 3.5 MeV (1$\sigma$), representing an improvement by a factor of three compared to the best current measurements. Telepresence robots (TPRs) facilitate remote operation and communication by serving as mobile virtual companions. As these systems become more advanced and capable of managing additional devices, they are also introducing new sources of frustration for users. This study investigates the cognitive demands and usability challenges inherent to TPR navigation. We conducted a cognitive load assessment and Fitts' law-based benchmarking to establish baseline metrics for TPR control. Furthermore, we performed a structured evaluation of cognitive loads during troubleshooting and introduced user-generated tasks to examine stress responses. These experiments covered decision-making, memory, problem-solving, and attention processes. Our findings indicate that TPR navigation imposes relatively low cognitive loads, with performance and cognitive effort aligning closely with Fitts' law predictions. Additionally, decision-related cognitive loads were observed to be lower than those related to motion. Ultimately, we demonstrate that interactive evaluations using TPRs offer a more realistic approach to assessing user experience than traditional methods relying on static stimuli. By incorporating user-generated tasks, interactive QoE evaluations capture workloads related to decision-making, memory, and attention that static methods miss, thereby providing deeper insights into the true demands of telerobotic operation. Hierarchical linear analysis (also known as multi-level, mixed-effects, or random-effects models) serves as a potent method for analyzing data characterized by non-independent observations. Within the statistical software R, the \texttt{lme4} package offers \texttt{glmer} for fitting generalized linear models with random effects and \texttt{lmer} for standard linear models. However, these tools focus solely on fixed and random effects, omitting any consideration of parameter uncertainty. In contrast, Bayesian hierarchical linear models enable the specification of uncertainty around parameters, the assignment of prior probability distributions to reflect initial beliefs, and the visualization of how prior beliefs are updated based on the data. This paper outlines an approach to integrating Bayesian methods into linear models using the \texttt{brms} package. It further addresses common data analysis challenges, including non-normal data, missing values, and data clustering. Finally, the discussion presents a linear model applied to a real-world dataset and explores strategies for handling unmeasured confounders. The exercises utilized in this paper can be accessed at \url{https://github.com/MichaelJGeyer/IGBM2019}. Additional resources are available at \url{https://mueller-axl.github.io/brms/}. The \texttt{brms} package is a comprehensive resource for implementing Bayesian linear models. This paper is designed for practitioners with foundational knowledge of linear models who are interested in adopting a Bayesian framework. No advanced mathematical background is required. The session aims to help attendees build robust linear models while gaining insights into their underlying uncertainties. By adopting a Bayesian perspective, practitioners can gain a more profound understanding of their data. Furthermore, this approach facilitates a more nuanced comprehension of causal relationships, a topic that will also be briefly addressed. The session will foster interaction and dialogue throughout. This paper introduces a rigorous mathematical framework for Mafia, defining its mechanisms, terminology, and end conditions with precision to enable research into the game's dynamics and conclusions. We provide a combinatorial analysis of initial state configurations for small populations, examining the probability that mafia players win in the first round of killing. Additionally, we simulate various strategies to analyze the variance of victory and analyze the impact of random number generation on the game's initial state. Finally, we conclude by discussing how this mathematical framework can inform the design of the game's parameters. The findings from our research can assist players in comprehending the underlying mechanics and stochastic nature of Mafia. Furthermore, this framework serves as a foundation for scholars to investigate the game's various aspects and facilitates designers in creating more engaging experiences through optimized parameter selection. **Aims.** Our primary objective is to determine how gas accretion influences the structural evolution of protoplanetary disks. **Methods.** To achieve this, we developed a self-consistent model that accounts for gas accretion onto multiple planets. **Results.** (i) Accretion onto a pair of giant planets (GP1 and GP2) significantly affects their mass gain and the disk's vertical structure. When the separation between GP1 and GP2 is small, accretion onto GP1 creates a shock wave in the disk that impedes flow toward the star, thereby accelerating gas accretion onto GP2. Conversely, if GP2 lies above GP1, accretion onto GP1 generates a wake in the upper disk layer that accelerates GP1's mass accumulation while suppressing gas accretion onto GP2. (ii) Accretion rates onto individual planets vary depending on their position relative to GP1 and GP2, as they are sensitive to local changes in gas accretion rates driven by disk structure modifications caused by GP1. (iii) The evolution of gas accretion rates onto the planets and the resulting mass ratios are highly dependent on the initial conditions of the disk and the planets. **Conclusions.** Accretion onto GP1 can either accelerate or suppress gas accretion onto GP2, contingent upon their relative positions. Consequently, the final mass of GP2 is not solely determined by GP2's own properties but is also influenced by GP1's characteristics. This study demonstrates that the accretion history of individual planets is inherently linked to that of their neighbors. Furthermore, the evolution of gas accretion rates onto planets and the resulting mass ratios depend on the initial disk configuration and planetary mass ratios, implying that the accretion histories of individual planets are not independent. These findings have significant implications for the formation and evolution of multi-planet systems. This work is based on a Japanese Research Fellowship (JSPS KAKENHI) grant (Grant No. 17K05370). Electronic transport within armchair carbon nanotubes is governed by phonon scattering. In this study, we present a carbon nanotube film utilizing a top-gate architecture, demonstrating clear signs of phonon-assisted electron conduction. Our findings indicate that electron-phonon coupling is substantial in this film, with a maximum gain of electron mobility driven by phonon scattering reaching approximately 100. These results offer the first proof of phonon-limited electron transport in a two-dimensional carbon nanotube architecture, a crucial advancement for carbon-based electronics. Furthermore, we propose a theoretical framework to interpret these experimental observations. This work underscores the critical role of phonon scattering in advancing carbon electronics and establishes a vital link between fundamental physics research and technological applications. Additionally, our proposed theoretical model is anticipated to find broad application in the field. This study introduces a novel fuzzy k-means algorithm designed for high-dimensional data, which incorporates variable feature weights. In many high-dimensional datasets, certain features possess greater relevance than others for clustering tasks. Traditional fuzzy k-means approaches treat all features as equally important and process them uniformly during clustering. To address this limitation, we propose an entropy-driven Variable Feature Weighted Fuzzy K-Means (EVFFK) algorithm. Initially, the method calculates the information entropy of each feature. Subsequently, it assigns a weight to every feature based on its entropy values, ensuring that more relevant features receive higher weights. Finally, the algorithm executes the fuzzy k-means process utilizing these weighted features. Experimental results demonstrate that EVFFK surpasses both the standard fuzzy k-means and other entropy-driven weighted fuzzy k-means algorithms in terms of clustering accuracy and stability on high-dimensional data. Furthermore, the method is effective for clustering high-dimensional data with missing values, an area where existing algorithms struggle. The proposed approach was evaluated on high-dimensional datasets from the UCI Machine Learning repository and various real-world sources, alongside synthetic datasets containing missing values, with consistent performance improvements observed across all instances. Additionally, the method's efficiency was confirmed through computational complexity analysis and benchmark testing. Ultimately, EVFFK emerges as a highly effective solution for high-dimensional data clustering. Finally, the paper concludes by outlining potential applications of this approach in bioinformatics and other fields.

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is a well-known class of nonconvex, nonconcave optimization problems with diverse applications, serving as the foundation for models like Adaptive Subgradient Method in the Dark (D-SGD) and Curiosity in recommender systems. This paper investigates the theoretical characteristics of general MoE structures. We first demonstrate that standard gradient descent (SD) fails to provide any guarantees for learning general MoE problems and can result in catastrophic performance degradation. Subsequently, we introduce a novel and unifying approach called "consistent SGD" (CoSGD), which unifies the analysis of various MoE types and ensures both convergence and statistical efficiency. We show that the number of samples required by CoSGD to achieve a specific estimation error matches the sample complexity of the corresponding population problem. Furthermore, we present a general framework for analyzing MoE structures, proving that with appropriate modifications to CoSGD, algorithms can be designed to achieve statistical efficiency for specific MoE forms. Finally, we apply this framework to analyze a general class of robust MoE regression problems, offering a comprehensive understanding of their convergence properties. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets confirm the superior performance of CoSGD compared to existing methods. This work advances the theory of nonconvex optimization by designing algorithms capable of achieving optimal sample complexity for nonconcave optimization tasks. The source code will be made available upon publication.

This study explores chip-firing games, visual directed networks, and specific abelian varieties linked to visual networks, extending the research found in [12] and [11]. While [11] establishes an analogy between non-aggressive monodromy graphs and Jacobians, this paper demonstrates that a similar relationship exists for monodromy graphs. Specifically, [11] identifies the fine Jacobian as the most appropriate geometric object, whereas this paper shows the Prym variety fulfills the same role. This connection to Prym varieties aligns with findings in the related field of factorization algebras [5]. The text also defines the visual open graph, visual open monodromy graph, and non-deforming open monodromy graph, drawing a Jacobian analogy for the latter two as well. Finally, the work investigates the relationship between these open graph varieties and the standard Jacobian or Prym variety, presenting a conjecture regarding this relationship along with a partial result. A significant component of this conjecture posits that open, or "sandwich," divisors constitute the most natural chip configuration for these graphs. While a complete result is derived for certain degenerate monodromy graphs, it remains an open question for general cases. The authors anticipate that this conjecture will prove valuable for ongoing research into chip-firing games, visual directed networks, and factorization algebras. Notably, this conjecture represents a distinct and potentially novel factor in the recently proven [2] relationship between the factorization algebra of a surface and its compactified linearized Picard scheme. Furthermore, the paper offers a fresh perspective on the classical Riemann-von Neumann theorem concerning the Jacobian of an open Riemann surface. Finally, the authors propose a conjecture suggesting that chip-firing games on visual networks may provide a new, independent, and potentially more intuitive proof of the Riemann-von Neumann theorem. This proposal stems from the authors' background in both chip-firing games and the algebraic geometry of Riemann surfaces, and the text includes a preliminary outline of this conjecture. The intended audience includes researchers and advanced graduate students in combinatorics, combinatorial mathematics, and related disciplines. No prior knowledge of chip-firing games, directed visual networks, or the specific forms of the Jacobian and Prym type theorems is assumed. Although string theory suggests that quantum gravitational effects could induce anisotropies in light propagation through photon birefringence, measurements of cosmic double refraction have shown these effects are negligible, implying corresponding limits on how many such operators exist. Since these birefringence terms originate from the non-minimal coupling of photons to global symmetries, our analysis demonstrates that cosmic refraction measurements restrict the number of quantum gravity-induced global symmetries. This finding offers a non-theoretical constraint on these symmetries, which is a fundamental component of both the Standard Model and string theory. Specifically, we examine constraints on $SU(N)$, $Sp(2N)$, and $F_4$ by comparing quantum gravity arguments regarding global symmetry breaking with empirical observations on cosmic double refraction. Additionally, we present constraints on $U(1)$ symmetries, which are less rigorously supported by quantum gravity, and explore the broader implications of our findings. Finally, we highlight that our conclusions are consistent with recent experimental results from optical metamaterials and with quantum gravity models featuring extended symmetry breaking. We report on the first UVIT observation of NGC 4147, a globular cluster located in the M31 halo. The cluster's age is estimated at 12.5 Gyr, with a metallicity of [Fe/H] = -1.95. Our analysis reveals a distance of 640 kpc and a line-of-sight velocity of 290 km/s. We identified 13 stars with absolute magnitudes greater than 25.5 and colors exceeding 0.2. Spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting indicates that 10 of these UV-bright stars are likely post-red giant branch (post-RGB) stars, characterized by effective temperatures greater than 28,000 K and masses surpassing 5 solar masses. The remaining three stars remain uncertain due to limited data. Additionally, we identified two candidate binary systems among the UV-bright population, with one exhibiting an orbital period of 1.5 days. Our investigation also uncovered two blue horizontal branch stars, two blue stragglers, and a candidate blue straggler. Furthermore, we detected two stars with circumstellar disks; one possesses a disk temperature of 100 K and a mass of 0.0002 solar masses, while the other has a temperature of 150 K and a mass of 0.0003 solar masses. Finally, we determined the distance modulus to be 24.97 ± 0.05. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the cluster's formation and evolution. The cluster's line-of-sight velocity and distance align with those of M31, suggesting NGC 4147 may be a member of the M31 halo. The presence of binary systems and stars with masses exceeding the typical horizontal branch mass further supports an early accretion scenario for NGC 4147. This study represents the most comprehensive investigation of UV bright stars in a globular cluster to date. The UVIT instrument's capability to detect and study such rare and unique stars in GCs underscores its significance for advancing stellar astrophysics. The data obtained from this observation will be valuable for future studies of the cluster. The UVIT observatory's sensitivity to UV radiation makes it an ideal tool for investigating the UV-emitting population in globular clusters. This expository note offers proof of the Mumford conjecture. The work is a condensed adaptation of the original proof, which incorporated technical refinements tailored to methods that were not available at the time. For further reading, see Brownlowe's notes. The demonstration of the Mumford conjecture relies on two primary components: first, an embedding of the stabilised second homotopy group of a closed orientable three-fold into the stabilised first homology of a closed orientable surface; second, a weighted version of this embedding. In each scenario, the weighted fundamental class of a source surface from a Morita map serves as the image. To establish finiteness, an additional argument is required: for the second claim, one must prove that mapping degrees are non-degenerate. In both instances, the mapping degrees of the images under the Morita map can be computed via intersection numbers within the mapping torus. These two claims are interconnected through a third assertion: that mapping degrees can be expressed as third Gromov-Witten invariants. Consequently, the third claim enables the reduction of the problem to Gromov-Witten theory, where the first two assertions are validated. The third claim follows from a weighted Gromov-Witten three-fold formula, which is derived through a weighted version of the Taubes isomorphism linking the third quantum cohomology of a Calabi-Yau three-fold to its Floer cohomology. To streamline the exposition, we have substituted original notations with more familiar alternatives and elaborated on certain arguments. We believe these simplifications will make the proof more accessible to a broader audience. Additionally, weighted techniques are not strictly necessary; instead, they can be reformulated using twisted methods, which are more aligned with the original proof's approach. We present both versions to illustrate the structural relationship between the weighted and twisted formulations. We anticipate that the weighted technique will prove more effective in future applications. Furthermore, we have expanded upon the original exposition regarding the relationship between the Gromov-Witten class and the mapping degree. The primary objective of this note is to elucidate the relationships among the three claims presented in the introduction and to provide a modern exposition utilizing weighted methods. This exposition prioritizes clarity regarding the relationships between these claims over historical fidelity to the original proof. A significant strength of deep learning is its ability to map complex input data into compact representations that facilitate downstream tasks like classification and clustering. While various transfer learning strategies exist, theoretical insights into why these learned representations achieve high performance remain scarce. This study examines the problem of clustering under both supervised and unsupervised transfer learning paradigms. We establish two key theoretical findings. First, we demonstrate that even when source and target clustering tasks differ, supervision can align the input data distributions of independent neural networks across both scenarios. Second, we prove that a neural network can learn a representation that maintains distribution similarity at multiple hierarchical levels, provided that multilingual and multitask learning constraints are met. These insights are validated through experiments on transfer learning tasks involving CIFAR-10, CUB-200, and NABE. Our results indicate that representing complex input data in a multi-level manner is a critical factor for deep learning transferability. Furthermore, we propose a novel training algorithm that integrates supervised, unsupervised, multitask, and multilingual learning to enhance transferability. Extensive experiments confirm that this proposed algorithm outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in deep transfer learning. Recent years have seen a surge in studying information diffusion within networked systems, driven by the need to mitigate outbreaks, fake news, and cascading failures in critical infrastructure. While many models rely on network structures characterized by communities or modules, the specific role these networks play in regulating the diffusion of infectious agents, phenomena, or behaviors remains largely unexplored. This study employs both analytical and numerical methods to investigate how modular structures influence information spread. Our findings indicate that modular networks significantly slow down diffusion compared to non-modular ones of identical structure. We demonstrate that high modularity restricts the diffusion process to local communities, thereby reducing the overall diffusion speed. Furthermore, we establish that low modularity allows for faster diffusion, with the exact relationship between modularity and diffusion speed dependent on the network's average degree. These insights provide a deeper understanding of how network topology influences information propagation, holding potential applications for controlling outbreaks, the spread of misinformation, and critical infrastructure failures. Our results can aid in the design of optimal intervention strategies to prevent or manage outbreaks and the dissemination of behaviors or trends. Specifically, our analysis reveals a threshold modularity (or connectivity) below which rapid diffusion occurs, offering guidance for implementing timely interventions. Finally, we present a novel analytical solution for predicting the final density of infected nodes in network models. This tool enables researchers to derive accurate estimates of key epidemic metrics, such as final infection prevalence and the basic reproduction number, without relying on numerical methods. This represents a significant advancement toward a more comprehensive theoretical understanding of network-based epidemics. We anticipate these developments will foster further research into network epidemiology. Our work offers new perspectives on how network structures impact the spread of information, with potential applications ranging from viral marketing to the spread of diseases. Additionally, we propose a novel algorithm for identifying network communities, which can assist in tailoring interventions to specific network structures. Our analyses uncover a fundamental link between network modularity and the final density of infected nodes, providing a comprehensive understanding of how network topology influences epidemic dynamics. These insights could guide the design of effective interventions to control or prevent outbreaks. Finally, we introduce an innovative approach to predicting infection outcomes, which could enhance our ability to manage and mitigate epidemics. Our research paves the way for future investigations into network epidemics, potentially leading to the development of more effective public health strategies. Our work also highlights the importance of considering network structure when designing public health interventions, which could improve the effectiveness of such strategies. Leveraging the Relative Entropy Conjecture regarding log-canonical thresholds within algebraic geometry, we demonstrate that the distinctiveness of random polynomials can be quantitatively assessed by examining the entropy of points in complex projective space relative to a fixed polynomial. This finding holds significant utility for measuring the distinctiveness of data within machine learning frameworks. Furthermore, the proof methodology is extensive enough to establish certain known results concerning random polynomials. Specifically, we establish that random polynomials exhibit essentially no critical points, satisfy the Chebyshev equioscillation theorem, approximate any complex function arbitrarily well, and approximate any complex shape arbitrarily closely. These attributes collectively indicate that neural networks trained on such polynomials could achieve superior generalization capabilities. Additionally, random polynomials facilitate highly accurate interpolation, allowing for the reconstruction of unknown data from a limited sample of known data points. This capacity to predict new data points with high precision is a highly desirable trait for many neural network applications. A key application of our findings involves the high-precision prediction of unknown stock market data, where historical data is utilized as input to a neural network to forecast future market trends. We have developed specific neural network training algorithms for distinct functions, demonstrating that training on random polynomials yields networks with exceptional predictive accuracy. Our approach utilizes data parallel training across multiple GPUs, enabling the training of large neural networks on extensive datasets. This scalability ensures that the quality of predictions remains consistent regardless of the volume of available historical data. To validate the distinctiveness of random polynomials, we computed the log canonical threshold for points in projective space relative to various polynomials using GPUMPI, an algorithm specifically designed for calculating this threshold. This computational framework facilitates the quick and accurate assessment of polynomial distinctiveness. The GPUMPI algorithm operates on the principle of relative log canonical thresholds, utilizing the property that the log canonical threshold of projective space points relative to the sum of two ideals is at least the minimum of the thresholds of the individual separate ideals. This allows for the determination of the log canonical threshold for random polynomials through the successive addition of summands, with error margins remaining small throughout the process. Our research demonstrates that the log canonical threshold for random polynomials is approximately 1, which is significantly higher than that of specific structured polynomials, thereby confirming their distinctiveness. This result underscores the potential of complex random polynomials for enhancing machine learning model performance. This paper presents discrete-time precision analysis for the time-domain regular perturbation model of an unmodulated direct-link scenario under conditions where perturbation is small. By leveraging the time-scale separation inherent in the model, we derive a recursion for the back-propagated field samples and subsequently develop a precision analysis. We demonstrate that the sample recursion can be precisely represented by a linear time-varying system, offering a more intuitive approach to deriving precision analysis for perturbation models. We derive exact upper bounds for the standard deviation of phase and complex envelope errors, as well as the variance of phase rate error, which exhibit exponential growth. Additionally, we provide approximations for perturbation power, variance, and co-variance, observing that perturbation power is negligible relative to transmission power, while variance and co-variance remain approximately constant and bounded. Finally, we examine the impact of increasing link distance on these metrics and identify a regime where perturbation power is small relative to transmission power, variance and co-variance are bounded, and their correlations are negligible. Simulations confirm that these metrics remain bounded in this regime. The discrete-time precision analysis and simulations are extended to a two-hop time-domain regular perturbation model where amplification is performed at the intermediate node. In this scenario, we show that perturbation power is small relative to transmission power, and both variance and co-variance are bounded. Furthermore, we analyze how these metrics vary with respect to transmission power, variance, and co-variance of the first hop's perturbation, as well as the gain of the intermediate node amplifier. Precision analysis for this model is also expressed using bounded co-variances of perturbation samples from successive time instances. Overall, the analysis and simulations indicate that, provided the intermediate node gain is not excessive, all metrics improve with increasing first hop distance and decrease with increasing second hop distance. However, when the second hop distance becomes large, perturbation power may become significant relative to transmission power. We also discuss the relationship between analysis results and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), noting that while all metrics correlate with SNR, they are not expressed directly as functions of it. Instead, we show that all metrics are monotonically increasing with respect to the SNR of the received signal at the intermediate node. The emergence of mobile devices has led to a proliferation of malicious applications, necessitating the development of various detection methods. While most research focuses on identifying features within the application package files, these artifacts can be easily stripped to generate obfuscated versions that bypass detection. This paper surveys a more fundamental level of analysis: the Android runtime environment. We provide a systematic exploration of runtime-based issue-space evasion attacks, offering a classification of prior work through a newly proposed taxonomy and examining specific case studies. Furthermore, we outline the challenges encountered in this field and suggest potential avenues for future research. We anticipate that this survey will assist researchers in navigating the extensive domain of Android runtime security and issue-space evasion. Additionally, we aim to contribute to the field by identifying gaps that can guide subsequent research efforts. Finally, we hope this work will inspire scholars to delve deeper into this critical area of Android security. Container orchestration |CO| represents a technology that enables containers to function as if they were on a single host, thereby enabling horizontal scaling and fault tolerance. However, current CO solutions face a dilemma: they either offer features and optimizations tailored to specific hardware, resulting in suboptimal resource utilization on diverse machines, or provide optimal local resource management but lack the flexibility to adapt to heterogeneous environments. To address this, we introduce a novel, universal, and lightweight orchestration container (|OC|). This framework enables containers to be deployed and optimized across high-performance computing nodes and cloud infrastructure. The |OC| consists of a light agent running on the host and a client for the container. Applications within the container utilize a unified programming interface that abstracts underlying resource specifics, allowing them to function as if they were local programs. We evaluated the |OC| against Docker and Mesos using benchmarks such as NBody, NAMD, and VASP. The results indicate that the |OC| achieves performance comparable to Mesos and Docker while consuming approximately 100 times less memory. Furthermore, our experiments demonstrate execution times on multiple hosts that are either similar to or faster than those achieved by Mesos and Docker. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ozy-project/ozy. Our findings suggest that an efficient, universal, and lightweight orchestration container is feasible. The primary contributions of this work are the proposed |OC| framework and the methodology for developing containerized, universal, and lightweight orchestration systems. The paper also details applications developed as proof-of-concepts for the |OC|. Finally, the study concludes with a discussion of future work and potential research directions. Research at the Dalian Institute of Physics at the Chinese Academy of Sciences identifies a reentrant, reconfigurable incompressible fluid at the 5/2 quantum Hall filling factor. This phase remains stable up to an electron density of $n=6.55\times10^{11}$ cm$^{-2}$, even in conditions involving moderate Landau-level mixing. This finding aligns with predictions for gapped non-Abelian states characterized by the 10$_v$ state counting rule. Additionally, conductance peaks observed at $2e^2/h$ and $4e^2/h$ suggest the presence of e/2 quasiparticles. These results provide essential context for evaluating 5/2 quantum Hall phases as potential candidates for topological quantum computation. Finally, the study introduces a framework for identifying quantum Hall phases through their state counting properties. This approach corroborates earlier proposals that zero-energy Majorana modes must arise from 10$_v$ phases, which can be either 5$_v$+5$_v$ or 9$_v$+1$_v$. Furthermore, it supports recent theoretical proposals regarding reentrant 5/2 phases that maintain non-Abelian character despite Landau level mixing. Specifically, these mixed-level 5/2 phases are either 5$_{vv5f}$ or 9$_{vv4f}$, where "v" and "f" denote empty electron modes and filled fermionic zero modes, respectively. The observational constraints from gravitational wave detections have recently sparked renewed interest in primordial black holes (PBHs). In a prior study, Thakur demonstrated that allowing the mass function $m(r)$ in the Thakurta metric to vary with radial distance $r$ enables cosmological black holes to exhibit behaviors inconsistent with general relativity. This work critically examines the physical interpretation of such black holes by analyzing their spacetime geometry. We establish the necessity of interpreting the coordinate radius as the areal radius, which necessitates redefining the mass function as areal-independent. Consequently, we establish a one-to-one correspondence between this generalized Thakurta metric and the regular dilaton black hole solution. Furthermore, we clarify the relationship between the advanced Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates employed by Thakur and those utilized by Johnson and Trivedi. Our findings indicate that Johnson and Trivedi's dilaton black hole can serve as an effective model for cosmological black holes, with its parameter space constrained by LIGO-Virgo observations. This implies that modeling cosmological black holes via the Thakurta metric does not yield any new viable candidates. Additionally, we show that Johnson and Trivedi's solution satisfies the standard Schwarzschild limit, addressing a gap in Thakur's formulation. Finally, as the first step toward a quantum description, we demonstrate that the Thakurta metric fails to generate a well-defined quantum state. Overall, this paper provides a comprehensive analysis of the Thakurta solution, revealing several inconsistencies. We anticipate that this critical review will prove valuable for future research. Accretion of small particles onto large planetesimals is a critical mechanism in the solar nebula for forming large planetary cores that can subsequently clear their orbits and initiate gap opening. While prior research has largely treated the density of dust in the nebula as uniform, this study investigates how dust density fluctuations influence planet formation via pebble accretion. We developed a model incorporating particle physics, including vertical settling, drift, and coagulation, to simulate dust behavior within the nebula. Our results indicate that coagulation causes dust density fluctuations to increase with radial distance from the sun. Consequently, planet cores formed under these fluctuating conditions grow significantly faster than in steady-state scenarios, with the effect being more pronounced in planetesimals located closer to the sun. Furthermore, the model demonstrates that planet formation is highly sensitive to initial dust density; even minor variations in dust density can result in the complete failure of planet formation. These findings underscore the necessity of accounting for dust density fluctuations when modeling planet formation. Additionally, our analysis reveals that the planet formation window is narrower than previously assumed, and the likelihood of forming super-Earths or gas giants in the inner solar system remains low. Finally, the model predicts the formation of multiple planetary systems, offering an explanation for the observed frequency of multi-planet systems. This research is based on a paper accepted for publication in the Astrophysical Journal. (Translation by Dongsheng)

It is widely recognized that statistical models often require overparameterization to match the degree of underparameterization found in effective regularized models. However, the parameter counts in these models differ significantly, raising the question of why overparameterization must be so extreme. This work demonstrates that the number of parameters in overparameterized models need only suffice to make brute-force brute force search feasible. Consequently, the substantial disparity in parameter counts is a consequence of computational constraints. Furthermore, we apply this insight to the analysis of semi-supervised learning across various generative models. Specifically, we investigate a linear classification framework where the signal lies within a low-dimensional subspace of high-dimensional input data, assuming noiseless observations are possible via linear measurements within that subspace. We analyze a learning scheme comprising two stages: first, collecting a small number of fully observed samples to fit a linear estimator; second, applying semi-supervised learning to partially observed data using the initial linear estimator as a bias term. We establish that the equivalent of brute-force search applies here as well, showing that the linear estimator's parameter count is correctly characterized by the subspace dimension rather than the total number of parameters. Finally, we establish that the sample complexity of the semi-supervised learning phase is necessary for ensuring that the risk of the resulting estimator is near-optimal. Empirical results indicate that the derived parameter and sample complexity bounds are tight. Additionally, we relate our findings to the analysis of variational autoencoders and implicit models. In the context of autoencoders, we demonstrate that the parameter count is dictated by the intrinsic dimension of the data distribution. For implicit models, we find that the parameter count is determined by the intrinsic dimension of the input space rather than the output space. Our theoretical analysis relies on a novel concept termed "weakly sparse" distributions, which encompasses discrete, product, and Gaussian distributions as special cases. We contend that the efficiency of brute-force search serves as a unifying principle for understanding the overparameterization of effective regularized models. Furthermore, the efficiency of such search is intrinsically linked to the concept of "easy" distributions, a category that includes most structured distributions. By examining the relationship between easy and weakly sparse distributions, we derive additional insights regarding overparameterization. Finally, our theoretical framework is supported by extensive experiments that validate the tightness of our derived bounds. These experiments explore the trade-off between the subspace dimension and sample size across three distinct generative models: discrete, product, and Gaussian. This study examines a dial-a-ride problem tailored for elderly individuals in a dense city environment, characterized by short travel distances, strict time constraints, and a high capacity for passengers per vehicle. We introduce a Branch-and-Cut algorithm that utilizes a vast collection of valid inequalities to tackle this scenario. Computational results demonstrate the method's effectiveness on instances with up to 100 requests and three vehicles, achieving a mean optimality gap of under 1% across 99 out of 100 instances. Furthermore, a collaboration with a daily operator revealed that the algorithm produces high-quality solutions in sufficient time for practical application. Finally, we explore several extensions to the basic model to address additional practical constraints. Through extensive experimentation, we identify several novel families of inequalities that significantly enhance solution quality. Our findings indicate that certain inequalities, such as those proposed by Cordeau et al. (2005), are particularly impactful in urban contexts. We also highlight the critical importance of a specific type of inequality for ensuring optimality, offering a technique to reduce its memory footprint. Finally, we investigate how to balance solution quality and computation time by introducing a scheme to dynamically adjust the level of detail during the search process. Experimental results confirm that this approach can yield substantial computational savings. To support future research, we have made our code publicly available for extensions to this problem variant. Our work also introduces a new class of inequalities to the literature and proposes a novel method for handling them. Finally, we suggest several directions for extending this problem variant to incorporate even more practical constraints. All experiments were conducted on a single Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-4790 CPU @ 3.60GHz. Our code utilizes the public version 1.2 of Concorde TSP Solver (http://www.tsp.sol.bham.ac.uk/concorde/).
