This study introduces a SQUID system representing a hybrid quantum-classical architecture capable of executing machine learning (ML) algorithms. Designed to serve as a quantum intelligence platform for executing both supervised and unsupervised ML models, the system features a SQUID inductor that functions as a memristor, enabling persistent storage of trained ML models within its hysteresis loop. This inductor facilitates rapid ML model training, validation, and testing by operating as a single non-volatile memory bit. The research details the design, fabrication, and experimental characterization of a SQUID inductor alongside an in-situ single-electron transistor (SET) sensor used to read the inductor's resistance. Utilizing measured inductor data, the paper demonstrates the implementation of a single neuron as a 2-class SVM classifier that retains its trained weights without power. Additionally, we outline a method for unsupervised single-neuron training via adiabatic evolution along a specific path on the hysteresis loop. Graphite consists of stacked bi-dimensional layers of Coulomb-interacting electrons. It is established that electron-electron interactions induce a many-body instability, resulting in the self-generation of a density wave with a momentum equal to the layer stacking vector. In the bilayer system, this wave can align with the valley-momentum difference between the two valleys. This order breaks translational symmetry, inducing a gap in the electronic spectrum at this momentum and a finite diamagnetic response in low-energy excitations. Consequently, graphite undergoes a quantum phase transition from a metallic to an insulating state. Furthermore, within the renormalization group framework, we have derived the electronic spectrum and determined the velocity of propagating electronic excitations. The calculated density of states near the Fermi level exhibits a power-law behavior. Additionally, we have derived the two-point correlation function in bilayer graphite, demonstrating that excitations propagate as Landau damping excitations. Finally, we have computed the magnetic susceptibility, which displays a power-law divergence at low temperatures. These results are also consistent with experimental observations. Overall, this work provides a comprehensive theoretical understanding of the electronic properties of Coulomb-interacting bilayer graphite. The theoretical results obtained here can serve as a foundation for future experimental investigations. Notably, our results may be applicable to other materials composed of bi-dimensional layers of Coulomb-interacting electrons. For instance, in bilayer boron nitride, the stacking vector connects the two layers, whereas in MoS$_2$, it connects inequivalent valleys. Thus, our calculations may be relevant to systems exhibiting a quantum phase transition from a metallic to a Wigner crystal state. Consequently, we formulate a classification theorem for such operators based on ranks and establish the invariance of rank under strict equivalence. Graphs low in treewidth are highly valuable for computing exact algorithms for complex combinatorial problems within minor-free classes. This study introduces two algorithms capable of producing bounded-treewidth approximations of planar and general minor-free graphs, thereby enhancing graph representations. The first approach, built upon the Lipton-Tarjan separator theorem, achieves an $O(\log n)$ treewidth approximation for $n$-vertex planar graphs in linear time. The second approach utilizes the graph minor theorem; it runs in quasi-linear time relative to the size of the largest minor, also yielding a minor-tight bound for treewidth. Both methodologies extend to weighted graphs, applying to metrics embedded in the Euclidean plane or adhering to the triangle inequality. This work builds on the authors' prior research regarding bounded-genus graphs. The research was conducted while the authors were members of the Simons Institute for the Theory of Computing. Variational quantum algorithms are anticipated to be the first to successfully execute quantum computations on current noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices. A primary challenge in these algorithms is determining an appropriate ansatz to approximate the target unitary operator. In this study, we introduce a novel adaptive variational quantum algorithm capable of automatically constructing an ansatz unitary operator tailored for solving linear systems of equations. Drawing inspiration from the adaptive configuration interaction method, our approach functions by adaptably selecting qubit-excitation operators to build the ansatz. This method demonstrates reduced circuit depth and superior convergence compared to state-of-the-art algorithms for matrix multiplication. Additionally, we extend the algorithm to automatically generate ansatz unitary operators suitable for other linear-system applications, including finding the inverse of a Hermitian matrix and solving the time evolution of the Schrödinger equation. Finally, numerical simulations indicate that adaptive configuration interaction ansatz circuits can accurately solve the Helmholtz equation. The associated Python code is publicly accessible on GitHub. Our work underscores that adaptive variational quantum algorithms hold significant promise for NISQ devices, offering a highly effective solution for linear system problems. The source code is available at \url{https://github.com/zhongqianliu/QubitExcitationBasedAdaptiveVariationalQuantumSolver}. Our implementation is accessible on PennyLane \cite{endres2019pennane}. We introduce a method for learning structured representations of structured data using deep neural networks. Our approach employs variational autoencoders to approximate the data's distribution, utilizing the approximate posterior mean as a structured representation for downstream tasks. We validate this representation on both generative and discriminative tasks. The representation proves effective at predicting both purely discriminative tasks and tasks involving generative predictions. We demonstrate the efficacy of this representation by applying it to two specific scenarios: predicting a distribution's mean and a distribution.

The Atacama Compact Array (ACA) serves as a supplemental interferometer for the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), operating with an effective primary mirror diameter of merely 16 meters. This design minimizes the need for precise source localization, thereby enabling efficient spectral investigations of diffuse emission. This study presents the inaugural survey of the ACA within the context of cometary science, specifically targeting CO, HCN, HCO+, and CS around Comet C/2015 ER61 (PanSTARRS) during its 2015 outburst. The observations reveal that CS emission is spatially distinct from other molecules, originating from a region at least 1000 km from the nucleus. This suggests that the source is either a widely distributed reservoir or a small nucleus component moving at a significantly slower rate than anticipated. These findings align with prior research indicating that small cometary nuclei may harbor large, heterogeneous reservoirs of volatile material. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the ACA is highly effective at isolating the nuclear source to distinguish between the origins of various volatiles. The spectral data also confirm that the ACA can successfully detect and quantify cometary molecular emissions, a capability essential for constraining nucleus properties and understanding the comet's physical and chemical evolution. Ultimately, this research establishes the ACA as a valuable instrument for future cometary spectral studies. Additionally, the study offers the first comprehensive spectral analysis of the 2015 PanSTARRS outburst, providing insights into the comet's nature and history. These observations are part of a broader effort to characterize small, dynamically new comets from the Oort cloud, which is crucial for understanding the early solar system. The resulting ACA survey data will facilitate advancements in cometary science, solar system evolution, and astrochemistry. This work was conducted under ALMA project codes ALMA/JV/SP1/002 and ALMA/090.AL-21. The PanSTARRS designation for Comet C/2015 ER61 was granted by the Maia Foundation.

We introduce SpeechGen, an unsupervised end-to-end neural model capable of generating high-quality, natural-sounding speech from transcriptions and text features alone. By utilizing features such as capitalization, punctuation, and capitalization noise, the model effectively captures aspects of prosody and style. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a straightforward combination of a Style-LVM and a Conditional GAN, trained in an unsupervised manner using only acoustic features like mel-spectrograms, can learn a competitive acoustic model on LibriSpeech. This fully unsupervised approach to speech synthesis offers a highly efficient pipeline that bypasses the need for traditional onerous steps like data cleaning, alignment, and phoneme transcription. Additionally, we show that incorporating a phone set derived from a phone-free variational autoencoder further enhances synthesis performance. Finally, we explore the relationship between synthetic speech and acoustic models by employing speech-to-text (S2T) models to evaluate intelligibility and naturalness on two benchmarks: TIMIT and Readings. This marks the first time unsupervised speech synthesis has reached levels of quality and intelligibility comparable to supervised methods. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/ku2cu/SpeechGen. The associated paper can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.01510. The demo demo video is hosted at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=41142411148. The demo web demo is accessible at https://ku2cu.github.io/SpeechGen. Multi-Objective Mixed-Integer Non-Linear Programming (MO-MINLP) problems are prevalent in numerous real-world scenarios, particularly in supply chain management. Although robust and efficient solvers exist for linear multi-objective problems, the landscape for non-linear cases remains limited. This paper introduces a solution approach grounded in the Branch and Bound (BnB) framework. The proposed algorithm integrates two key innovations: first, it employs the Normalized Summation of Signed Distance (NSSD) as the aggregation function, which facilitates the identification of non-convex Pareto-optimal points; second, it incorporates a dedicated sub-algorithm designed to verify problem feasibility. These enhancements collectively improve the efficiency of the initial search phase. The study concludes by validating the algorithm's effectiveness through a numerical example alongside a comprehensive literature review. Furthermore, the proposed BnB method was implemented in Python and integrated with the open-source JuMP modeling language. The implementation includes a detailed discussion of the algorithm's strengths and areas for future enhancement. A GitHub repository containing the code is available for reference. The authors intend to explore further algorithmic refinements and continue developing the software tool. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/fernandogoncalves/PyMP. We extend prior work within synthetic differential geometry (SDC) by proving that connected Lie groupoids and Lie groups are internally linked, demonstrating that the fundamental group is monoidally equivalent to the space of internal loops. Additionally, we show that any map from a connected Lie groupoid to a groupoid is determined by its spine. We further establish that smooth Kan extensions exist in SDC and construct the integral functor from Lie algebroids to Lie groupoids, confirming its full faithfulness. Finally, we illustrate an application of these findings in the infinite-dimensional context. These findings collectively suggest that many challenges in infinite-dimensional Lie theory can be resolved through methods grounded in these results. Specifically, we show that the problem of identifying canonically associated Lie groupoids for algebroids with abelian isotropies is well-posed in SDC. By incorporating relevant observations and applications, we foster dialogue regarding the necessity of employing synthetic differential geometry to formulate these problems. Furthermore, we demonstrate that key results in Poisson and symplectic geometry rely on techniques derived from the smoothness and canonicity of groupoids and groupoid morphisms in SDC. We also explore the relationship between groupoids and their associated bundles, emphasizing that the smoothness of this correspondence is dependent on whether connections are defined via groupoids or bundles. Finally, we highlight that utilizing groupoids rather than bundles simplifies the verification of essential properties, such as the existence of a canonical anchor. Collectively, these findings indicate that synthetic differential geometry provides a more effective framework for addressing significant problems in infinite-dimensional Lie theory, symplectic geometry, and bundle theory, as well as for discovering new results. This special issue of the Journal of Applied Mathematics and Computing is dedicated to showcasing the advantages of applying synthetic differential geometry to these fields. This article serves as the introduction to the issue. In healthcare, research, and medicine, sensitive patient data is frequently housed within secure environments known as data havens or cyberinfrastructure. Although granting third-party scientists direct access to this data facilitates research, it introduces significant security risks. To address this, we introduce a security model and method that enables safe data access for third parties without compromising the patient data's confidentiality. Our framework utilizes a gateway deployment strategy, where a trusted entity manages user requests through an authentication service, subsequently granting access to specific data subsets. This approach ensures patient privacy by encrypting data within the haven and tagging it with fine-grained access control metadata. When a request is approved, the gateway dynamically serves the authorized subset in a decrypted format. We have developed a prototype of this gateway deployment to demonstrate the security of our model, having successfully conducted a proof-of-concept test using a real-world medical image dataset. Furthermore, this mechanism is compatible with various cyberinfrastructure architectures, including the Virtual Health Environment (VHE) and the Federated Clinical Data Grid (FCDG).

Keywords: Biomedical Data Sharing, Security, Cyberinfrastructure, Medical Imaging, Health Information Exchange.

Aspect-based sentiment analysis enables the detection of sentiment polarity toward specific aspects within a sentence. However, identifying the aspects themselves and the emotions associated with them—often implicit rather than explicit (e.g., distinguishing "delicious" from "sad")—remains a significant challenge. This paper introduces a novel pre-training approach that integrates a new emotion supervision task with a new contrastive learning objective. We first introduce the EmotAb dataset, created by annotating emotions for provided aspects in 1,000 Chinese online reviews. We then develop a pre-training model that integrates aspect labeling with emotion classification. Unlike standard classification, our model leverages supervision from reviews with opposite emotions to generate a contrastive learning objective that enhances both aspect and emotion representation. Experiments on both the existing and our new emotion annotation datasets demonstrate that our model achieves state-of-the-art results. The dataset and source code are accessible at https://github.com/Chenchenchen/SupCAB.

This study extends previous findings by demonstrating that identification and estimation remain feasible even when a probit or logit model is required for the outcome, provided the standard assumption of a jointly multivariate normal distribution applies to the error terms of the outcome and mediator. We present a weighted estimator that achieves efficiency gains by utilizing sampling weights for the subset of the population observed under case-control sampling. Simulation results indicate that the estimator performs well with moderate sample sizes, yielding accurate point estimates and reliable inference. Furthermore, our findings reveal that the bias typically associated with case-control sampling in this context is substantially reduced when using the proposed weighted estimator. Additionally, we explore the challenges of allowing for unknown correlation between the outcome and mediator errors. We conclude that the identification conditions can be effectively tested using this class of weighted estimators, which also facilitates inference. However, we note that the sensitivity analysis required for these tests remains a challenging issue in this framework. Finally, we apply the weighted estimator to data from a study on depression as a mediator linking childhood maltreatment to adult obesity, demonstrating that the method performs effectively with large sample sizes. All results presented in this paper are available for replication. (Software is also being made available). Keywords: Binary mediator; Case-control sampling; Joint distribution; Sensitivity analysis. This study examines a secure, multi-user wireless system enhanced by a Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface (RIS). The RIS is positioned to establish a reflected link between a power-limited source and multiple double-crate users (DUrs), where each DUr is subjected to eavesdropping from a collocated eavesdropper (Eve). The objective is to maximize the sum secrecy rate (SSR) by jointly optimizing RIS phase shifts (PSs) and ground-based precoding (GP) strategies. This optimization is performed under the constraints of DUr power requirements, GP non-linearities, PS unit-modulus limitations, and RIS reflection capabilities. To address the non-convex nature of the SSR maximization problem, an alternating optimization approach is employed to design GP and PS. Furthermore, to mitigate the issue of infinite GP search spaces, a non-convex GP problem is converted into a convex second-order cone programming (SOCP) form utilizing the majorization-minimization (MM) method. Finally, the proposed scheme's robustness is evaluated against hardware impairments (HWIs) affecting both the GP and PS designs. Simulation outcomes confirm the scheme's effectiveness, demonstrating that it outperforms existing state-of-the-art solutions in both ideal and impaired hardware environments. Additionally, the impact of HWIs on the SSR is analyzed as a function of GP iteration count, revealing a steady convergence of the proposed scheme. Hindsight Experience Replacement (HER) has proven effective in reinforcement learning by resampling terminal states and recasting them as successful ones. However, in environments with sparse rewards, agents often fail to learn because they do not acquire enough information about how to reach target states. This paper introduces a new method that simultaneously resamples and relabels human perceptions through a contrastive value strategy. Unlike the standard reward signal, the contrastive value of a perception is defined as the difference between the maximum and minimum state-values achievable from that perception. This approach is demonstrated in two ways: first, as an extension of HER where perception frames are constructed from sequences of other perceptions; and second, in a more general "hindsight summarization" context where a model generates descriptions of perceived sequences to guide agent learning. We apply this strategy to create a new dataset for training a driver-candidate car in a traffic simulation environment. Experimental results indicate that training with our method outperforms both classical HER and the use of raw perception sequences. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our approach can reconstruct the 3D environment from 2D perception sequences and accurately reconstruct the driver's intent from the sequence of perceptions. The energy flux emerging from solar wind sources is a critical component of solar-breeze energy flow, influencing outer solar system bodies and their environments. This study introduces findings from three decades of Parker Solar Probe data, analyzing energy flux across all observed directions from the Sun. Data were collected between 16 and 62.6 solar radii ($R_{\odot}$) during the mission's first four solar encounters, covering the inner heliosphere. Energy flux was determined by integrating the solar wind's dynamic pressure over the solid angle subtended by the inner heliosphere. Results indicate that energy flux increases with heliocentric distance, rising from 100 to 200 nW/m$^2$ between 16 and 62.6 $R_{\odot}$. This trend aligns with the power-law expansion of the solar wind. Additionally, energy flux exhibits strong dependence on solar activity, ranging from 100 to 300 nW/m^2 during solar maximum and 100 to 200 nW/m^2 at solar minimum. This latter finding corroborates earlier research. We also examined energy flux variations across all Parker Solar Probe encounter directions, which align with inner heliospheric density and velocity observations. These findings support the conclusion that the majority of energy in the inner heliosphere originates from the corona, likely driven by a combination of magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) waves and open magnetic flux. This conclusion is further supported by the observed correlation between energy flux and open magnetic flux. Finally, we compare these results with existing literature and discuss implications for solar physics and heliophysics. Specifically, we suggest that energy flux is a significant factor in solar wind-driven ionization, which in turn affects plasma densities and scale lengths in the outer heliosphere. These outer heliosphere characteristics are crucial for understanding the heliosphere's interaction with the interstellar medium. Consequently, the Parker Solar Probe's observations of energy flux in the inner heliosphere are highly relevant to current and future missions targeting the outer heliosphere and beyond. These observations may also inform future missions dedicated to studying the solar wind and its evolution. Rotational spectra observed in even-even nuclei from A=150 to A=182 indicate increasing complexity, which cannot be adequately described by standard models such as the Bohr-Mottelson framework for collective motion or the shell model for single-particle dynamics. The Two-Rotors Model offers an alternative description by positing nuclear motion as the interaction between two rotors. By applying a local canonical transformation grounded in a specific Hamiltonian, an analytical solution is derived that successfully reproduces the experimental rotational bands. This approach also provides a description of scissors modes within the same A mass region. Furthermore, numerical investigations into a generalized, locally canonical transformation—utilizing complex angles—have been conducted. In this context, the target Hamiltonian features an additional local phase factor compared to the standard local canonical transformation version. The study reveals a new R-parity-odd scissors mode in the two-body problem, which vanishes when the generalized local canonical transformation Hamiltonian reduces to the standard local canonical one. Additionally, the influence of the local phase factor on the rotational characteristics of this two-body system is examined. These findings are supported by numerical results. This paper introduces a neural network-based approach designed to address these drawbacks. Crucially, these neural networks do not rely on any mesh, thereby eliminating mesh-related computational expenses. The method is demonstrated using the 1-D heat equation and the 1-D wave equation as test cases. Results indicate that the proposed cell-mean based neural networks achieve higher accuracy and demonstrate greater computational efficiency compared to existing neural network solutions. Furthermore, the study confirms that the method converges to the exact solution of the 1-D wave equation. Additionally, the approach achieves substantially lower training losses within the same number of training steps compared to Collocation Neural Networks (CNN). Finally, the method is shown to yield results with minimal dependence on the specific set of cells selected for defining the cell-mean-based neural networks. The presented results are consistent with those obtained using Finite Difference Methods (FDM). The ALICE experiment, operating within the LHC's heavy-ion collision facility, specializes in creating and investigating the quark-gluon plasma. It excels in heavy-flavour physics, hadronic and nuclear physics, four-particle correlations, hadronic and hadro-nuclear probes, and the study of heavy ions. To advance its research into physics models and theories for the next few years, a new dedicated ALICE upgrade is proposed. This initiative aims to significantly boost heavy-ion data collection rates and detection capabilities for the post-2030 era, specifically addressing heavy flavour, hadronic and hadro-nuclear, four-particle, and nuclear physics. A key component of this proposal is the Heavy Ion Tracker (HIT), which, when combined with existing ALICE detectors, will facilitate a comprehensive, multi-dimensional analysis of heavy-ion physics. This document outlines a technical proposal for the ALICE upgrade and its associated detector research and development initiatives. It provides a detailed description of the HIT and a summary of the progress made thus far. Additionally, the proposal outlines research and development activities for ALICE sub-detectors and their readout systems, detailing their current status and required efforts. Finally, it presents a statement of work covering the next few years. The HIT is designed to deliver a unique comprehensive heavy-ion dataset, offering unprecedented particle identification and momentum resolution. This will enable a thorough investigation of heavy-ion physics, including heavy-flavour hadrons and their decay products, across a vast kinematic range. Furthermore, the enhanced capabilities for four-particle correlations and electromagnetic probes will allow for a systematic analysis of heavy-ion physics and heavy flavour production. These advancements will provide a deeper understanding of the heavy-ion phase diagram, particle production mechanisms, and the initial conditions of the quark-gluon plasma. Ultimately, the comprehensive heavy-ion data set will significantly advance our knowledge of heavy-ion physics and their underlying models. The development of the HIT and its research and development activities are considered crucial for advancing ALICE physics in the upcoming decades. The proposed upgrade is expected to be completed in time for LHC Run 3. Specifically, the construction of the HIT is anticipated to begin in 2024, with the installation of all HIT components and their integration into the ALICE data acquisition system scheduled for 2028. This timeline allows for a two-year period to commission the HIT alongside the other ALICE sub-detectors. This unambiguous signature of thermal noise in the quantum vacuum field arises from the entanglement between future and past light cones. These findings indicate that quantum effects linked to accelerated motion can be observed in a broader frequency range compared to existing experiments. Additionally, we demonstrate that our methodology can be used to detect thermal noise in curved spacetime, including the Unruh effect, Hawking radiation, and the Penrose process. The Berry phase linked to atomic acceleration can then be measured through interference patterns. We show that the observed oscillations in the Berry phase, relative to the acceleration parameter, serve as clear evidence of thermal noise in the quantum vacuum field. The concept of a global vector bundle extends the traditional transitive action of a Lie group $G$ on a manifold $M$ by allowing a Lie group $H$ to act globally on $M$ in a way that may fail to be transitive. Here, $H$ serves as a structure group for $G$-equivariant maps, while $G$ acts as a parametric group, thereby unifying ideas from homogeneous spaces and parameterized manifolds. This framework yields novel insights into well-established theories, such as the geometry of smooth or algebraic families of manifolds, generalized equivariant de Rham cohomology, and equivariant characteristic classes for $G$-manifolds where $G$ is a subgroup of $H$. We demonstrate that the equivariant Pontryagin classes for a $G$-manifold can be realized through the curvature of a connection on a global vector bundle. Building on this, we derive a new proof of the Grothendieck-Riemann-Roch theorem within algebraic geometry by utilizing the push-forward formula for a flat connection on a global vector bundle. This approach bypasses rigorous obstructed integrations, reducing the problem to establishing a relation between two instances of a single type of equation. Furthermore, we prove that the characteristic forms of a global vector bundle exhibit clear positivity relative to a specific form on a dense submanifold. Finally, we outline applications of global vector bundles to the geometry of algebraic families and generalized equivariant K-theory. This note focuses exclusively on the smooth category, with a corresponding paper addressing the algebraic setting forthcoming in this journal. Additionally, we present an example of a vector bundle over a global vector bundle that is not necessarily smooth. These constructions enable the definition of a category of vector bundles over a principal bundle, whose objects are global vector bundles and whose morphisms are bundle maps. We also define associated bundles over this new category and examine their relationship with associated bundles derived from a representation of the Lie group $H$. Finally, we present a construction that generates a vector bundle over a global vector bundle whose curvature is expressed via a generalized Cartan structure equation. This method extends the concept of a Cartan connection to global vector bundles, offering a tool for analyzing the geometry of algebraic families of manifolds. The hard spectral state of Cyg X-1 is characterized by a multi-component spectrum comprising a thermal disk component, a thermal Compton component, and, during certain epochs, a low-energy thermal component attributed to the "stellar breeze." In this study, we present the first spectral-timing analysis incorporating this breeze component. Using the first 10 Ms of data from the 2018 NuSTAR observation of Cyg X-1, we fitted the stellar, thermal disk, and thermal Compton components with both standard and "breeze" models. Our findings indicate that the amplitude of the thermal component varies with the stellar component, whereas the amplitude of the Compton component remains independent of the breeze. Consequently, we demonstrate that a non-negligible contribution from the stellar wind to the X-ray spectrum exists in the hard state, and we discuss the implications of this discovery for current theoretical models. Finally, we highlight that this phenomenon is potentially detectable in other black hole X-ray binaries. We investigated post-merger outflows generated by magnetized neutrino-cooled disks resulting from binary neutron star (BNS) mergers, utilizing a coupled neutrino radiation hydrodynamics and magnetohydrodynamics framework. Our analysis examined the impacts of BNS system parameters, including total mass, mass ratio, and the magnetic field configuration of the accretion disk. Our results indicate that the initial mass of the merger product (the BNS remnant or black hole) does not influence the outflow mass, whereas the mass ratio significantly affects it. Specifically, systems with a mass ratio under 0.4 produce massless winds due to insufficient magnetization in the collapser's polar axis. In contrast, mergers with a mass ratio exceeding 0.4 generate jets with mass rates ranging from approximately $10^{-3}$ to $10^{-2} M_{\odot} \text{s}^{-1}$ and velocities between $0.1c$ and $0.3c$. Furthermore, the orientation of the magnetic axis relative to the spin axis is a critical factor; systems with misalignment angles greater than 45 degrees produce negligible outflow mass. Finally, we compared our findings with outflows from non-magnetized BNS systems, noting that while both produce jets with similar mass rates and velocities, the chemical composition of the post-merger outflows differs significantly. This study is the first to systematically explore how BNS system parameters affect outflow mass rates and velocities, offering valuable insights for understanding electromagnetic counterparts to gravitational wave signals from BNS mergers. Additionally, our results suggest that the observed lack of post-merger outflows in GW170817 can be attributed to a magnetic axis misalignment angle exceeding 45 degrees. Finally, we highlight that the observed dimness of GW170817's post-merger outflow is likely due to the low mass rate of the ejecta. We utilize deep imaging from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Pan-STARRS Survey on Photospheric Photometry of Galaxies (HSC-SSP) to examine tidal features in early-type galaxies (ETGs). Our analysis focuses on galaxies with stellar mass between $10^{10.5}$ and $10^{11.25} M_{\odot}$ at redshifts $0.03 \leq z \leq 0.15$, a sample of approximately 10,000 objects. We identify and measure the angular size and flux of tidal features for 1,015 ETGs, determining the fraction of these galaxies that host such structures. We establish a flux limit for "gigantic" tidal features, which we apply to investigate the relationship between feature size and flux, as well as to analyze correlations between galaxy morphology, color, and stellar mass regarding the presence of massive features. By integrating our findings with existing literature, we derive the merger rate for ETGs possessing gigantic tidal features, yielding a rate of $1.5 \pm 0.3$ Gyr$^{-1}$, which is roughly 1.5 times higher than the rate for galaxies lacking such features. This discrepancy is attributed to the extended duration over which tidal features remain visible. Our findings indicate that galaxies with gigantic tidal features are predominantly red and massive, suggesting that the gas required to form these features was already present during the early stages of early-type galaxy evolution. This aligns with the hypothesis that these structures arise from major mergers between early-type galaxies. Furthermore, our results imply that major mergers between early-type galaxies can generate gigantically large tidal features, a phenomenon previously observed only in rare, massive galaxies. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for understanding galaxy evolution. These results are based on a sample of 1,015 ETGs, and our findings are broadly consistent with previous studies. The paper is publicly accessible. This study extends the previous research (I) by deriving the Axially Symmetric Bipolar Outflow Gravity Solution (ASOBGS) from the Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation (ASTG). Similar to the bipolar point solution within the full GR theory (GR), the ASOBGS features two parallel bifurcated spacetime metrics operating at distinct velocities: one aligned with the central star and another supporting outflow propagation. The initial metric is characterized by a gravitational potential peaking at the center and diminishing radially outward, mirroring the bipolar point solution, while the second metric facilitates bipolar outflow movement. The separation between these metrics is governed by the mass ejection rate. The paper also addresses the singular nature of ASOBGS at the origin and examines the gravitational field equation solutions, generating solution curves for various astrophysical objects. The resulting field line curves demonstrate a bipolar outflow pattern driven by gravitational forces, with flow speed regulated by star rotation. The model successfully replicates outflow morphologies observed in young stellar objects and active galactic nuclei. Furthermore, predictions regarding rotation velocity and mass ejection rate align with empirical data. Ultimately, this research proposes a novel interpretation of gravitational forces as a repellent phenomenon. Additionally, the ASOBGS provides a theoretical basis for understanding star formation, bipolar jets, and outflows, as well as the mechanisms behind the formation of black holes and neutron stars. Finally, the model offers a theoretical foundation for investigating the origins of black holes and supermassive black holes, as well as jets and gamma-ray bursts. The ASTG also holds potential for explaining planetary formation and orbital dynamics. These outcomes may significantly advance our comprehension of gravitational forces and the dynamics of young stellar objects and active galactic nuclei. This study examines optical searches for both simultaneous and delayed signals from eight well-defined fast radio bursts (FRBs) that occurred in compact nearby galaxies. The first six FRBs were observed using the Large Binocular Telescope, while the last two were detected via the Large Binocular Sun Telescope. No optical signals were found from any of the FRBs. We establish 99% confidence upper limits on the fractional radio-to-optical flux ratio at radio frequencies, ranging from 1.2 to 3.1 times the optical bandpass. These constraints are notably more stringent than the most recent reported optical emission limits associated with FRB 121102. Furthermore, we set 99% confidence upper limits on the optical fluence of any potential delayed emission originating from the FRB bursts themselves, with peak wavelengths between 500 and 600 nm and durations between 0.1 and 10 seconds. Our most restrictive limits are obtained for FRB 190523, where no optical emission was detected within 10 seconds of the burst, and for FRB 20200418F, where no emission was detected within 100 seconds. We conclude that any optical emission linked to these FRBs must be either significantly weaker or occur at wavelengths different from those probed by visible-light searches. These results are consistent with prior findings regarding the lack of optical emission from FRB 121102. Additionally, we discuss the implications of our findings for the origins of FRBs. Our results do not contradict or support the hypothesis that FRBs are caused by fast rotating compact objects, such as millisecond pulsars, and they impose constraints on the viability of neutron star mergers as the primary burst mechanism. However, our findings strongly argue against the scenario in which FRBs are triggered by the tidal disruption of a star by a compact object. Finally, we highlight the necessity of conducting high-cadence, wide-field optical surveys to achieve a comprehensive and simultaneous search for optical counterparts to FRBs. We also outline the capabilities and scientific goals of the upcoming CaT (Chilean Astronomical Telescope) project. We trained a visual grounding model to extract a text description of the video's actions, which was then fed into GPT-2 to generate a narrative. Our results demonstrate that GPT-2 can produce descriptions that align with both the text and visual inputs, confirming that the model can process "double grounding." Furthermore, we found that GPT-2 can be directed to prioritize visual information over the initial prompt sequence. Finally, we highlight the potential of this method to enable visual grounding techniques to automatically compose complex visual descriptions. This paper introduces Delegated RingCT, a ring currency protocol incorporating zero-knowledge proofs. Our approach achieves performance superior to both current ring currency systems and traditional zk-SNARKs, executing faster than the former and consuming less power than the latter. We evaluate this method against two benchmarks: delegatable anonymous credentials and halting zk-SNARKs. By employing aggregation techniques and eliminating the need for trusted setup, our proposal significantly outperforms both comparison groups. Future enhancements could involve implementing batch aggregation to further accelerate transaction speeds. Ultimately, we believe our framework will aid cryptocurrency designers in achieving their objectives by offering a versatile, privacy-focused solution that is both efficient and secure. Specifically, it enables users to transition from public blockchain currencies to private, ring-based alternatives with minimal performance degradation. Additionally, the scheme supports delegation, allowing users to appoint representatives to manage their funds on their behalf. The brightness profile of a particle beam along one spatial dimension can be determined by analyzing the spatial intensity distribution of a screen illuminated by beam particles that have been scattered. This technique, known as the brightness scan method, is applicable to all relativistic beam energies and relies solely on first-principle calculations without empirical calibration. However, screen-based diagnosis is restricted to low particle energies because high-energy hits damage the screen. In this work, we present a new technique for illuminating the screen that extends brightness scan analysis to any beam energy. This innovative approach is particularly valuable in the field of free electron lasers, where it enables the determination of bunch shape for ultra-short, ultra-intense particle bunches used to excite other particles. We validate this method using simulations of relativistic proton beams. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the bunch shape derived from this approach matches the result obtained through numerical analysis of microbunching in free-electron lasers. This confirmation underscores the technique's utility as a diagnostic tool for free-electron laser experiments. Additionally, we show that the method can measure bunch shape for multi-Gaussian beams containing multiple populations. Finally, we discuss the technique's potential as a way to study space-charge effects in intense proton beams traveling at sub-relativistic speeds. In this context, bunch brightness serves as a key parameter that quantifies the strength of space-charge forces. The bunch shape can be derived from a brightness scan by measuring the radial intensity profile of the space-charge halo formed by scattered protons. We illustrate that scattering beam particles provides an advantage over other scattering methods, such as gas jet scattering, when dealing with ultra-short bunches. Specifically, we show that this scattering technique can reveal the ultra-short bunch structure that is typically obscured by the long tail caused by emittance growth from scattering in conventional gas jet methods. We also demonstrate that this technique is capable of identifying the ultra-short bunch structure hidden within a broad background formed by multiple beam particle populations. Finally, we show that the scattering particle rate can be optimized by adjusting the pressure of the jet. These findings are achieved without any empirical calibration, relying exclusively on first-principle calculations. This paper serves as a foundational reference for implementing such scattering-based diagnostic techniques. Furthermore, we provide a code to assist researchers in planning and analyzing brightness scans. The code is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/tae-kyu-lee/BrightnessScan}. Data-driven modeling is widely recognized for delivering accurate and reliable forecasts, yet it faces challenges related to model interpretability and the need for extensive historical data. To address these issues, a new collaborative approach has emerged, operating under the premise that diverse models can contribute to a unified forecasting solution. This contribution offers a comprehensive review of this paradigm, providing a detailed theoretical and mathematical framework along with an analysis of current applications. Furthermore, it formalizes the connection between collaborative data-driven modeling and collaborative filtering, and explores potential research directions. The paper concludes by reviewing the field's progress and highlighting opportunities for future advancement. This work seeks to deepen understanding of collaborative data-driven modeling and its role in data science. Additionally, it serves as a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners engaged in forecasting, operations research, machine learning, and related domains. Finally, it is intended to inspire continued interest and further development within the field. This paper introduces AskewSGD, a novel quantized optimization technique designed to minimize convex or low-complexity non-convex functions. By employing a variable step-size strategy, AskewSGD achieves a linear convergence rate for convex functions and improves upon the expected convergence rates of first-order optimization methods. The method is straightforward to implement, requires no specific quantization hardware, and can be seamlessly integrated into end-to-end training pipelines. Experimental results demonstrate that AskewSGD surpasss current state-of-the-art quantized optimization approaches in both performance and energy efficiency. Furthermore, when applied to neural network training, AskewSGD surpasses existing quantization methods on classification tasks, such as those using ResNet architectures. Soft robotics has gained significant traction due to the unique capabilities offered by these systems. At the core of any intelligent robotic platform lies a control system that translates the robot's physical model into actionable outputs. Soft robots present distinct control challenges compared to their rigid counterparts, primarily because of the complex, nonlinear dynamics inherent in their materials. Consequently, leveraging these physical models as the foundation for the control system has emerged as a promising and rapidly evolving approach. This survey provides a comprehensive overview of model-driven control techniques for soft robots, examining various methods grounded in mechanics, electronics, and mathematics. Furthermore, it analyzes current methodologies, identifies gaps in research, and proposes directions for future advancements. Finally, the survey concludes by addressing critical challenges that must be overcome to enable more widespread industrial adoption of soft robots. (This work appears in Advanced Intelligent Systems, 2021).)

Our approach begins by outlining the strategy for covering the classical Jacobi group, followed by a detailed analysis of the covering classical symplectic group. Subsequently, we develop a cover and a "generalized" Jacobi group by applying the Araki method to subgroups of the covered symplectic group. We demonstrate that these constructed groups align with Araki's genuine Jacobi group and Bohlman & Böhme's generic covering Jacobi group, respectively, provided certain topological conditions are met. Furthermore, we present two distinct constructions for the covered genuine Jacobi group: one based on the semi-direct product of three abelian groups and another utilizing the generalized Satake-Tate model. We also establish an isomorphism between these two coverings of the genuine Jacobi group. Finally, we identify the Lie algebras associated with both covered groups. To support our work, we include an appendix offering a novel proof of the covering short exact sequence for the classical symplectic group, which relies on our findings from that section. We anticipate that the techniques and results from this appendix will be valuable for future research. Overall, this work serves as a comprehensive summary of our findings, with our methodology being more algebraic compared to the original proof by Araki. Additionally, we provide an alternative construction of the covered genuine Jacobi group using the generalized Satake-Tate model. We aim to contribute to the fields of covering Lie groups, covering Lie algebras, and the theory of covering automorphic forms. Table-based fact verification focuses on determining the validity of a fact by examining a support dataset. Most existing methods treat the table as a static structure, neglecting the hierarchical relationships between rows and columns. We propose that fact verification through F-acts involves multiple disassembly steps to isolate the fact's core components. To model this process, we introduce ID-structure, a dynamic table structure where F-acts are decomposed into row units and column units. These units are discrete fragments of rows and columns linked by shared cell IDs. Furthermore, we present Table Disassembly for Fact Verification (TDFV), a framework for verifying F-acts based on ID-structure. Our experiments demonstrate that ID-structure effectively captures core components and enables the modeling of verification processes. Additionally, TDFV surpasses prior models, showing that disassembly significantly enhances table-based fact verification. The code is accessible at id-structure.github.io. We present a method for incorporating conditional information into the latent space of a trained generative adversarial network. Our approach employs a conditional discriminator that evaluates if the synthesized image aligns with an specific condition, such as an image segment mask or a class label. By optimizing the generator to maximize the discriminators joint output, we navigate the trade-off between the global coherence of images within the generated batch and the local accuracy of the target condition. Our framework is versatile, supporting various information types including segmentation masks, bounding boxes, and textual descriptions. We successfully applied this method to open-set in-filling, open-set image cropping, conditional image generation using segmentation masks, and conditional image generation using bounding boxes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that bounding boxes offer superior local fidelity compared to masks, whereas masks provide greater flexibility and are more suitable for human-in-the-loop applications. Finally, we show that combining both conditioning methods yields the most robust results. To our knowledge, this represents the first application of conditional GANs to large-scale open-set in-filling and cropping tasks. Bayesian nested sampling serves as a method for computing evidence and conducting inference regarding the posterior distribution of model parameters. A critical component of nested sampling is the "step selector," a user-defined function that determines how the live points pool contracts during sampling. This study introduces three novel step selector algorithms designed to enhance the exploration of parameter spaces, particularly for high-dimensional scenarios. The authors evaluate these methods against an existing algorithm through numerical experiments involving both a simple one-dimensional case and a more complex scenario featuring degenerate parameter spaces. These findings indicate that the new algorithms outperform the existing one, demonstrating superior convergence to the posterior distribution in both scenarios. Furthermore, among the proposed methods, the nested nested sampler exhibited the fastest convergence. Additionally, the authors developed a general framework to calculate the Bayesian coverage probability for any step selector when estimating specific parameter values. This approach was utilized to determine coverage probabilities for both the nested nested sampler and the existing algorithm across various scenarios, including those with degenerate parameter spaces. Results indicate that nested samplers employing the new step selector methods achieve coverage probabilities closer to the ideal 0.5 (indicating accurate parameter estimation) compared to those using the existing algorithm. Finally, a Python package implementing these step selectors, alongside utilities for estimating coverage probabilities, is made available to facilitate their use. This package, along with a Python implementation of nested sampling that supports arbitrary step selectors, can be accessed via: https://github.com/JamesBuckley123/nestpython. This resource is particularly valuable for researchers conducting MCMC sampling. By default, the package employs the nested nested sampler, which utilizes adaptive importance sampling to construct step selectors inspired by Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. Users may also choose to implement and utilize their own custom step selectors. Keywords: Bayesian inference; Monte Carlo integration; Monte Carlo integration; Monte Carlo importance sampling. The objective of distance labeling in graphs is to assign specific labels to vertices such that the shortest distance between any two vertices can be derived from their labels using a basic function. While numerous resilient variants exist, most existing solutions for planar graphs rely on complex labeling schemes. In this work, we demonstrate that for every $c \geq 1$, there exists a constant $k$ where each vertex in a planar graph with maximum degree $\Delta$ can be assigned a polynomial-time computable, $c$-resilient distance labeling of size $O(\log n)$. Furthermore, each neighbor of a vertex $v$ can be uniquely identified by a small subset of size $O(\log n)$ within $v$'s shortest path neighborhood of radius $\Delta$. To our knowledge, this represents the first application of distance labeling to planar graphs that avoids the intricate schemes typical of previous approaches. Our method builds on a recently introduced embedding of planar graphs into the Boolean hypercube, which we adapt to a higher-dimensional Hamming space. This space facilitates the construction of hypercube expanders, a key component in ensuring the labels' distance properties. We anticipate that this framework will have broader applications in planar graph theory. Specifically, we utilize our labeling scheme to establish an $O(\log n)$-time randomized distributed algorithm for planar graph coloring. This solution achieves a $(\Delta + 1 - \frac{1}{\log \log n} - \varepsilon)$-coloring with high probability, improving upon the previous best distributed result by Datta et al. (SODA'21), which only improved the bound by $\frac{1}{\log n}$. Additionally, we introduce a novel application of distance labeling to the distributed graph algorithm paradigm, yielding a new randomized distributed algorithm for planar graph matching. This algorithm computes a matching that covers at least a $1/2 - \varepsilon$ fraction of vertices in $O(\log n)$ time with high probability, surpassing the prior best result by Byrjalty et al. (PODC'19), which achieved this improvement in only $\log \log n$ rounds fewer. Both of our distributed algorithms operate in the strongly congested model, which differs from the congested model by allowing $O(n)$ messages per node per round rather than $O(\log n)$. This study examines time- and frequency-domain two-particle correlations $C_2(x, t)$ and $S_2(\omega)$ within a driven, dissipative Bose-Hubbard model, comparing these findings against two-particle quantum quench dynamics. We demonstrate that the short-time behavior of $C_2(x, t)$ is primarily dictated by the two-particle density of states (DOS), $D_2(\omega)$, which is defined in Appendix A. For $S_2(\omega)$, the relationship between the DOS and spectral function is largely governed by the interplay between the two-particle DOS and the two-particle DOS filtered through the single-particle DOS. Specifically, in the dissipative Mott insulator phase, the spectral function exhibits a single-peak structure at high temperatures, while in the superfluid phase, it displays a double-peak structure. Conversely, in the driven dissipative fluid phase, both $C_2(x, t)$ and $S_2(\omega)$ exhibit double-peak structures. We attribute this transition from single- to double-peak behavior to the interference between the two-peak structure of $D_2(\omega)$ and the two-peak structure of the filtered single-particle DOS. These results are derived from both analytical and numerical methods, with the latter utilizing the time-convolutionless projection operator formalism. Our findings indicate that the correlation between the two- and single-particle DOS is most significant in the superfluid phase. These insights are anticipated to be applicable to other quantum systems, such as those in the Haldane model. Finally, our findings regarding the relationship between the two- and single-particle DOS are expected to be extendable to other quantum systems. This paper investigates the regularity of weak solutions to divergence-form elliptic equations where the lower-bounded term is represented as a current whose $L^2$-coefficients fail to be extendable to distributions. While representing solutions functionwise leads to issues with duality pairing due to the non-distributional nature of the coefficients, working with currentwise coefficients avoids this specific problem. We establish Caccioppoli-type inequalities, local $L^p$ estimates for gradients, and Wiener criteria for solvability and continuity. The findings are closely tied to harmonic functions exhibiting linear growth and admit counterexamples based on current coefficients that preclude distributional extension. Notably, continuity criteria for scalar and vector-valued functions with linear growth are highly sensitive to the regularity assumptions made at the solution level. As an application, we extend the Calderón problem to a setting involving a resistance current whose $L^2$-components are not extendable to distributions. Furthermore, we demonstrate the existence of currents with extendable $L^2$-functions possessing a positive Green current yet lacking any distributional extension with a positive Green function, thereby highlighting the significant role of distributional extendability in potential theory. Finally, we extend distributional extendability to a broader class of functionals and provide a criterion for the semi-continuity of positive functions with respect to convergence in flat currents. These extensions are deeply connected to flat currents with extendable $L^2$-functions and the convexity of their $L^2$-norms. We also address a question raised by Burdzy regarding the non-uniqueness of the fine extension of positive functions with linear growth and the existence of positive functions with linear growth possessing positive superharmonic extensions. Additionally, we derive an explicit formula for the Riesz measure associated with a function of finite energy and examine the relationship between the original function and its Riesz measure. A significant portion of this work relies on novel results concerning positive functions with linear growth, positive functions exhibiting superharmonic behavior, and their connections to line measures and line distributions. Recent advancements in out-of-distribution (OOD) detection utilize probabilistic models to establish uncertainty bounds for identifying anomalous inputs. However, Gaussian Processes (GPs), a prevalent probabilistic method, face challenges in accurately quantifying uncertainty due to their point estimate nature, lacking mechanisms to account for model parameter uncertainty. This paper introduces a novel Bayesian GP framework that quantifies both model parameter and prediction uncertainties. By leveraging the Gaussian nature of GP predictions and Gaussian process regression, we model parameter uncertainty as a distribution. Consequently, Gaussian processes are transformed into distributional Gaussian processes, where mean functions and covariance functions become random variables. This approach facilitates the construction of a uncertainty Baysian network (UBN) for OOD detection. Experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses state-of-the-art techniques in OOD detection performance. The code and data are accessible at https://github.com/ahmedhassan1992/DGPSOS. Periodically driven quantum systems, or Floquet systems, exhibit diverse and intriguing phases. While periodic heating in isolated systems is well-documented, its behavior in open systems remains poorly understood. This study theoretically investigates the phase diagram of an open driven system featuring a noncondensable repulsive interaction, characterized by low dissipation and moderate particle loss. We demonstrate that a specific configuration of dissipation and loss yields a phase in which particles form a Bose-Einstein condensate within a single-mode "scar-like" ground state of the Floquet Hamiltonian. We further confirm that this phase boundary aligns with the critical point where the Floquet system transitions into a fully disordered state. These findings highlight the efficacy of scar states in driven-dissipative contexts and offer a novel approach for generating and manipulating quantum states. Additionally, our framework may hold promise for modeling and controlling non-equilibrium phenomena in biological systems. Finally, we propose experimental implementations using ultracold atoms within optical-lattice setups. Notably, these proposals do not require time-resolved detection, as the scar-like condensate can be identified through standard in-situ imaging. Our proposed method is applicable to various experimental setups, including those utilizing Raman coupling, Floquet engineering, and Floquet metrology. Furthermore, the proposed scheme is compatible with recent experimental achievements in achieving quantum enhanced metrology. Finally, we outline avenues for future research. According to a recent finding by DePuegniet and Ghiraldin, solutions to the Monge–Ampère equation featuring a bounded right-hand side situated between $-1$ and $1$ demonstrate uniform Hölder continuity. This paper presents an alternative proof of that result by employing an enhanced Alexandrov maximum principle applied to specific supersolutions of the equation. Furthermore, this approach yields a proof of the same result for the more general case where the right-hand side is any real number. Finally, our methodology extends to establishing the uniform Hölder continuity of viscosim solution within the context of the double-obstacle problem. This specific application constitutes a streamlined proof compared to the recent, more intricate argument provided by DePuegniet and Ghiraldin. Additionally, our proof employs a straightforward covering lemma applicable to open sets in $\mathbb{R}^n$ with a straightforward condition. This condition is satisfied when the set possesses a rectifiable boundary, thereby facilitating the demonstration of uniform Hölder continuity for viscosity solutions of the double-obstacle problem. This solution was recently achieved by the second author in a doctoral dissertation. Our approach circumvents the necessity of additional assumptions required in other proofs of this result. Finally, this paper serves as a substantially simplified exposition of DePuegniet's proof strategy by eliminating the need for the additional assumptions utilized in that original work. Specifically, our argument avoids requiring the supersolutions under consideration to exhibit additional flatness at the origin or to be defined on convex domains. The statistical analysis utilizes the test statistic $Z=\frac{T-\mu}{\sigma}$, which is approximately normally distributed with a standard deviation of unity and a mean of 0. The null hypothesis is defined as $H_0:\mu=\mu_0$, where $\mu_0$ represents the mean of inter-glitch arrival times, and the alternative hypothesis as $H_1:\mu\neq\mu_0$. For non-periodic pulsars, the false alarm probability (FAP) is approximately $2.87\times10^{-5}$. Additionally, we propose a chi-squared test for non-periodic clocks, which employs the inter-comparison of variances and also achieves a FAP of approximately $2.87\times10^{-5}$. These findings offer valuable theoretical insights for understanding the behavior of neural networks during training. Holographic error correction codes offer a different perspective on quantum entanglement. This paper introduces a new holographic code called Hyper-INVARiant MERA (HIEM), which is constructed by stacking invariant tensor networks together. This architecture enables power-law entanglement entropy at a fixed code distance and facilitates the analysis of how distance affects error correction. This approach introduces a novel dimension to the holographic error correction problem. We outline a straightforward and direct method for calculating the minimum global distance, demonstrating that it scales at least linearly. Furthermore, we derive the error threshold, which also scales linearly. Our findings indicate that HIEM exhibits hyperbolic geometry, with entanglement entropy for a region of length $A$ in the code space scaling logarithmically ($\sim \log A$) in the physical space. Additionally, we present an efficient classical decoding algorithm for a specific class of HIEM codes, which runs in polynomial time on a classical computer. This marks the first instance of an efficient holographic error correction code that supports both a hyperbolic geometry and a corresponding classical decoder. Our results provide the first non-trivial example of a tensor network that is invariant under continuous symmetries and can be solved efficiently on a classical computer. This establishes a new link between tensor networks, holography, and continuous symmetries. Finally, we show that HIEM can be embedded within a larger, higher-dimensional holographic error correction code, maintaining a bulk geometry resembling anti-de Sitter (AdS) space. This demonstrates the first explicit and systematic method for building holographic error correction codes with power-law entanglement scaling. Our work paves the way for exploring a new category of tensor networks, which may hold significant potential for quantum computing. This category includes continuous symmetry-invariant tensor networks, which are crucial for quantum many-body systems with symmetries, and holographic error correction codes, which hold promise for practical quantum error correction. This family of tensor networks is built upon HIEM. We anticipate that HIEM will serve as a foundation for investigating quantum many-body systems, quantum field theories, and quantum computing. This study investigates the axial spacing between filaments within the Galactic Center to assess their alignment. Utilizing 1.3 mm continuum emission data from the ALMA B1-10 field, we analyzed the sky coverages of 11 identified filaments. By examining the inter-filament spacing distribution, we determined that the mean spacing is 1.1 arcminutes, which corresponds to a physical distance of approximately 0.02 pc at a Galactic Center distance of 8 kpc. The distribution of inter-filament gaps reveals a strong clustering tendency, with a characteristic clustering scale of 2.5 arcminutes (0.06 pc). Furthermore, the mean gap size is calculated to be 0.7 arcminutes (0.02 pc). We also found that the distribution of spacing variance is well-described by a log-normal distribution, indicating that the morphological structures of these filaments are likely driven by supersonic turbulence. Additionally, a significant correlation exists between the fractional brightness of the Galactic Center and the mean inter-filament spacing, suggesting that these filaments may originate from the condensation of molecular gas. These findings provide valuable insights into the physical origins of the filaments in the Galactic Center. Finally, we propose a new model to explain the physical characteristics of the Galactic Center molecular cloud. By comparing this inter-filament spacing with other existing spacing metrics, we conclude that these filaments are not merely remnants of earlier molecular cloud fragmentation but are actively forming through the collapse of dense cores. The resulting distribution of spacing variance is consistent with a two-stage filament formation model. This paper introduces a new method for robustly reconstructing complex dynamical systems from noisy, time-resolved measurements. We prioritize inversion techniques that inherently account for experimental noise within the system's natural dynamical basis. By reformulating reconstruction as a forward-optimization (FO) problem, we define a specific loss function that quantifies the discrepancy between observed data and simulated trajectories generated by an FO process using the reconstruction as its initial condition. This formulation unifies various reconstruction approaches, including those relying on deconvolution, deblending, or dephasing, which are essential in contexts like super-resolution microscopy. Furthermore, it allows for the flexible integration of additional data or physical constraints, such as thermodynamic principles, into reconstructions. The core innovation lies in combining FO inversion with a specialized trajectory basis derived from model-system dynamics. This basis is constructed adaptively from observed data and physical laws, ensuring that reconstructions remain consistent with both the measurements and the physics of the underlying processes. This approach is implemented via a straightforward algorithm that is both robust and computationally efficient. We validate the method's effectiveness across a range of examples, including reconstructing nonlinear dynamics from noisy observations, leveraging physical constraints, and extending the technique to high-dimensional data. The method's broad applicability is demonstrated through high-speed time-resolved imaging of complex, nonlinear processes in biological samples. These results show that our approach can resolve fine spatial details, achieve quantitative accuracy, and detect subtle temporal features, even in experiments where conventional techniques fail. This paper introduces a channel estimation technique designed for OFDM systems utilizing printed U-shaped metasurfaces in wireless environments characterized by short line-of-sight paths. The method is further refined to function under conditions of a reduced cyclic prefix and hardware imperfections caused by inconsistent element spacing on the metasurface. While enhanced empirical machine learning models typically struggle with hardware imperfections, the proposed model achieves high accuracy by effectively capturing the impact of these issues through a feature map derived from the physics of propagation and reflection. This approach maintains robust performance despite minor deviations in array element spacing, a factor often overlooked in previous studies. Furthermore, the proposed model demonstrates superior performance compared to traditional OFDM channel estimation methods, even when using a significantly shortened cyclic prefix. Results indicate substantial gains, achieving at least a 20 dB improvement in normalized mean square error across all considered scenarios. Finally, a sparsification algorithm is implemented to further boost performance, yielding an additional 20 dB gain. The overall model exhibits scalability, with estimation performance improving linearly as the number of training samples increases. This paper presents a novel interpretation of single energy measurements, characterizing them as the application of non-projective positive operator-valued measures (POVs). We demonstrate that the change in energy during the measurement process equals the product of the distance between the POV elements and the conjugate momentum, evaluated at the system's real-time position probability density. Furthermore, we establish the relationship between the variations of system properties before and after a measurement. These findings are illustrated using both pure and mixed states. Finally, we examine an energy measurement followed by a time evolution, which can be interpreted as a sequence of two single POV measurements. This analysis confirms the integral variation theorem regarding the comparison of system properties prior to these combined measurements and subsequent interferometric observations. Additionally, we verify that all derived results align with existing literature. Finally, we analyze the characteristics of the states subsequently evolved following an energy measurement. Notably, this study is the first to provide a direct link between energy measurement and POVs. These results hold significant importance for understanding the post-measurement state, systems accessed via energy measurements, and quantum thermodynamics. Moreover, they offer a new perspective on interpreting energy measurements. To the authors' knowledge, these findings represent a new result in the field. This work examines the stability of $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons within nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$ geometries, specifically focusing on the associative case. By employing Fourier expansions of perturbations, we demonstrate that the linearization of the ASD instanton equation in this setting is not elliptic. Furthermore, we establish the existence of non-trivial deformations for both non-parallelizable and parallel $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons, contrasting this with the strict $\mathrm{G}_2$ geometry where the deformations of an irreducible instanton are known to be four-dimensional and integrable. In contrast, the coprojective case yields no such deformations, consistent with established $\mathrm{G}_2$ geometry. The paper concludes with a discussion on non-linear deformations. Our findings reveal a significant disparity between the deformation theory of instantons on nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$ manifolds and that on rigid $\mathrm{G}_2$ manifolds; consequently, we suggest investigating weakly integrable geometries to determine if the concept of an instanton can be precisely defined in that context. Ultimately, this study represents the initial step toward understanding instanton theory within the context of the holonomy reduction to $G_2$. Additionally, we outline several potential applications, including defining special associative 3-folds, redefining harmonic maps, and exploring the relationship between these $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons and Calabi-Yau manifolds. Finally, we introduce a class of non-linear deformations termed "deformations of type II." Utilizing this concept, we demonstrate that every associative 3-fold possesses non-trivial deformations of this type, offering an alternative proof for a theorem previously established by Edith Czernia. Through this methodology, we also generate explicit examples of associative 3-folds exhibiting non-trivial deformations of this nature. Notably, this represents the first instance of such a result for 3-folds that are not cohomariant. Our findings suggest that deformations of type II may serve as a more natural analogue to K\"ahler manifolds possessing non-trivial deformations. To substantiate this claim, we examine specific families of 3-folds and explicitly calculate their associated deformations. Furthermore, we illustrate that 3-folds lacking deformations of type II are exceptionally rare. This study examines the connections between Hurwitz zeta functions and Ramanujan's series for odd zeta values. Specifically, we demonstrate that the Hurwitz zeta function, evaluated at positive integers and $1/2$, serves as a bridge between these two formulations of Ramanujan's series. Consequently, our paper presents several novel identities for odd zeta values and extends certain of Ramanujan's results. We also investigate the implications of these findings for the Birch and Bernstein conjecture regarding the Birch congruent number equation. Furthermore, we introduce new identities linking the harmonic numbers and Ramanujan's $p$-symbol. Finally, our results yield novel identities for Bernoulli polynomials and offer novel proofs for specific identities concerning Stirling numbers of the second kind. Additionally, our upper bound for the integral of the absolute value of the Riemann zeta function over a single period refines an earlier estimate by Ivić. Our methodology draws upon techniques from the theory of umbral calculus, including Faulhaber's formula, Faulhaber's polynomials, and Bernoulli polynomials. In our proof of Ramanujan's series for odd zeta values, we provide a concise and elegant alternative to the original argument found in his 1918 paper. Finally, our work offers a fresh perspective on the relationship between the Riemann zeta function and the harmonic numbers. Furthermore, we explore how integrating this data-driven perspective with algebraic topological tools can establish the necessary conditions to design new, potentially exotic states of matter. Our goal is to offer insights for advancing this emerging data-driven methodology, which holds the promise of uncovering novel physical phenomena. We also discuss specific applications in quantum Monte Carlo simulations, aiming to inspire researchers in algebraic topology, machine learning, and condensed matter physics regarding the future intersections of these fields.
