This study examines the dynamics of charged particles subjected to both a magnetic field and a reduction in their charge due to collisions with a resistive material medium. The drive reduction force (RDF) and Lorentz force generate a complex motion characterized by an expanding spiral, with the spiral's area increasing at a rate proportional to the square root of time. The research also explores how the particle's co- or counter-rotation within the magnetic field influences the motion across different spatial dimensions. Furthermore, the integration of the equation of motion with the continuity equation yields a solution for the current density of the moving charge. These findings may find applications in diverse fields, including the study of cosmic ray motion, plasma physics, and the design of magnetic field line separators. Additionally, the study demonstrates that the path length of the particle increases exponentially over time. Finally, it is shown that the co- or counter-rotation depends on the path length and remains invariant with respect to the magnetic field strength. A corresponding 3D model is available for download. In classification tasks involving significantly imbalanced classes, where one group vastly outnumbers another, the dominant class often dictates the decisions of robust estimators such as nearest neighbor algorithms. This occurs because most predictions are frequently directed toward the larger class. This study aims to address the issue of inconsistent classification in such statistical environments by introducing a robust closest neighbor algorithm. Specifically, we propose utilizing the depth function of kernelized Shapley Additive Explanations (SAE) to enhance the robustness of closest neighbor classification when handling high-dimensional, imbalanced, and noisy data. Numerical methods are employed to demonstrate the efficacy of this proposed approach, highlighting its superior performance in classification accuracy, particularly in the presence of a significant number of mislabeled points within the training set. Additionally, the robustness of this method is evaluated against the L1-norm closest neighbor algorithm. The analysis of classification results derived from both SAE depth and L1-norm weighting is conducted using various proximity measures, including Euclidean, L1, and L2-norm distances. Ultimately, the findings indicate that the L1-norm closest neighbor method outperforms it under clean data conditions, whereas the SAE depth-based method achieves more consistent and reliable classification outcomes when the training data contains noise. The results further reveal that the SAE depth-based approach yields more consistent outcomes than the traditional L1-norm method across all tested scenarios. Furthermore, the study confirms that the SAE depth-based closest neighbor method remains highly effective across varying noise levels, including scenarios with a high proportion of mislabeled training points. Finally, the SAE depth-based closest neighbor method demonstrates consistent classification accuracy across all tested conditions, regardless of whether the data is clean or noisy. The source code for this work is available at: https://github.com/ahmedmohamed1989/Robust-Closest-Neighbor-Classification. Keywords: Robustness, Consistency, Depth, Kernelized Shapley Additive Explanations (SAE), Closest Neighbor, Classification, Imbalanced Data, Noisy Data.

By cross-referencing this data with the Sydney-Dark Energy Supernova Survey (Sydney-DES) and Sydney-DES2, we discovered 67 quasars with $z \geq 2.5$ that have not been previously studied. Leveraging multi-wavelength data from Sydney-DES, Sydney-DES2, Sydney-DES3, and Sydney-DES4, we conducted redshift measurements and spectroscopic follow-up on these 67 objects, achieving secure redshifts for 61 quasars with $z \geq 2.5$ and seven additional quasars spanning $0.5 < z < 2.5$. The combined catalogue now includes 1,060 quasars ($z>0.5$) with $g \leq 15.5$, featuring 400 quasars ($g \leq 13.5$) that are brighter than any other existing catalogues. We present the second iteration of the Quasar Bright End Luminosity Function (QBEL-LF), which has been updated to incorporate these new entries. Furthermore, we identified 11 quasars with $M_g \leq -27.5$ and $z \geq 2.5$ that are brighter than any in other catalogues. We present the first direct observation of quantum dot charge-tunneling events into a superconducting island, achieved by monitoring the frequency shifts of quantum dot artificial atom transitions. We vary the dot-level energy relative to the superconducting island's Bogoliubov states. Tunneling events are detected as transient changes in vacuum capacitor coupling, which manifest as brief shifts in both resonator reflection and resonance. Furthermore, we observe that the tunneling rate into the superconducting island is orders of magnitude slower than tunneling out, suggesting a tunneling bottleneck. Finally, we demonstrate that this suppressed rate can be enhanced by gate tuning to reflect the interaction of the dot with both the superconducting island and an adjacent metallic island. This work illustrates that gate-sensing methods can effectively detect charge tunneling between quantum dots and normal-metal-based hybrid devices. Additionally, the technique is compatible with readout methods suitable for scaling, indicating its potential application in studying tunneling mechanisms between dots and larger hybrid devices during operation. Understanding these mechanisms is crucial for advancing coherent electron transfer in small ensembles of such devices. Additionally, we discuss how this approach can characterize decoherence in a wide range of solid-state artificial atom systems. In one specific instance, we demonstrate that spin flips occurring during tunneling into the superconducting island cause the observed suppression, providing evidence that this mechanism can be overcome by employing Josephson charge pumping. This finding is particularly relevant for future experiments aiming to demonstrate coherent electron transfer between quantum dots and quantum devices based on larger electron ensembles. In the context of circuit QED, this also implies that these spin flips cause dephasing of artificial atom transitions, offering a means to quantify such dephasing. Given that these phenomena occur on sub-microsecond timescales, they are likely responsible for dephasing observed in similar experiments involving electron coupling to microwave resonators. Finally, we highlight that gate-sensing techniques can facilitate the study of various other phenomena, such as spin relaxation and exchange interactions. Quantifying these effects is essential for current and future efforts to achieve coherent electron transfer between small ensembles of hybrid devices. Furthermore, these methods can aid in developing new strategies to overcome the identified tunneling bottlenecks. This is particularly pertinent for future efforts to demonstrate coherent electron transfer between quantum dots and larger electron ensembles in quantum devices. To achieve this, it is necessary to identify and address the specific mechanisms causing tunneling bottlenecks between quantum dots and the discrete electronic states of larger ensembles. The Murozuma-Jiannelli (MJ) contraction is a specific instance of a broader category of contractions defined for systems of conservation laws. This paper establishes the Lipschitz continuity of an entropic discontinuity map associated with this general class of contractions, provided certain technical assumptions are met. Furthermore, the proof offers a novel interpretation of these assumptions through the lens of the associated vector field. The demonstration relies on recent findings by the first author concerning the differential properties of convex functions on a simplex, which may prove valuable in other contexts. Additional contributions include a novel characterization of these functions and an explanation for why the simpler combinatorial nature of the differential on a simplex is insufficient to address the problem directly. Finally, the paper presents a proof of a recent result by the second author, which refines a well-known condition by Bressan and Jin. This refination is essential for establishing Lipschitz continuity. The conclusion of the work presents an outline of a proof for the Lipschitz continuity of an entropic discontinuity map, with only one step remaining unresolved. Specifically, the proof requires demonstrating that a particular convex function defined on a simplex—the domain of a difference between two states—remains within a compact subset of that simplex. While the methodology to achieve this is clear, identifying the appropriate compact subset remains the final challenge. Completing this step would fulfill the second author's open problem. However, this difficulty appears inherent to the proof strategy, suggesting that a more fundamental issue may exist. Consequently, the paper ends with a discussion of this obstacle and explores potential alternative approaches. Overall, the work advances the understanding of contraction metrics for hyperbolic systems of partial differential equations. Such metrics are valuable in various applications, including the design of contractively consistent numerical schemes, the analysis of contractive discretizations, and control theory. A primary motivation is the recent discovery that contraction analysis can identify stability regions for nonlinear control systems that extend beyond traditional stability regions derived from standard control theory methods. Furthermore, these regions can be significantly larger than those obtainable using existing techniques. The current paper serves as a step toward achieving contraction analysis on a broader range of nonlinear systems. By advancing our comprehension of contraction regions, we can enhance efforts to develop efficient numerical methods and control strategies that leverage these areas. Finally, the paper demonstrates that a refinement of the Bressan-Jin condition is necessary to guarantee Lipschitz continuity, thereby improving upon previous efforts in this direction. Perpetual view generation, which involves creating new views of a single-view scene, has recently gained significant attention. Although current methods generate high-quality, photorealistic, and diverse images, they often fail to reliably produce a complete 360-degree view due to occlusions and artifacts. To address this, we introduce DiffDreamer, a novel, fully unsupervised framework that utilizes conditional diffusion models to generate high-resolution, complete, and varied novel views. Our results show that a single trained model can be flexibly applied to various downstream tasks, such as novel view synthesis and virtual try-on. We have also released an extensive single-view dataset featuring diverse subjects like landscapes, rooms, and outdoor/indoor scenes to facilitate research. Extensive experiments confirm the effectiveness of our approach. The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/1000x1000/DiffDreamer. The paper is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.01011.

Networks are ubiquitous across various domains, ranging from social and biological networks to communication systems and the internet. In each of these areas, numerous processes occur simultaneously, necessitating the study of networked systems that integrate network topology with process dynamics. A critical challenge in controlling such systems lies in the high dimensionality of their state variables, which correspond to every agent within the network. This paper introduces a fully data-driven approach for predicting, optimizing, and controlling networked processes, requiring only the basic understanding of network topology and access to system state data. Specifically, the proposed method utilizes the Koopman operator to create a high-dimensional lifted state space where the original nonlinear dynamics are approximated as linear. This enables the application of efficient control and optimization techniques directly in this lifted space. The framework's efficacy is demonstrated on a nonlinear and homogeneous networked SIS (Susceptible-Infected-Susceptible) epidemic model, for which a control law is designed to minimize infection spread. The model's parameters are subsequently estimated from simulated data, and the proposal is evaluated against the baseline scenario lacking any prior knowledge of network processes. The results indicate that the data-driven approach achieves performance nearly equivalent to the scenario with known model parameters. Furthermore, a comprehensive analysis reveals that the proposed framework is applicable to diverse network processes, provided the agents' states can be appropriately observed. The computational cost remains low, as both the epidemic model and the corresponding networked process are simple. Overall, the results demonstrate that this data-driven method offers significant advantages when network process parameters are unknown. The networked epidemic model serves as a representative example of various networked processes, including the spread of misinformation, where the proposed framework is highly relevant. The network structure influences both the natural process evolution and the control design, and this is effectively illustrated through the case study of the networked SIS model. The paper is organized as follows: Section II presents the problem formulation; Section III outlines the proposed control framework; Section IV details the application to a networked SIS model; and Section V concludes with a discussion of open research questions. The networked SIS model is selected because it captures essential characteristics of information dissemination networks, such as the interaction between network topology and process nature, the impact of network size on control performance, and the high dimensionality of the state space. These aspects are examined through a comprehensive analysis of model performance across different networks of varying sizes. This study theoretically and experimentally examines the Rayleigh-Plateau instability affecting a liquid film on a solid cylinder. While prior research primarily focused on films draining under gravity, this work investigates film thinning driven by capillary forces, incorporating a slip boundary condition at the cylinder's solid surface. Our theoretical framework predicts the formation of droplets on the cylinder, within a capillary bridge between them, and at the final break-off point from the fiber. These predictions align well with experimental results, which also demonstrate that including slip in the theoretical model is essential for accurately capturing the observed instability dynamics. Furthermore, we explore the potential of capillary thinning for achieving precise placement of droplets on a solid cylinder. Finally, the findings are made relevant to thin films on other cylindrical geometries, offering predictions for scenarios where liquid drains from a solid or is supplied to it. These outcomes hold significance for applications spanning microfluidics to atmospheric science and industry. The theoretical predictions are supported by open-source code available at github.com/instability2021. In summary, our findings indicate that utilizing capillary thinning for accurate droplet placement on a solid cylinder is highly feasible. Additionally, we observed that slip at the solid surface enhances the Rayleigh-Plateau instability of a liquid layer, leading to faster thinning and droplet formation. Our theoretical predictions regarding droplet formation, including both spatial arrangement and temporal evolution, agree well with experimental results. Furthermore, our theoretical framework remains applicable to other cylindrical geometries, such as thin films on other cylinders and liquid bridges. Overall, our findings suggest that employing capillary thinning for precise droplet placement on a solid cylinder is highly feasible. This study investigates the initial-boundary value problem for the Hunter-Saxton model. We establish global Lipschitz stability for this model by introducing a novel energy functional that incorporates both the initial data and the source term. This newly developed functional not only demonstrates Lipschitz stability but also offers an alternative proof for the result previously presented in [10]. Furthermore, it serves as a foundational tool for other researchers to generate additional findings. In the process, we also achieve an $L^2$ Lipschitz stability result. When the source term $f$ belongs to $L^\infty((0,T)\times(0,\pi))$, these stability estimates hold. Additionally, under the condition that the initial data $(u_0,v_0) \in H^1((0,\pi))\times L^2((0,\pi))$ and the source term resides in $H^1((0,\pi))$, we obtain an $H^1$ Lipschitz stability result. Finally, we strengthen the Hunter-Saxton model to address the well-posedness issue identified in [11]. For this extended model, we derive the Lipschitz stability of strong solutions and provide a complete description of blow-up scenarios. These results are accompanied by a corresponding blow-up criterion. To achieve these findings, we have also developed a new technique that may prove useful for other researchers in related areas. Finally, the stability estimates are validated through several numerical examples. The increasing adoption of ultrasound-based scoliosis screening in schools and community programs has raised concerns regarding image interpretation reliability, specifically whether it differs between self-trained operators and clinical sonographers. This study aimed to evaluate the consistency of ultrasound imaging for scoliosis assessment by comparing the results from both self-trained high school students and experienced clinical sonographers against traditional radiography. Additionally, we analyzed the inter-rater reliability among five clinical sonographers. The results demonstrated strong agreement between ultrasound and radiography findings (intraclass correlation coefficient, ICC = 0.83; 95% confidence interval, 0.68–0.92; p < 0.001), with correlation coefficients for scoliosis angle and lumbar kyphosis exceeding 0.7. Furthermore, measurements by self-trained students yielded results statistically indistinguishable from those obtained by clinical sonographers (ICC = 0.83; 95% confidence interval, 0.68–0.93; p = 0.40). In contrast, variation among clinical sonographers led to statistically significant differences in scoliosis angle measurements (ICC = 0.72; 95% confidence interval, 0.50–0.85; p = 0.001). Ultimately, ultrasound proved to be a reliable and cost-effective tool for scoliosis assessment, though its application in school settings warrants careful consideration. Future research should explore the potential of artificial intelligence to further enhance the reliability of scoliosis evaluation through ultrasound imaging. This study evaluates the efficacy of the median duration of word families as a synthetic duration strategy for speech synthesis. Adopting a non-parametric approach, the findings indicate that while the median duration is sufficiently accurate for natural-sounding synthesis when employed alone, it fails to accurately model significant variations in speaker-specific durations across the top and bottom 10% of word families. Consequently, a more effective algorithm for selecting synthetic durations must be capable of adapting to a given speaker's extended word family durations. This paper also examines the benefits of augmenting median-based duration selection with a parametric speech synthesis duration model for application in TTS synthesis. This model is trained on speech data from multiple speakers to forecast a target speaker's word duration based on the preceding spoken word, thereby accounting for speaker-specific effects and speech naturalness. The proposed solution for generating synthetic durations using a speaker-adaptive, non-parametric model is demonstrated to substantially reduce speaker-specific effects between extreme word families, thereby enhancing speech synthesis quality. This improvement is quantified through speech intelligibility scores and mean opinion scores for speech naturalness. Identifying hate speech online is crucial for fostering healthy social interactions and maintaining community well-being. This study focuses on detecting anti-Asian hate speech within social media contexts. To address the limited feature set available for a community-specific model, we employed feature selection techniques, specifically Gain Ratio, to identify the most predictive attributes. We tested the generalized hate speech model on Twitter using the Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) and Fast Fourier Transform (FFT), comparing our results against prior research. Our findings demonstrate that the DCT-FFT approach outperforms other methods, while also highlighting the effectiveness of integrating feature selection to enhance model accuracy. Multi-input multi-output (MIMO) architectures have emerged as a promising approach for accelerating deep neural networks (DNNs) on embedded hardware. By replicating network components, these structures allow for feature sharing, enabling the summation of outputs from parallel paths. However, despite their potential, current empirical evaluations of the impact of local feature sharing on optimization and resulting model performance remain scarce. This study investigates how reducing the degree of feature sharing in submodules of subnetworks affects optimization and model accuracy. Our findings indicate that increasing the sparsity of shared features within subnetworks can enhance both optimization quality and model performance. Furthermore, we introduce a family of MIMO architectures featuring block-sparsity designed to facilitate local feature sharing. Unlike traditional space-sharing designs, which often suffer from poor convergence, our time-sharing designs achieve both superior optimization and higher accuracy. To support reproducible research, we have released an open-source library containing custom optimizers and MIMO architectures for experimental use. This work offers critical insights into the relationship between architecture design, convergence, and model performance, fostering more informed and effective architectural choices. Historical manuscripts offer windows into the past through their handwritten content, yet deciphering these documents often requires knowledge of historical scripts and handwriting styles that may differ from contemporary handwriting. While existing approaches frequently rely on modern scripts, leveraging both historical and modern handwriting features can enhance decoding accuracy. To advance research in deciphering handwritten historical documents, this paper offers a systematic review of publicly available benchmark image datasets covering five regions: Europe, Asia, Africa, and the Americas. Our analysis examines each dataset's characteristics, including handwriting periods, languages, styles, and sample sizes. Additionally, we identify 137 existing methods that utilize these five regional benchmark datasets and propose a classification for their contributions. Finally, we outline potential future research directions. This study aims to facilitate future deciphering efforts by providing a comprehensive reference for historical manuscript datasets, methods, and their applications. Furthermore, we hope this paper will encourage researchers to contribute to benchmark development by sharing public datasets, fostering a broader global community dedicated to deciphering historical handwriting. This study addresses the tracking and regulation of a DC motor driving an industrial joint on a KUKA KR 1000 Robot Arm without modifying the primary voltage control loop. This strategy avoids disrupting closed-loop performance metrics like rise time and damping, which are typically optimized for tracking. The approach utilizes three low-resolution quadrature counters (secondary encoders) installed on the drive belt, the motor, and the joint arm. By applying a flatness-based feedforward technique, the system predicts the voltages required at the secondary encoders to achieve a specific joint trajectory, effectively converting a tracking challenge into a stabilization problem. This is accomplished by measuring secondary encoder positions and adjusting the primary encoder's voltage to maintain the robot arm's mechanical structure. The method was validated through both simulations and experimental results using the secondary encoders on the industrial robot. These findings demonstrate that the proposed solution can modify trajectory rise times while simultaneously enhancing tracking accuracy. Furthermore, simulations and experiments indicate that, given adequate low-pass filtering, the system can mitigate errors arising from parameter mismatches and unmodeled dynamics. Consequently, the technique is applicable to other secondary encoders or sensors, such as current or voltage measurements, to improve position tracking in industrial robots. Additionally, the method is easily adaptable to other robotic systems. The proposed approach enables the reconfiguration of off-the-shelf industrial robots for high-precision tasks without requiring costly upgrades. This facilitates the development of new robotic systems by leveraging existing, mass-produced, high-power robots and integrating affordable, low-cost sensors. Ultimately, this allows for the creation of specialized robots tailored to specific applications while maintaining the high power and power density characteristic of contemporary industrial robots. Finally, the method is easily extensible to other systems that already employ secondary encoders or sensors for the control of high-power joints. The extensibility of this strategy is illustrated by its successful application to low-resolution secondary encoders on an industrial robot originally designed for tracking with higher resolution. The method was implemented via an external controller, ensuring that the primary controller remains independent of any specific trajectory. This independence allows the primary controller to be developed and tested in a laboratory setting, separate from the robot itself. **Background:** Multiple time-to-event data are common in medical research, yet their analysis remains challenging due to the frequent interdependence of events. Traditional approaches often attempt to model these dependent events directly, which can result in inaccurate results and misleading conclusions. **Multiple State Examination (MSE)** offers a novel analytical framework that utilizes a multi-compartment Markov model to examine multiple time-to-event data. By employing a Markov model, researchers can investigate the transition probabilities between various health states, while the compartment structure enables the modeling of time-dependent health states. **Objectives:** This study aims to introduce MSE, apply it to multiple time-to-event data within a Myocardial Infarction (MI) cohort, and evaluate its utility for generating hypotheses regarding life course health trajectories. **Methods:** We developed a 10-compartment Markov model to analyze a dataset comprising 1,000 individuals with MI. Compartment states were defined as: 1) post-MI survival, 2) stroke, 3) cancer, 4) other disease, 5) non-fatal cardiovascular disease, 6) non-work-related disability, 7) work-related disability, 8) death by cardiovascular disease, 9) death by cancer, and 10) death by other causes. **Results:** The analysis yielded 90 transition probability estimates, including age-specific multiple time-to-event survival curves, hazard ratios, and the average age of state transitions. Notably, the study identified that: 1) post-MI survival probability increases with age, 2) work-related disability is more prevalent in younger patients, 3) non-work-related disability is more common in older patients, and 4) non-fatal cardiovascular diseases are more frequent in younger patients compared to older ones. **Conclusions:** This study demonstrates that MSE is a valuable tool for elucidating life course health trajectories. Furthermore, it provides a new methodological perspective for analyzing multiple time-to-event data. This study examines the decisional metric dimension problem, which involves determining whether a graph $G$ possesses a resolving dominating set with a size no greater than $k$. We demonstrate that when parameterized by the size of a feedback vertex set, this problem is fixed-parameter linear (FPT). Additionally, we analyze the problem parameterized by the distance to an induced star forest and a clique minor, establishing fixed-parameter completeness for both cases under 2-cyclic minor containment. Finally, considering parameter $k$ as the difference between the smallest and largest vertex cover sizes, we outline an algorithm with complexity ${2}^{O(k^2)}\cdot n^2$. These findings are built upon an exact algorithm for the decision problem, which runs in ${2}^{O(k^3)}\cdot n^2$ time. Our results rely on an auxiliary problem, Resolving Dominating Set by Deletion, for which we provide a linear-time reduction to the Feedback Vertex Set problem. This auxiliary problem is also fixed-parameter linear when parameterized by the feedback vertex set size, is fixed-parameter complete for parameterization by the distance to an edgeless graph, and admits an exact solution via deletion in ${2}^{O(k^3)}\cdot n^2$ time using $k$ as the difference between the largest and smallest vertex cover sizes. Notably, all algorithmic complexities mentioned are tight. Furthermore, our framework is flexible and can be adapted to other deletion problems, such as the Independent Dominating Set problem, which is also fixed-parameter linear parameterized by the feedback vertex set size. Our approach utilizes a novel technique that establishes a general connection between deletion problems and their corresponding decision problems. Finally, we provide an exact algorithm for the Independent Dominating Set problem, which runs in ${2}^{O(k^3)}\cdot n^2$ time when parameter $k$ is the difference between the smallest and largest vertex cover sizes. This complexity is tight, and the algorithm is a straightforward extension of our previously described technique. In this final step, we establish a relationship between Independent Dominating Set and Independent Set, which is tight. Our findings are supported by an independent result: Independent Set is known to be NP-complete for 2-cyclic graphs, implying that Independent Dominating Set lacks a polynomial-time algorithm unless $P=NP$. Consequently, our algorithm is tight for 2-cyclic graphs. This outcome underscores the tightness of our algorithm and the potential tightness of our upper bound for Independent Dominating Set.

We extend the theory of power domains by introducing directed, point-based frameworks for them. These examples demonstrate that directed power domains cannot be modeled as metric spaces equipped with continuous distance functions. In contrast, when directed information is represented as a metric space, metric extension is both feasible and achievable. Furthermore, we enhance the existing distance function associated with the suspension domain by incorporating a novel component derived from its lattice structure, thereby enabling a metric representation for all basic power frameworks. Consequently, this implies that the metric representation of power frameworks is solely contingent upon the lattice information of the underlying domain. Additionally, we incorporate the metric representations of several other fundamental directed frameworks, including the domains for lists and for multisets. Our approach leverages existing metric extension methods as components in the extension processes for all mentioned directed frameworks. Finally, we conclude by outlining several opportunities for future research.

As simulated hothouse climates evolve, the frequency of extreme precipitation events is expected to rise. This study examines such episodes in 1.2 CO$_2$ hothouse simulations of early Earth, which were driven by a moist greenhouse condition. These simulations featured a substantial steam atmosphere, surface temperatures averaging 330 K, and global precipitation rates 10 to 100 times higher than present-day levels. Despite the intense rainfall, hothouse climates exhibited distinct episodic behavior, characterized by climate cycles lasting 100 to 1,000 years. These cycles alternated between "wet" phases, marked by widespread rainfall, and "dry" phases, defined by subsidence and minimal precipitation. During wet periods, precipitation rates were 2 to 3 orders of magnitude higher than during dry ones. Consequently, hothouse climates experienced extreme downpours, with raindrop fluxes reaching 100 to 1,000 times those observed in the modern climate. These downpours lasted only 10 to 100 days but occurred with a frequency 100 times greater than in a CO$_2$-driven icehouse climate. The extreme nature of these downpours stemmed from the combination of high precipitation rates and vast vertical convective scales. Furthermore, downpours were not merely amplified versions of wet periods; they represented a distinct climatic state characterized by the collapse of the upper tropospheric branch of the Hadley circulation. This collapse triggered the evacuation of the upper troposphere, leading to the shutdown of convective rain and the onset of episodic behavior. These findings suggest that hothouse climates on Earth-like planets could experience extreme downpours, potentially causing significant damage to any life forms present. Additionally, these results may have implications for the habitability of early Earth. We introduce the natural generalization of the twistor action for (self-dual) Yang-Mills theory to arbitrary integer spins, applicable both globally and locally. Our findings indicate that global actions of this type exist only when the little group is little(4). For higher spins, local twistor spaces exhibit dependence on the higher-spin field amplitudes. These twistor actions for higher-spin Yang-Mills theories feature simple extensions of the (F, G)-integrals present in the Yang-Mills version. The corresponding equations of motion yield equations of motion for self-dual tensors of all integer spins, where each corresponds to a higher-spin extension of the Yang-Mills condition. We also present self-dual Yang-Lang interactions for all integer spins. These results provide compelling reasons to anticipate the existence of a 4d space-time formulation for all-rank (self-dual) tensors. Anticipating such a theory, we construct a non-linear self-dual action in four dimensions that reduces to a sum of twistor actions upon twistor compactification. We demonstrate that this action is gauge invariant and derive its equations of motion. Additionally, we provide a non-linear extension of the multi-spinor formulation by Tomasiello. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for higher-spin Yang-Mills theory. Deep neural networks (DNNs) have demonstrated remarkable success across numerous computer vision applications, including medical image classification. However, their performance is often constrained by noise within training labels. Although existing methods attempt to address label noise, they frequently overlook the underlying causes of noise generation. This study investigates how statistical distributions of training samples influence learning, revealing that within-class distributions are often non-uniform. Such non-uniformity causes standard DNNs to allocate disparate attention to different data points, resulting in inferior generalization. To counteract this, we propose a novel approach called Bayesian Statistics Guided Label Rejuvenation (BSGLR) to mitigate the impact of non-uniform distributions. Our method utilizes Bayesian statistics to quantify the uncertainty associated with each sample. Subsequently, we employ an attention mechanism to assign varying importance weights to samples during training based on this uncertainty measure. Additionally, we demonstrate that BSGLR can identify the relative class relationships of test samples. Consequently, BSGLR enhances the efficacy of standard DNNs by boosting classification accuracy and robustness against noisy labels. Experimental results validate the superiority of our approach. For a connected graph with a simply vertex $v$, the study establishes relationships between the spectrum of the transition probability matrix for the associated random walk on $G$ and the number of spanning trees of $G_{\{v\}}$. Leveraging these relationships, the authors define the characteristic polynomial of the transition probability matrix of the associated random walk on $G$ as the set of all possible spanning tree counts of $G_{\{v\}}$. We introduce a novel data-driven strategy for enhancing instantaneous velocity field-based wall-bounded turbulence models, which forecast wall shear stress and heat flux. This framework utilizes neural networks to refine conventional coherent structure dynamics into a robust predictive framework. We initially train a baseline neural network using synthetic turbulent data, validate its performance against synthetic and experimental data, and subsequently employ transfer learning to further enhance prediction accuracy. When applied to experimental datasets from the Coherent Structures in Wall Bounded Flow (CSWBF) experiment, our approach yields state-of-the-art predictions for instantaneous wall shear stress in wall-bounded turbulence. By leveraging physical insights from the underlying model, we effectively integrate synthetic training data with real experimental data to boost accuracy. The resulting neural network-corrected model demonstrates a 20% improvement in root mean square error compared to the best previous modeling techniques. Furthermore, we assess the transferability of this framework by training it on synthetic data and testing it on the more complex Johns Hopkins Turbulent Boundary Layer (JHTBL) dataset. This analysis reveals that while the model significantly surpasses the performance of the original model, it still lags behind when evaluated against techniques specifically trained on the JHTBL data. These findings underscore the transferability constraints of the framework and highlight the necessity of training on representative experimental data to achieve optimal accuracy. The source code for our framework is publicly accessible at: https://github.com/PrashanthiSrinivasan/DeepWBF. The computational resources required to train these networks are minimal, making the framework highly scalable. Consequently, this data-driven framework holds significant potential for real-time flow control and turbulence modeling applications. The trained networks are also available on Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7200000). Finally, we have released an open-source Python library, DeepWBF, which implements the framework and streamlines the training process for users. The library can be installed via pip: pip install DeepWBF. Additional implementation details are provided in our recent paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.07774. Our results suggest that deep learning offers a highly effective pathway for developing accurate wall-bounded turbulence models. Furthermore, our framework is versatile and can be extended to other wall-bounded turbulence models, including large eddy simulations and Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes models. This study demonstrates that Hofstadler superlattices on topological insulator (TI) surfaces generate Hofstadler Weyl metals (HWMs) that break time-reversal symmetry. These HWMs exhibit novel electromagnetic responses, including a nonreciprocal anomalous Nernst effect (NAE) and a nonlocal anomalous Nernst effect (lNAE). The magnitudes of NAE and lNAE can be amplified by adjusting the magnetic field within the Hofstadler regime. Furthermore, we establish that these Hofstadler NAEs and lNAEs are sensitive to surface terminations and can be further controlled by modifying the growth direction. These findings indicate that Hofstadler Weyl metals offer a pathway to precisely manipulate topological transport responses through surface engineering. Additionally, we anticipate that these results will be applicable to other systems hosting HWMs. Finally, our predictions are supported by first-principles calculations. We introduce a hybrid dielectric-plasmonic system designed to create a strong hybridized localized surface plasmon (H-LSP) mode. Functioning as a unidirectional nanoantenna, this structure couples an embedded silicon nanosphere with a split-ring metallic nanoantenna to concentrate electromagnetic energy in a specific direction. This configuration supports a highly symmetric antenna dipole characterized by high quality factors, large localization volumes, and significant Purcell factors. Leveraging these exceptional properties, we propose splitting the silicon nanosphere into two small dielectric oligomers to convert the nanoantenna into an efficient and unidirectional photon source. Numerical simulations confirm that this hybrid device achieves high emission efficiency (Ex>0.95) and precise directional control, directing nearly all radiation (Ex>0.99) into a narrow 20° cone. Furthermore, the narrow emission spectrum (Delta Lambda<100nm) and robust optical response to structural dimensions make this hybrid nanoantenna a promising candidate for applications in nano-photonics and nano-electronics. Additionally, the all-photonic nature of the system ensures minimal heat generation, ensuring stability and reliability for nanoscale optical components. This research opens a pathway for developing new hybrid nano-photonic devices with superior performance. Finally, we have established a comprehensive design protocol to facilitate the fabrication of these hybrid nanoantennas. This protocol enables the customization of the Purcell factor, localization volume, emission efficiency, directional control, and spectral response to meet diverse application needs. The entire design workflow is fully documented in our accompanying video. This innovative hybrid nano-photonic design establishes a new platform for the development of high-performance nano-photonic devices. Key features of this work include: 1) The creation of a novel hybrid nano-antenna structure capable of achieving tunable and efficient photon sources; 2) The demonstration of tunable emission efficiency, directional control, spectral response, and localization volume through structural parameter optimization; 3) The provision of a complete protocol to guide the design of various types of nano-photonic devices. This study experimentally validates the Anomalous Screening Theory (AST) regarding stress transfer in granular matter. Theories of stress transfer in static granular assemblies are crucial for both fundamental comprehension and the engineering of granular components. The stress transmission mechanism in granular systems is complex, stemming from the interaction of various factors, including the geometry of the assembly, the characteristics of the applied load, and the physical properties of the individual particles. The stress tensor within a granular assembly, derived from the average of local stresses, is typically asymmetric. AST specifically addresses the phenomenon of an asymmetric stress tensor in granular materials. The underlying cause of this anomaly is the disparity in force transmission between horizontal and vertical directions; specifically, vertical forces are significantly stronger than horizontal ones, resulting in distinct local stresses. Consequently, when a load is applied to a small surface area, vertical columns bear the majority of the stress, causing the stress distribution to spread more rapidly in the vertical direction than in the horizontal one. This results in a stress state that diverges from the classical elastic theory of continuous media. The AST was initially validated using a granular rheometer. In the current study, we extend this validation by applying a localized load to a small surface area and measuring the stress tensor through 3D particle tracking. Furthermore, we conducted an extensive comparison of simulation results against experimental data to confirm the validity of the AST across different particle properties. Our numerical simulations were performed using the discrete element method, which models individual particles as rigid spheres subject to contact forces. We conducted a systematic comparison of simulation and experimental results to further validate the AST. The comprehensive results demonstrate that the AST accurately predicts the stress distribution in a granular assembly. This confirms the theory's applicability across diverse physical conditions, thereby facilitating the theoretical analysis of various engineering components. Additionally, we demonstrate the efficacy of combining experimental and numerical methods for verifying and understanding the behavior of granular matter. Our methodology involves a systematic comparison of simulation and experimental results, which can be adapted for verifying and analyzing the behavior of other complex systems. The results indicate that the AST is a general theory applicable to granular matter composed of various particle types. This is achieved by incorporating the specific properties of the particles into the simulation model. Consequently, our findings provide a comprehensive understanding of the behavior of granular matter, which is essential for both fundamental research and engineering applications. This study evaluates seven data synthesis methods across four NLP tasks spanning three datasets. Results indicate that a single synthesis technique does not consistently excel; however, SAS and TITAN emerged as the most effective, performing comparably to both enriched and augmented model results. The Fast Multipole Method (FMM) is a widely utilized technique for accelerating the calculation of particle interactions within large systems. However, numerical errors, particularly those resulting from the truncation of multipole expansions, can cause significant deviations between the computed potential energies and the exact analytical values. This study investigates these errors and demonstrates that, while FMM can break translational and rotational invariance, it preserves the system's total angular momentum. Consequently, for isotropic two-body potentials, the translational and rotational energy errors in FMM calculations scale at the same order as the multipole expansion truncation. Our findings are derived from employing multipole expansions for source groups and spherical harmonoids with a degree and order of $l = N_p - 1$, where $N_p$ represents the count of particles within each multipole group. This specific choice of expansion order ensures that the error in the approximate potential energy of particles within a group remains independent of the analytical potential function $V(r)$. We also note that the relative error in the approximate potential energy for a group scales with the number of particles within it. Furthermore, relative errors in FMM potential energy calculations are proportional to the square of the inter-particle distance, provided the potential function $V(r)$ is sufficiently smooth. Finally, we establish that the relative errors in FMM potential energy calculations are bounded by the error in the potential energy of the particles within each group. These insights enable the derivation of an a priori bound on the number of particles per group required to ensure that the relative error in FMM potential energy calculations remains below a specified threshold. Additionally, FMM is shown to be applicable for calculating potential energies in systems composed of particles with mixed sizes. We also present a method to evaluate the relative error in FMM potential energy calculations, which is independent of the force model's analytical form and relies solely on the particle positions. Finally, we illustrate that the relative errors in FMM potential energy calculations are directly proportional to the number of particles within each group. These conclusions are validated through potential energy and force calculations for various models, including the Lennard-Jones, Yukawa, and soft-sphere potentials. The study also examines potential energy preservation in non-isotropic systems, such as those featuring ellipsoidal particles. Our results indicate that FMM accurately calculates potential energies for ellipsoids when the ellipsoids are non-overlapping. However, for overlapping ellipsoids, the relative errors in FMM potential energy calculations are bounded by the maximum value of the analytical potential function

We introduce a method that automatically identifies samples with high learning potential to boost the training efficiency of a distributional expert. This expert generates samples by sampling from its learned probability density function. Our approach is straightforward: it calculates the Fisher information matrix for each parameter and subsequently selects gradients of samples relative to those parameters. We demonstrate that these selected samples exhibit significantly greater variation among themselves compared to standard Monte-Carlo sampling from the expert. These varied samples prove valuable for training downstream models, such as regression experts or generative adversarial networks, thereby enhancing their training efficacy. Evaluations on two synthetic datasets and one real-world dataset confirm that our method achieves substantial improvements in both sample quality and the training speed of downstream models. Furthermore, we provide within-model and between-model empirical evidence to substantiate these findings. Finally, our approach requires no modification to the expert model or its training procedure. This study examines the di-Higgs process within the decay modes of 2 Lepton + 2 Lepton Searcher, 2 Photon + 2 Lepton Searcher, 2 Photon + 2 Jet Searcher, Z + 2 Lepton Searcher, and 2 Photon. The analysis utilizes an integrated luminosity of 139 fb$^{-1}$ from proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV, acquired by the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider during 2015 and 2016. Results are presented using a simplified effective field theory (EFT) model featuring a single coupling, $\kappa_{\mathrm{W}}$, which perturbs the gauge and Yukawa interactions of the Higgs boson. The search identifies no significant signal above the background-only hypothesis. Consequently, 95% confidence level upper limits on the product of the cross-section and branching ratios are established for each event category, which are subsequently combined. For a coupling value of $\kappa_{\mathrm{W}} = 1$, effective cross-section upper limits relative to the Standard Model are determined to be 1.9 $\times$ 10$^{-3}$, 1.7 $\times$ 10$^{-3}$, 1.4 $\times$ 10$^{-3}$, 1.0 $\times$ 10$^{-3}$, and 1.0 $\times$ 10$^{-3}$ across the respective channels. The combined channel yields an upper limit of 1.0 $\times$ 10$^{-3}$, representing an improvement by a factor of two over prior searches for this process at the 13 TeV center-of-mass energy. These findings are also interpreted in the context of an alternative parameterization that incorporates a coupling between the Higgs boson and the vector boson. This work serves as a foundation for future investigations into Higgs boson pair production in association with a vector boson. The analysis code is publicly accessible via GitHub. A digital spin laser operating on $^{133}$Cs$^+$ ions in solution has been developed. By subjecting the ions to millisecond-scale radio-frequency pulses, the spin population is either fully polarized or depolarized with high precision. This digital control over the spin population enables an optical transition threshold occurring at a milliwatt level. Although the emitted light is not a coherent laser beam, it displays laser-like characteristics, including a narrow linewidth of 100 kHz, a far-field diffraction pattern, and a divergence angle of 10 degrees. This digital spin laser paves the way for all-optical radio-frequency control and sensing based on the optical properties of polarized ions in solution. Furthermore, it addresses the challenge of generating a stable and intense light source for quantum information processing and quantum communication in solution. Finally, this system offers a unique platform for investigating the interaction between light and matter in quantum solutions. The primary challenge in dark matter research involves identifying the specific physical particles that constitute it. In the standard model, no particle can serve this role. However, extensions to the standard model, such as supersymmetry, include additional heavy neutral particles. If these particles are sufficiently massive, they could constitute dark matter. Although direct detection of such heavy neutral particles remains beyond current experimental capabilities, indirect methods offer a way to investigate them. These methods involve analyzing the byproducts of particle-antiparticle annihilation. This study investigates the effectiveness of transfer learning for detecting hate speech in Hindi and Bengali by employing a multilingual BERT-based transformer model. Our primary contributions include the creation of Hindi and Bengali hate speech corpora through manual annotation and the implementation of various transformer-based strategies for cross-lingual transfer learning. Evaluated both independently and in combination, our enhanced models demonstrate a significant performance boost, rising from 0.82 to 0.87 for Hindi and from 0.76 to 0.81 for Bengali. Furthermore, this transfer learning approach facilitates more effective training of transformer models on limited datasets, a common constraint in these domains. Consequently, this research supports more sustainable Hindi and Bengali hate speech detection systems, which serve as a crucial component of automated content moderation on social media platforms. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive codebase supporting both independent training and cross-lingual transfer learning for future evaluation and extension. We introduce a novel approach to time projection chamber signal analysis that separates electron drift and pulse-formation times with high precision. By exploiting this separation, we demonstrate that the charge, drift duration, and residual gas pressure of individual photons can be measured for each event, enabling the calculation of event-specific total ionization and other observables. These findings are based on data from a 1.5 L, 2 cm diameter Borexino-style gas TPC featuring a high-definition readout plane. The resolution achieved provides valuable observables for direct detection of dark matter, neutrons, and other nuclear recoils. We illustrate the potential of these observables for direct dark matter detection by demonstrating how they can reduce the electron-recoil-to-nuclear-recoil ($e/n$) background by a factor of 100 at a fixed energy threshold. Furthermore, we show that such substantial improvements in $e/n$ separation can be realized across a wide range of gas TPC geometries and target volumes. This methodology represents a significant advancement for the upcoming generation of gas-based recoil detectors, including those within large liquid xenon experiments and small-volume, high-resolution devices utilizing TPCs with multi-pixel readout planes. Additionally, this technique offers a new means to monitor and correct for spatially varying photon yield and detector stability in gas TPCs. Finally, we discuss the potential for employing these observables to derive in-situ, local, and event-specific metrics for gas pressure, temperature, and electron lifetime. To facilitate adoption by other groups, we have made the analysis code publicly available. All results are presented using open data and analysis code. This paper presents the results of the Out-of-Categorization challenge, which evaluated model performance when applied to tasks outside their trained domains. The event utilized the Semantic Role Annotation (SRA) benchmark, pitting two categories of state-of-the-art models against each other: neural network-based systems trained on substantial datasets and transformer models trained on minimal data. The primary goal was to compare generalization capabilities across these architectural and data regimes. The study demonstrates that transformer models excel in scenarios with limited training data, though they do not consistently outperform neural models in out-of-category benchmarking. Both approaches exhibit a significant decline in performance for categories absent from their training sets. The analysis concludes by proposing promising directions for future research in out-of-category research and briefly explores the broader implications of these findings. </s>

The results demonstrate that as the dimension increases, geodesic lengths converge in distribution to a sum of independent chi-distributions, with corresponding implications for the positions of critical points. Our findings include a detailed asymptotic analysis of the algorithm's computational complexity and its numerical performance. Finally, we validate these results through applications to graph theory and image analysis. A key outcome of this work is a rigorous proof of the asymptotic independence of critical points of geodesic lengths, a result that aligns with the predictions of Cox process theory. This paper investigates distinct values of the L-functions associated with modular forms with level $N$ and weight $k$. We demonstrate that the denominators of the distinct values corresponding to distinct slopes of the Dwork crystal, derived from the Todorov zeta function, are bounded by a expression that depends solely on the level $N$ and the slope, remaining independent of the weight $k$. Additionally, we establish that the boundedness of the denominators of distinct slopes within the Grothendieck-Lefschetz zeta function for a projective variety over a finite field can be deduced from the result concerning the denominators of distinct slopes in the Todorov zeta function. To achieve these bound results, we employ the theory of generic formal functions and the Sato-Tate theory of distinct values for L-functions of modular forms. Furthermore, we provide two distinct proofs for the theorem on the boundedness of denominators for distinct values of L-functions of modular forms. The first proof utilizes an elementary theory of distinct values developed by the second author, which relies on the explicit formula for the second derivative of the Sato-Tate measure and the theory of moments of random variables. The second proof is based on the theory of formal measures. The authors intend to extend these boundedness and equidistribution theories for distinct values of L-functions to other automorphic forms in forthcoming research. This study investigates spin-dependent transport within armchair graphene nanoribbon (GNR) structures by employing a tight-binding model and numerical calculations. Specifically, we analyze a double-barrier resonant tunneling diode consisting of two source-drain electrodes, source and drain barriers, and an intermediate GR region. Using the nonequilibrium Green's function approach, we evaluate the system's current-voltage characteristics while incorporating spin effects via the noncollinear spin-orbit coupling mechanism. Our results demonstrate that spin-orbit interaction generates significant spin polarization in the current, alongside hysteresis effects inherent to double-barrier resonant tunneling diodes. Furthermore, we successfully explore strategies for achieving spin-polarized transport by modulating both the noncollinear spin-orbit coupling strength and the GNR geometry. These findings indicate that spin-polarized current can be observed through adjustments to GNR dimensions or the noncollinear spin-orbit coupling configuration, thereby enabling the development of spin-polarized electronic devices based on GNRs. Ultimately, this research advances the understanding of spin-dependent physics in graphene-based systems and holds potential for practical applications. This study extends Korovkin-style convergence theorems to weakly nonlinear and monotone operators acting on Banach lattices of multivariate functions. These operators maintain sufficient regularity, including continuity, monotonicity, and convexity or concavity, which are essential for analyzing spatially distributed physical phenomena. For instance, in fluid dynamics, the Navier-Stokes operator is weakly nonlinear and concave in its velocity variable, a property that enables the application of the methods developed here. Similar characteristics are observed in other weakly nonlinear operators within the same field. The framework allows for the estimation of norms based on pointwise evaluations at specific locations and addresses various partial or integral operators, such as those defining the $L^p$-norm of a function along a particle trajectory in hydrodynamics or a fluid element's moment of inertia tensor. Furthermore, the methods presented provide a unifying approach to existing literature results and facilitate new advancements. Specifically, the paper derives novel extensions of the Banach and Zakrzewski theorems and establishes a new result regarding the Sobolev operator, demonstrating how norms can be assessed using pointwise values, semi-norms, or specific semi-norms of derivatives at selected points. Additionally, it formulates new inequalities capable of tightening existing bounds and broadens the applicability of the direct method of variations. Finally, an illustrative example highlights how the developed theoretical framework can support a posteriori error analysis. Notably, the first author has implemented a variational algorithm based on these results and its generalizations to solve a specific problem in fluid dynamics. This implementation allows for the generation of highly accurate approximations alongside rigorous, provably tight error bounds, a capability unique to this approach. Crucially, the algorithm achieves these results without requiring the a priori construction of special test functions or the derivation of partial or integral operator estimates, which are typically necessary prerequisites in similar methodologies. Finally, the paper concludes with a discussion on generalizations and potential future applications of these techniques. A key motivation for this work is the demonstration that the direct method of variations can serve as a highly effective alternative to the perturbation method, which is widely used in stability analysis across mathematics and physics. This equivalence is particularly significant for physics applications, as it enables the direct derivation of both stability and a posteriori results from the same set of computations. Specifically, in fluid dynamics, this means that stability estimates can be obtained using the identical algorithms employed to calculate the vorticity and Reynolds stress tensors. This study demonstrates that the hamiltonicity of such graphs $G$ can be characterized via the positive semidefinite matrix associated with $G$. Furthermore, assuming the conjecture by Ollinger regarding the independence count of bipartite graphs, the pancyclicity of $G$ would likewise be derived from this same matrix. Additionally, these findings are applied to construct a family of bipartite graphs that are both pancyclic and Hamiltonian. Finally, the methodology employed to prove the Hamiltonicity of $G$ is utilized to establish a new, concise proof of a theorem by Chudnovsky, Kim, Kim, and Kim, which characterizes the pancyclicity of graphs based on their chromatic number and clique number. The argument used to demonstrate the pancyclicity of $G$ also characterizes the Hamiltonicity and pancyclicity of graphs with chromatic number $r$ and clique cover number of $r-1$. The latter result is achieved through an application of the recently introduced rank function of a graph. This paper examines the directed flow of forward and backward luminosity hadrons, specifically pions, protons, and kaons, as well as muons, generated in soft hadronic showers resulting from high-multiplicity Au+Au and isobar collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\textrm{NN}}}=$ 200 GeV. The muon transverse momentum spectrum in these collisions is modeled using a hadronization model coupled with a muon tagging efficiency derived from experimental data. This muon sample selection is subsequently analyzed with hydrodynamic models to explore potential QGP signatures within the directed flow of p and $\K^-$ in the 1–2 GeV/$c$ range. The study reveals that pion directed flow exhibits a distinct signal in Au+Au and isobar collisions, whereas the signal for kaons shows no significant difference between them. Furthermore, the directed flow of muons demonstrates a clear signal in isobar collisions, with a $4.1\sigma$ significance. These findings suggest that while hydrodynamic models may not adequately describe the directed flow of p and $\K^-$, they remain viable for interpreting the observed directed flow of muons. This implies that the directed flow of forward luminosity hadrons may originate from mechanisms linked to initial geometry and/or early-time dynamics, rather than those associated with particle production. Consequently, the directed flow of muons serves as a valuable probe for investigating the characteristics of the QCD phase diagram. These results highlight the value of isobar collision experiments in enhancing our understanding of QCD matter. The analysis was conducted using PHENIX data from Au+Au and (Nb$^{95+}$W$^{183}$)+ (Nb$^{93+}$W$^{183}$) collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\textrm{NN}}}=$ 200 GeV. The data collection utilized two distinct methods: one involving the tagging of muons with charged pions in the same event, and another based on the reconstruction of muon pairs. The former approach yielded a larger dataset, while the latter, though yielding a smaller sample, offered superior muon momentum resolution. The study utilized both datasets to analyze the directed flow of p and $\K^-$, as well as muons. Additionally, the analysis incorporated measurements of directed flow for protons and Kaons, alongside prior PHENIX results on charged pions, to ensure a comprehensive understanding of directed flow across various charged particles. This paper introduces a new adaptive spectral Koopman operator framework designed for nonlinear state estimation in control systems with complex dynamics. Traditionally, spectral approaches to the Koopman operator have struggled with data richness, particularly when exogenous noise is present. Our method addresses these limitations by utilizing sparse grid training sets that combine polynomial chaos expansions with finite element method spatial discretizations. This strategy effectively manages the "curse of dimensionality" inherent in nonlinear systems. Additionally, the approach incorporates adaptive polynomial degree selection and hyperparameter learning to enhance data efficiency and improve performance across diverse control problems. We validate the efficacy of this framework through two case studies derived from real-world applications: nonlinear model predictive control for an unmanned aerial vehicle and optimal feedback control for an insulin-glucose homeostasis system. In both scenarios, the proposed framework demonstrates superior performance compared to existing literature. Furthermore, we establish a link between our work and dynamic mode decomposition, showing that the method can be implemented via the projection of sparse grid finite element basis functions onto Fourier basis functions. This approach minimizes the need for normalization operations during iterative solutions and steers clear of minor bound state solutions when analyzing strong-field continuous states. Furthermore, we derive a simple analytical formula for the effective principal quantum number of outer bound states in DC fields, facilitating the swift estimation of accurate eigenvalues. This technique is particularly valuable for systematically constructing bound state configurations required as initial guesses in DC-field photoionization simulations utilizing the outer-in method. Finally, we propose a novel and efficient DC-scale transformation to recover standard spatial scales for presenting DC photoionization rates and scattering phase shifts. This study measures the top-quark pair production cross-section in proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}=5.02$ TeV using the ATLAS detector at the LHC. The analysis relies on events featuring two leptons (ee, e$\mu$, or $\mu\mu$) and significant jet activity within the central region. Data were recorded in 2018, following an energy upgrade to 13 TeV, with an integrated luminosity of 13.9 fb$^{-1}$. The total cross-section is determined to be $\sigma_{\mathrm{t\bar{t}}}=382.2\pm1.5\mathrm{(stat)}\pm1.8\mathrm{(syst)}$ pb, which aligns with both the standard model prediction and a recent calculation incorporating next-to-next-to-leading order QCD corrections and the perturbative resummation of soft-gluon radiation effects. Although statistical models of localized systems typically predict that the fraction of localized states approaches zero as disorder decreases, it is conceivable that specific initial conditions yield trajectories remaining close to an initial localized configuration. This paper investigates the validity of such states in a ring of Josephson circuits connected to a central reservoir, demonstrating the existence of initial conditions capable of sustaining localized steady states even at low disorder levels. We contend that these states arise from a competition between the coupled system and the reservoir, leading to a bifurcation. This phenomenon is elucidated through a two-state analysis and numerical simulations of various rings, supported by a statistical state analysis of different initial conditions. Furthermore, we show that these states can be induced by preparing initial conditions within a metastable basin of attraction, characterized by an average lifetime that increases with system size. Finally, we explore potential applications of this phenomenon. This study extends our prior research published in *Chaos* (Vol. 29, 087001, 2019). Urban environments are renowned for their diverse social interactions, income exchanges, and cultural exchanges. However, the global pandemic triggered strict lockdowns that drastically curtailed these interactions, thereby intensifying social and economic polarization. The current surge in income inequality is a pressing concern that demands immediate attention. This study examines the pandemic's impact on income diversity within urban encounters, specifically analyzing how behavioral shifts during the pandemic modified interaction patterns. Our findings indicate that the diversity of interactions experienced by individuals across different income levels rose by 17% post-pandemic, while diversity in interactions for every income group except the lowest rose by 26%. Consequently, encounter heterogeneity increased by 20% for all income groups except the lowest, and interaction reciprocity improved by 10% for every group apart from the lowest. These results suggest that the pandemic, through modifications to behavioral patterns, has worsened income diversity in urban interactions, with this effect being most pronounced in the post-pandemic period. Furthermore, we observed that the post-pandemic period saw greater income diversity in interactions for lower and middle-income groups, while higher-income individuals maintained higher diversity in their interactions. These observations highlight the need for targeted policies aimed at reducing income polarization in urban encounters, particularly during the post-pandemic phase. We conclude that future research should explore additional metrics of income diversity in urban interactions, such as those related to interaction frequency, duration, and geographic distribution. Additionally, we recommend that policymakers consider implementing measures to promote income diversity in urban encounters, such as increasing access to education and training opportunities for low-income individuals, fostering entrepreneurship and small business development, and promoting social safety nets and support systems for vulnerable populations. Finally, we suggest that researchers continue to investigate the relationship between income diversity and urban encounters, examining how income diversity affects interaction patterns, how interactions influence income distribution, and how urban interactions can be leveraged to promote economic growth and social cohesion. By addressing these issues, we can work towards creating more equitable and sustainable urban environments for all residents. Numerical simulations employing nonlinear field splitting facilitators effectively generate realistic flow patterns in porous media with channelized heterogeneities, thereby revealing distinct flow paths between immiscible fluid pairs. Within two-phase flow simulations utilizing these facilitators, a capillary barrier effect typically forms at the interface between high and low permeability regions, facilitating the injection of fluids into favorable zones. This study examines the impact of a facilitator of equivalent viscosity across these zones on the flow patterns achieved at specific times, considering various facilitator viscosities. Simulations were conducted using two distinct facilitator viscosities: one matching the mobile phase and another being ten times higher. By directly comparing the two scenarios, we identify specific times during the simulation where flow patterns diverge significantly due to the variation in facilitator viscosity. These results indicate that the facilitator viscosity exerted during the initial stages of the simulation is the most critical factor in achieving an optimized flood sweep. Consequently, utilizing a facilitator with a higher viscosity than the mobile phase during the early simulation stages is recommended to achieve the desired flow patterns during the later stages. This insight is derived from a single simulation, and further research is necessary to validate these findings using a broader range of facilitator viscosities. Additionally, the influence of the breakthrough time of the injected fluid into favorable regions warrants further investigation. Ultimately, the findings of this study could inform the selection of facilitator viscosities in future applications. Finally, the potential for applying facilitators of higher viscosity than the mobile phase during later simulation stages remains an area warranting further research. Utilizing a metat surface, we propose an all-optical method to produce single-handed chiral resonator modes. This approach leverages the off-resonant coupling between a spin-polarized dipole source and a spherical dielectric resonance, with the resulting mode's chirality governed by the source's spin chirality. This fully dielectric system offers straightforward fabrication and design, making it highly suitable for integrating with existing photonic circuits. Furthermore, this technique can be employed to engineer the handiness of photonic quantum emitters, potentially enabling the study of topological quantum phenomena. Our proposed solution presents a promising pathway for developing efficient, tunable chiral photonic devices. Additionally, we investigate the possibility of achieving higher-order order-parameter symmetry breaking within the system. Finally, we discuss the potential for detecting and analyzing the order-parameter field using a single photodetector. These capabilities could facilitate the study of non-equilibrium and topological effects in future quantum and photonic technologies. Our work paves the way for achieving highly efficient resonator excitation, thereby advancing the pursuit of strong light-matter interaction. Specifically, this could enable the direct detection of chiral photons and channel chiral excitations into quantum matter. Our findings may also contribute to achieving the fundamental limit of light-matter interaction strength. Moreover, we address several promising avenues for future research in this field. Finally, all simulations were conducted using our open-source platform, CHORUS. It also includes a topological module to explore topological quantum effects within photonic quantum circuits. The platform is accessible at: https://github.com/Chorus-Group/CHORUS. Furthermore, we have released an interactive demonstration of our work at: https://chorus-group.github.io/TOPUS/demo/. This allows for the direct observation of the connection between the helicity of the single photonic qubit and the topology of the photonic band structure. These scenarios are relevant for investigating the formation of artificial wormholes and for space-time manipulation aimed at space travel. These theoretical findings are directly compared against experimental data regarding Cu or Ag nanoparticles coupled with CuS or MoS$_2$. Our results indicate that a quantum treatment of electronic structure, even in simple systems, is essential for accurately describing electromagnetic effects in QT-ERS. Furthermore, we observe a significant correlation between the HOMO-LUMO gap and LUMO energy. These insights provide a foundation for future experiments aiming to optimize QT-ERS signals. Notably, systems exhibiting low-energy LUMOs or high-energy HOMOs—characterized by small HOMO-LUMO gaps—yield substantially larger signals. This demonstrates the critical role of electronic structure in QT-ERS, suggesting that materials such as Cu$_2$S, which are promising for SPR-ERS, should also be high-priority candidates for QT-ERS applications. Additionally, we highlight a qualitative distinction between SR and QT SPR resonance, alongside quantitative estimates of electron transfer between semiconductor-nanoparticle interfaces under SR excitation.
