We introduce a nearly linear-time algorithm to compute vertex dividers for $N$-vertex graphs with treewidth $W$ under a constrained node-decomposition. Although such near-linear divisor algorithms are established for various decomposition types, including $O(W)$-shallowstree-trees and $O(W)$-bitangent forests, the algorithmic gap for vertex dividers remains in the context of treewidth. Our approach bridges this gap, achieving a running time of $O((N + W)\log N)$ operations using $O(N + W)$ words of memory. This method leverages the properties of a treewidth-$O(W)$ bitangent forest inherent to the pre-provided decomposition. While the resulting vertex dividers differ slightly in structure from those derived from the input decomposition, they retain the same divisor size and cost parameters. Consequently, our technique can facilitate nearly linear-time algorithms for specific vertex-divisor applications, such as approximating the minimum vertex separator for clustering graphs with treewidth $O(W)$ in linear time. Furthermore, our approach establishes a new equivalence between treewidth and bitangent forests: given any $O(W)$-bitangent-forest-decomposition for an $N$-vertex graph, we can construct a treewidth-$O(W)$ decomposition in $O((N + W)\log N)$ time using $O(N + W)$ work space. This contrasts with the $O(N)$ time and space required by standard algorithms that convert a treewidth decomposition into a bitangent decomposition. Although the resulting bitangent decomposition is not necessarily optimal, it maintains a treewidth of $O(W)$. The remaining $O(\log W)$ gap between these two parameters is noted to be challenging. Additionally, we outline how to adapt our method to other forms of treewidth decomposition, such as shallowstree-decomposition and bitangent-forest-decomposition, provided the treewidth and depth bounds are $O(W)$ and $O(D)$ respectively. In these scenarios, our method yields a nearly linear-time algorithm to transform the given decomposition into one with the corresponding target form. While these target decompositions may lack certain desirable traits of the input versions—such as treewidth or depth—these attributes can be recovered via standard algorithms at the expense of an additional $O(\log W)$ or $O(\log D)$ factor in the running time. Grouping algorithms are increasingly being applied to combine information from multiple networks, a trend driven by the growing availability of data across various levels and formats. This process involves clustering nodes based on their connections within one or more networks. However, when dealing with more than one network, a critical question emerges: how should differences in node degrees and edge weights influence the grouping outcomes? The standard approach, maximum weighted mutual information, treats a "step" to a neighbor as proportional to the edge weight. We argue that for specific applications, this model must be adapted to account for heterogeneity in the available networks. Specifically, when at least one network is inferred rather than directly observed, or when nodes in the inferred network possess lower entropy than in the measured network, modifications are necessary. If group membership is inferred for a network, the choice of using absolute or relative weights becomes paramount. We outline the criteria necessary for selecting the most appropriate model for a given application and provide heuristics to guide users in making informed decisions. Finally, we demonstrate how to apply these considerations to real-world data and develop a Python package to facilitate such analyses. This package is designed to be extensible and can serve as a foundation for implementing custom grouping methods. By providing the means to examine how a specific algorithm responds to changes in input weights, it offers valuable insights for both practitioners and researchers. We demonstrate its utility through a case study of how mutual information can be leveraged to integrate both measured and inferred networks. Additionally, we include a collection of custom weighting schemes that can be easily extended to support both weighted and weighted and directed grouping analyses. Finally, we provide a tutorial on utilizing the package for custom weighting. Overall, we contend that understanding the implications of weighting schemes is essential for researchers and practitioners to ensure that their grouping analyses are appropriate for their specific applications. Furthermore, we provide resources, including exercises and code, to support teaching these concepts. All materials are available at: https://github.com/rossi-lab/NetworkIntegrationExamples/tree/master/TeachingMaterials. Our goal is to foster a community where weighting choices are openly discussed, ensuring that both the advantages and limitations of these decisions are transparent. We believe this transparency is vital for advancing the field of network integration. We acknowledge that various applications may require different approaches to weighting, and we invite the community to discuss how to address the questions we have raised. We welcome contributions from both practitioners and researchers to help establish clear guidelines for when and how to apply weighting in network integration. We look forward to your input. Thank you. Ross

This paper introduces a novel approach to estimate and certify errors in physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) by leveraging recent advances in machine learning robustness. Specifically, we develop a method to quantify prediction errors at test points where the underlying forward problem has not been solved, even though these points violate the governing differential equation. By utilizing certified robustness techniques, we derive an upper bound for the maximum error in such test points, thereby providing a guaranteed error bound. We demonstrate the effectiveness and practical utility of this method on the advective heat equation and the shallow water equations. Our results show that this technique effectively identifies incorrect PINN predictions in regions of the input space where the differential equation is not satisfied, even under significant noise. This capability is essential for certified machine learning, ensuring that model outputs are reliable and trustworthy. Furthermore, this method is broadly applicable to any forward problem, including those addressed by other PINN variants such as those solving hyperbolic conservation laws or employing operator learning. Ultimately, this contributes to the creation of robust, reliable, and safe machine learning solutions for real-world applications. To our knowledge, this represents the first application of machine learning robustness to the certified mistake analysis of PINNs. Additionally, we have made our code public to facilitate further research and replication. Finally, this work serves as a foundation for our future efforts in creating robust, reliable, and safe machine learning frameworks for practical applications. Air pollution serves as a major risk factor for numerous diseases, including cancer, cardiovascular, and respiratory conditions. While epidemiological studies have established the links between air and disease, they often lack precise data on individual air pollutant exposure. Consequently, researchers have developed models to estimate exposure based on environmental monitoring and various analytical methods. This paper evaluates and compares different approaches for modeling air pollution exposure within an epidemiological context. It outlines the benefits of integrating geostatistics and machine learning in model development, alongside appropriate validation strategies. The discussion emphasizes geostatistics' utility in interpolating spatially correlated data and machine learning's capacity to handle complex data structures and enable automated model selection. Finally, several illustrative examples demonstrate the application of these modeling techniques to asthma and leukemia. Keywords: air pollution, exposure assessment, epidemiology, geostatistics, machine learning, spatial modeling.

Linear contextual bandits are a widely adopted framework for sequential decision-making under uncertainty, yet they often suffer from suboptimal sample efficiency when action spaces are vast. This issue is particularly critical when utilizing bandit methods for downstream inference, as inefficient exploration can result in subpar models. This work introduces and analyzes novel regret bounds for linear bandits with extensive action spaces, demonstrating that the number of actions significantly influences regret. We propose two algorithms, $\alpha$-LinUCB and $\alpha$-LinTS, which expand popular linear bandits by allowing regret to depend on the log of the action space size. These algorithms maintain the simplicity and interpretability of their predecessors while learning action representations that are more concise by an order of magnitude. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between regret performance and the quality of inferred representations for various LinUCB variants. Our findings indicate that current regret bounds fail to guarantee the optimality of these representations. We also present a new regret bound for LinUCB that is independent of the action space size, thereby ensuring the optimality of its learned representations. Finally, we validate our theoretical contributions on both synthetic and real-world datasets. From an applied perspective, $\alpha$-LinUCB and $\alpha$-LinTS outperform existing methods by up to 1000% in terms of reward. From a theoretical standpoint, we establish that achieving regret independent of the action space is impossible for CUCB and LinTS, and we provide the first regret analysis for Thompson Sampling in this setting. Collectively, these results underscore the vital role of theoretical analysis in guiding the application of bandit algorithms. Although the orbital Hall effect in time-reversal symmetric systems was recently observed in topological insulators, it remains elusive in band-insulating graphene due to its unique geometry, where the Berry curvature vanishes everywhere. By incorporating substrate-induced gaplessness and exploring a potential pathway to fully gap the system, we demonstrate that the orbital Hall effect persists. Specifically, we show that the orbital Hall effect in gapless graphene cannot be fully understood as a bulk phenomenon characterized by accumulated valley Chern numbers in Berry curvature space. Instead, it is more accurately described as an alternative to the valley Hall effect, where valley Chern numbers play a pivotal role in defining the orbital Hall conductivity. Furthermore, we illustrate that this orbital Hall effect in graphene can be experimentally detected through spin-valley coupling. This work establishes a promising direction for investigating the orbital Hall effect within unique geometries. Additionally, our findings regarding gapless graphene are directly applicable to Kagome and other geometries where the sum of valley Chern numbers is non-zero. The research code is accessible at https://github.com/zhaozhongwei1990/Graphene-CHHE.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are machine learning models specifically engineered for processing and analyzing graph-based data. Their efficacy in real-world graph datasets often hinges on how effectively they integrate structural information with node attributes; however, their performance can be significantly compromised by data contamination. This issue arises when a portion of graph nodes, labeled or unlabeled, are corrupted during training. To investigate this problem systematically, we introduce RL-GNN, a novel framework utilizing reinforcement learning to contaminate graph data within a GNN training context. Our approach employs a custom reward function designed to maximize the discrepancy between GNN predictions on test and train sets while simultaneously ensuring the contamination remains undetectable. Experimental results demonstrate that RL-GNN successfully introduces targeted contamination in a manner that is difficult to identify, thereby causing substantial performance degradation in downstream tasks. Furthermore, we find that standard graph augmentation techniques offer limited protection against our proposed contamination strategy, as these methods tend to fail when the contamination is severe. Finally, we conclude that while transfer learning can provide robustness, it remains vulnerable to the systematic application of RL-GNN. Overall, our findings suggest that current defenses are insufficient against this targeted data contamination approach. By demonstrating the feasibility of our method, we aim to raise awareness of the risks associated with GNN training on contaminated graphs and encourage the research community to develop more robust defenses. Our code is available at: https://github.com/ashishkumar2001/RL-GNN.

Catalogue matching serves as a critical method for assigning physical properties to astronomical sources, such as distances and proper motions. This study investigates the combination of multiple information sources to enhance catalogue matching efficiency. We developed and applied a catalogue matching algorithm that integrates various observational data, specifically photometric information and astrometry. Our findings indicate that incorporating photometric data significantly improves the completeness of common source identification. Additionally, we examined the impact of merging observations from different instruments on matching performance and demonstrated that catalogues can be effectively matched even when no astrometric data is available. These results have direct implications for future large-scale surveys, including Euclid, which will generate multi-instrument photometric catalogues for over 100 million sources. Through multi-colour photometry, our approach achieves a completeness of approximately 60% for common source identification among realistic catalogues of 10 million objects, even in the absence of astrometric data. This level of completeness is essential for accurately measuring cross-correlation counts and ensuring the homogeneity of photometric source lists. For distance-based matching using astrometric data, completeness is expected to exceed 80%, thereby facilitating the construction of reliable sample cross-matches. Ultimately, this work illustrates that catalogue matching can be substantially optimized by jointly utilizing all available observational information. The described methods are fully automated and have been implemented in the public software library PMML, which is designed for processing photometric and astrometric source catalogues. The code is accessible at https://github.com/astrometry净/PMML. Ontologies serve as formal, explicit specifications of categories within a particular domain and the relationships between these categories. Current ontology visualizations often fail to clearly display non-hierarchical associations, which are crucial for understanding large ontologies. We present OntoPlot, a new visualization that enables the inspection of these important associations. OntoPlot builds on the concept of association graphs, where nodes represent concepts and edges signify relationships. This allows users to identify associations linked to a specific concept by simply selecting its node. Standard vision pipelines for autonomous robot navigation typically involve a sequential workflow: a deep network generates predictions from sensor data, which are subsequently mapped to control signals via an optimization process. We introduce a novel method to enhance this pipeline by utilizing an active predictor to generate sensor inputs based on the current output. This approach incorporates a model of the environment's posterior states and employs a deep generative network to create sensor readings that maximize the probable posterior likelihood. This work demonstrates the benefits of active prediction through a simulated robot navigation scenario. In this setup, the active predictor optimizes for sensor inputs—specifically, the selected environment state—for which the predictor exhibits the highest confidence. Consequently, the interaction between the active predictor and the primary predictor results in the robot navigating more efficiently by focusing on the most significant states. Furthermore, we establish a correspondence between this mechanism and model-based reinforcement learning techniques, suggesting that our method could offer a new perspective for understanding and enhancing existing autonomous robot navigation systems. We validate the efficacy of this framework using both simulated and real-world 2D navigation scenarios. Representational meta-learning aims to acquire a robust, task-agnostic representation from multi-task data that facilitates efficient adaptation to novel tasks with limited examples. While numerous methods claim success in labeled settings, few have been rigorously evaluated on their ability to generalize to 1-example scenarios across diverse domains. This paper presents Demonstrable Meta-Learning (Demo), which offers a rigorous, representation-agnostic framework for systematically evaluating such generalization. We apply Demo to widely used linear meta-learning techniques and establish a new state-of-the-art systematic evaluation framework for this class of methods using our Lithograph benchmark, which consists of 100 image classes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our Gated MAML approach achieves the first system-level evaluation beyond linear methods on the more challenging YACCB benchmark, comprising 200 classes. Finally, extensive empirical evaluations reveal that these methods fail to meet the demanding criteria of learning from a single example on open-domain image classes, prompting us to propose Open-domain 1-Set (ODS1) as a new 1-example benchmark. Extremely limited 1-example learning necessitates unsupervised adaptation, leading us to develop ODS1-unsupervised, the first systematic benchmark for unsupervised meta-learning. Comprehensive evaluations across multiple benchmarks show that our gate-unrolled approaches outperform all prior state-of-the-art methods by up to 150% in accuracy. Additionally, we introduce a practical codebase for both implementation and evaluation. Deep learning models for supervised tasks typically necessitate extensive labeled datasets. In medical imaging, acquiring large collections of labeled scans is often prohibitively expensive and time-consuming. This study investigates the feasibility of reducing the training data requirement for binary segmentation of lung nodules in CT scans by employing image augmentations. Using a standard binary segmentation dataset of lung CTs, we trained and tested a U-Net convolutional neural network. Our results demonstrate that image augmentations can significantly lower the number of images required to train accurate segmentation networks. Specifically, we utilized a dataset of 200 labeled lung nodules from 50 binary lung CT scans. To prevent overfitting, we employed K-fold cross-validation. To evaluate the impact of image augmentations, we performed training with data replicated through geometric transformations, random scaling, random rotations, and random horizontal flips. We tested various replication factors ranging from 1 to 10 times the original data volume. We assessed network performance using the Dice coefficient for segmentation accuracy and mean absolute error for lesion size prediction. The findings indicate that network performance improved with augmented data up to a 10-fold increase, after which performance plateaued. Consequently, we utilized a 10-fold increase in data for subsequent analysis. Furthermore, we compared the effect of these augmentations on U-Net architecture selection against using only a quarter of the original data. Finally, we examined the influence of different augmentation types and determined that the selected architecture combination yielded the best segmentation results. Ultimately, we conclude that image augmentations substantially reduce the number of images needed for training, thereby lowering the cost and time required for data labeling. This approach could significantly impact medical image analysis, particularly for applications like lung nodule segmentation where data acquisition is challenging. This paper introduces MMLSpark, a MlFlow-enabled scalable Spark extension designed for deep learning applications. Built on the popular Spark platform, MMLSpark offers the extensive ecosystem of Spark and PySpark, enabling easy integration with major deep learning frameworks such as TensorFlow, Dask-TF, and TuriCreate. To address common deep learning challenges, MMLSpark provides key building blocks for processing images, tabular data, and text, including distributed data access, augmentation, normalization, one-hot encoding, embedding, feature engineering, feature selection, hyperparameter tuning, model ensembles, and pipeline management. Furthermore, it supports advanced techniques for classification, clustering, regression, anomaly detection, and recommendation engines. As deep learning applications grow in complexity, MMLSpark allows for horizontal scaling across clusters and organizations. Additionally, this paper explores related work, execution and optimization, deep learning patterns, deep learning APIs, and migration guides to assist practitioners in adopting MMLSpark. Voice translation involves converting speech from one language into another without translating the accompanying text. This work introduces the first zero-shot voice translation system, capable of translating between any two languages even in their absence. Our method leverages pre-trained, non-speech audio models to generate on-shot voice conversion and copy commands, which are used to modify base multilingual audio to satisfy voice and language-specific requirements. We evaluated our approach across three English-to-foreign language tasks, including voice conversion, cross-lingual text-to-speech, and voice translation. The results demonstrate that our method achieves competitive performance in voice conversion and voice translation tasks, matches state-of-the-art performance in cross-lingual text-to-speech, and successfully addresses an entirely new voice translation problem. Additionally, to ensure the generated audio remains suitable for speech recognition, we incorporated an on-site on-average phoneme distribution loss. Accurate localization and identification of vertebrae are critical for numerous diagnostic and therapeutic applications, including vertebral body lesion detection, surgical planning, and radiation therapy treatment. However, this process is difficult due to the high density of vertebrae within the spine and the presence of degenerative conditions. To address these challenges, we introduce a cost function that combines a regularization term, designed to enforce Grad-Shafranov equations on tubular structures, with a level-set-based data term. This formulation is adaptable to various segmentation and identification tasks. We demonstrate that optimizing this function is equivalent to solving a combinatorial problem that integrates vertebral shape constraints with vertebra labeling. Furthermore, we provide a novel branch-and-cut algorithm to solve this problem and a corresponding continuous algorithm for joint shape reconstruction and identification. When applied to CT scans, our approach achieves a mean localization error of 1.1 vertebrae and an identification error of 1.8 vertebrae, surpassing state-of-the-art methods. In semi-automated radiation therapy planning, our method reduces the mean localization error to 2.1 vertebrae compared to 3.7 vertebrae achieved by leading automated techniques. Additionally, we validate the capability of this approach to accurately identify vertebrae in CT images affected by severe degenerative conditions, such as spondylolisthesis. To our knowledge, our technique represents the first to successfully localize and identify vertebrae in such complex spinal cases. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/IMAGINeuralNetworks/VertebraLocalizationAndIdentification. The Non-Riemannian (NR) formulation of gravity offers a framework grounded in a metric defined on an orthogonal decomposition of tangent spaces, allowing for a more unified and geometric comprehension of physical phenomena. This approach eliminates the necessity for extra degrees of freedom found in the Riemannian case. Recently, a comprehensive set of NR gravitational actions has been established, linked via specific field redefinitions. In this work, we employ the double field theory (DFT) framework to derive these NR actions, leveraging DFT's inherent global $O(D,D)$ symmetry. We demonstrate that incorporating a specific DFT term yields a metric formulation, which can then be Fierz-expanded to produce nonlinear sigma-model-like actions. Furthermore, we establish that all derived DFT actions remain equivalent under a restricted symmetry encompassing generalized Scherk-Schwarz projections and T-duality. Finally, we identify the appropriate T-duality orbits within the DFT formulation that correspond to various NR gravitational formulations in the metric approach. These methods enable the systematic generation of gravitational theories, facilitating a deeper investigation into the physical properties of potential candidates for a quantum theory of gravity. Additionally, these theories may assist in understanding the nonperturbative aspects of string theory. A key advantage of the NR formulation is its capacity to describe certain non-standard geometries, such as those found in the near-horizon regions of black holes, as a product of two distinct geometries. This capability is particularly relevant for addressing the information paradox. Finally, we explore the potential of these theories as effective descriptions for quantum gravity. Specifically, the nonlinear sigma-model formulation, characterized by a low-energy spectrum, is a natural candidate for this role. This insight could be valuable in analyzing the nonperturbative structure of string theory and in exploring distinct solutions to the Einstein equations. To illustrate this, we examine the cosmological applications of the Fierz double copy. In this context, we show that the theory predicts a big-crunch scenario, whereas standard Riemannian gravity would result in a big-rip. These findings underscore the significance of nonlinear sigma-model formulations within the broader context of NR gravity formulations in DFT. Ultimately, these results provide a pathway to identify promising candidates for quantum gravitational theories. Finally, the NR formulation of gravity represents a significant step toward a unified description involving both perturbative and nonperturbative string theory components. This advancement is essential for a holistic understanding of spacetime and for investigating the various aspects of the universe. The rise of high-bandwidth applications has created a channel load-awareness problem, particularly within indoor IEEE 802.11 networks, where excessive client associations with access points (APs) cause significant performance degradation. This issue is compounded by extenders, which are designed to improve performance but often inadvertently worsen it. A key solution involves selecting appropriate APs and extender modes based on channel load to mitigate these effects. While the IEEE 802.11k and 11v amendments offer Channel Load (CHL) data for this purpose, the 11w amendment provides Accounting, Billing, and Restriction (ABR) accounting that tracks client association and disassociation events. This paper introduces a protocol enabling an AP to query neighboring APs for CHL information regarding a disassociating client. Using the gathered data, the AP can evaluate whether another network offers a superior match by considering both the target AP's current load and the client's preferred AP. This approach ensures that no network is overloaded by the client's arrival while simultaneously addressing the performance issues linked to extender deployment. The study also includes a detailed analysis of 802.11k/v/w/n/ac/be frames and demonstrates the protocol's effectiveness through simulations. Results indicate that the proposed method reduces client disassociation rates by 20% to 40% compared to the baseline, alongside a notable improvement in overall network performance. Furthermore, the protocol introduces only a minor computational and memory overhead for the AP, with negligible overhead for clients and a slight increase in the beaconing process. Finally, the research concludes with an analysis of the challenges involved in implementing this protocol in production environments. Finally, the paper presents an Android-based application for monitoring CHL information. This app allows users to view all nearby APs and their load status, displays available extendor modes, and recommends the optimal network choice. Users can view real-time load updates every 10 seconds, with an option to refresh the data manually. Additionally, the app recommends the best extendor mode based on the user's current location and the available options. This tool is particularly beneficial for users who are not technical experts, empowering them to make informed decisions regarding network selection and extender configuration. By utilizing this application, users can significantly enhance their wireless experience. The paper also details the underlying mechanism of the app and the efforts made to optimize its performance.
